20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3443
WEDNESDAY, 20 MAY 2015
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m.
Prayers.
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus
1. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement in his Budget speech last year, “we are in surplus”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, because the Treasury forecasts then
showed a small surplus for 2014-15.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why has he persisted in making that promise or that undertaking to
New Zealanders, including after the election, when he knew he could not keep it?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not believe that that statement is at all accurate.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why does he or other Ministers in his Government persist in making
excuses about milk prices and inflation when he knows that dairy prices began falling
last February and inflation has been stagnant since 2013?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member may have such a lack of  grasp of economics that
he does not realise the impact that inflation has on the Government’s books. We know
that Grant Robertson has got his training wheels on, so he does not know what $15
billion worth of less expenditure means. By the way, during the entire election
campaign, Labour got up and said that the Government should take no credit for higher
dairy prices, because that is just a function of something else. But, apparently, with
the—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have heard enough.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Now that he is set to be the first Prime Minister since Robert
Muldoon to deliver seven straight deficits, why should the public believe him when the
Government promises a surplus next year?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What the New Zealand public have done , year after year after
year, is judge this Government on its economic performance. They have see n the mess
we inherited from Labour when it came to ACC, the massive build -up in expenditure,
the failure to have a competitive tax  system, and the fact that it left the books in such a
shocking state, and they have actually seen us get that down, get debt down, and get
growth up. That is why business confidence is high. That is why New Zealanders in
droves have voted for National. Ma ybe the member needs to look in the mirror and ask
himself why his messages are not getting through. Here is an idea: he does not have any
messages. He has not—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What reports has the Prime Ministe r received on getting back to
surplus based on the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update  forecasts before the
election last year?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I have seen one report from last year’s election campaign on
the 2014 -15 surplus: “Oh, lo ok, absolutely stand by the numbers, calculated and
checked on the same basis as the Government’s own numbers and absolutely verified,
all banked, all paid for. We are still running a surplus every year. It is absolutely
fantastic and people can have every confidence in it.” That was David Cunliffe claiming
that Labour was running a surplus, even from Opposition.
3444 Oral Questions  20 May 2015

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: What other promises for Budget 2015 are now also under threat, and
will the Budget show we are on track for the 150 ,000 extra jobs by 2016 and a $7,000
average wage rise by 2017, as promised in his open letter after last year’s election?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member will have to wait —only one more sleep,
actually—until the Budget tomorrow. I am sure he  will be able to do that. What he will
see tomorrow in the Budget, though, are  good growth numbers . He will see surpluses
out in the years in front. He will see debt levels that are the envy of the Western World.
That is why I can be absolutely sure that when New Zealanders look at this Government
and its economic leadership they do not have buyers’ remorse; they are very happy that
they dispatched Labour to Opposition for 3 more long years.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: How much can the fiscal numbers move around between Budget
forecasts and the Government’s annual accounts being published the following year?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: According to that economic powerhouse Grant Robertson, not
at all. But, actually, history shows that fiscal forecast s and out-turns move around quite
substantially. For example, in Budget 2008 the then finance Minister was forecasting a
$1.3 billion operating balance before gains and losses surplus in 2008 -09. As it actually
turned out, he left the Government’s books in  deficit by $3.9 billion that year. I say just
this one thing: why in this country do we have the Public Finance Act? I know —
because Labour rorted the books so much that they could no longer be trusted. That is
why.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: In light of that answer, and returning to reality, what happened to his
promise to act on child poverty and make it the centrepiece of his third term?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: One more sleep.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Is not the truth of it that this  is a Government with a surplus of
empty promises and a deficit of ideas, a Government that took credit for a short patch of
economic golden days on the back on high dairy prices and the Canterbury rebuild but
has no plan now that the storm clouds are gath ering? Is that not the truth of this
Government?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Here is the truth of this Government. Unlike the countries that
we actually compare ourselves with, we have got on top of deficits despite the
Christchurch earthquakes. We have got employment rates that are rising. Of the OECD
countries, of which there a re 36, only four have higher levels of employment than us,
and 31 have lower levels of employment. We have low inflation and we have strong job
creation. We have low levels of public sector debt  and we have high levels of consumer
confidence. The record ac tually speaks for itself. It happens to be a record I am very
proud of.
Child Poverty—Government Initiatives to Address
2. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand
by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How can he be “proud of the Government’s record in tackling child
poverty” when he said this week that it is probably numerically correct that the number
of children in poverty has grown under his watch?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As we know with this, there are many, many measures, but
what I can be absolutely sure of is that  there are 42 ,000 fewer children, for instance,
living in benefit-based households over the last 3 years. I can be sure that we have done
a great deal for those children who live with hardship, including free GP visits and
prescriptions, including the work we have done  with charitable organisations that , for
instance, provide breakfast in schools, including the work we have done with social
workers, including the work we have done with Children’s T eams, and including the
20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3445
work we have done on insulating homes. During the worst of all times, this Government
actually maintained benefits and entitlements for New Zealanders. There were plenty of
people who wanted to slash them; this Government supported them.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: How many, if any, of the 260,000 chi ldren currently in poverty will
no longer be in poverty as a result of the Budget tomorrow?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not have an exact answer for that, and even if I did have, I
would not give it to the member a day before the Budget. What I can say, though, is that
the fastest way out of poverty is through work, and this Government is doing two things
in that regard. One is it is underpinning, with its policies, strong economic growth and
strong job creation. We know this because there are 4 2,000 fewer children living in
benefit-based households than there were 3 years ago. The second thing that this
Government is doing is invoking the investment approach when it comes  to people who
are on benefits —making sure that they have got skills, makin g sure that they have got
training, and making sure that they have access to the opportunity to look after
themselves. Again, I am actually very proud of what this Government is doing to help
people to help themselves.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why did the Prime Minister abandon the thousands of children who
turn up to school hungry every day by voting against my bill to feed them lunch at
school, and even stood in this House and denied that those children existed?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, I reject the last part of the member’s question. I think
she overexaggerated those numbers, and I think we demonstrated that on the day.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why is the Prime Minister abandoning young New Zealanders in
their 30s, for whom hom eownership has plummeted under his watch faster than it has
for any other age group?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Again, I reject that proposition. If the member cares about
young people in their 30s getting a home, why did the member not support the
HomeStart package that we have? Why does the member not support Resource
Management Act reform? Why does the member not actually support the work we are
doing with special housing areas? I know: because the member likes to jump up and
down and complain, b ut when it comes to actually doing anything, she has never done
anything because she has never been in Government.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why is the Prime Minister abandoning young parents by refusing to
fix Working for Families so that young parents who lose work hours or who fall on hard
times do not also lose the $60-a-week in-work tax credit lifeline that they rely on?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As the member knows, that policy, which was introduced by
Labour—and I think, in this instanc e, was correctly positioned that way —ensured that
there was always a gap between welfare and work. And if there are not those incentives,
all of the academic evidence shows you, actually, that there will be less incentive for
people to move off welfare int o work. I think that if you have a welfare system in New
Zealand, it is a sign of a decent society that looks after people. But it is also a system
based on obligation, and, actually, we owe it to the millions of New Zealand taxpayers
who work hard to pay their taxes that people who are on welfare feel the obligation that
they should go out and work if they possibly can.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Prime Minister at least agree—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member ask her supplementary question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Would the Prime Minister at least agree that an economy that is not
working for everyone —that includes young New Zealanders under 40 who are
struggling to buy a home, who are struggling to get dece nt paid work, who are trying to
raise their children in increasing financial insecurity —is an economy that is simply not
working?
3446 Oral Questions  20 May 2015

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Far from not working, the economic credentials and
performance of this Government over the last 7 years, even in contrast to like -minded
countries, demonstrate that this Government has been performing well. We live in the
real world, and in the real world there has been a global financial crisis and many other
issues. Actually, some of these iss ues, when it comes to either people on benefits or
children living in benefit -based households, have been very longstanding, complex
issues. They will not actually be resolved overnight, but the work that this Government
is doing, breaking down the silos and the barriers that are there, is working pretty well. I
think the member actually speaks with great ignorance when she rejects what the
Government is doing there.
Budget 2015—Future Investment Fund
3. JAMI-LEE ROSS (National —Botany) to the Minister of Finance : How will
the Government’s responsible fiscal management support better public services for New
Zealanders in Budget 2015?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government has managed the
finances that are paid for by the taxpayer by being careful with new spending and
focusing consistently on reprioritising —that is, shifting money from programmes that
either do not  work or are low priority to new, more effective spending. For instance,
over the previous six Budgets the total new discretionary spend of this Government has
been around $3 billion. Over the last six Budgets of the previous Labour Government
the total new spending was $20 billion. The Government has, over the last six Budgets,
been able to shift around $15 billion of spending from ineffective or low -priority
programmes to more effective programmes, and that has been at least as important as
the new spending.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I wanted to wait until the
Minister had finished his answer before raising this, because he had already begun his
answer. I was expecting that you may have had a comment on the primary question set
down because of the assertion that it contains within it and your previous rulings on our
questions that contain such assertions. If it is acceptable for Government members to
ask about “responsible” fiscal management, can we ask about “irresponsible” fiscal
management?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I certainly examined the questions and did not pick up that at 11.30.
It was accepted and tabled in the House. It was only when an interjection came from my
left during the question that I really focused on the meaning of that word. I think it
would have been a better question without that word there. I should have picked it up at
11.30, but I did not.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: How is the Government using capital reprioritisation to improve
public services and avoid further overseas borrowing?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The main tool the Government is using is the Future
Investment Fund. Th e sale of electricity assets raised $4.7 billion, which was allocated
to the Future Investment Fund, and we are now able to use that money to invest in other
public assets. So far the Government has invested around $700 million in health, nearly
$400 milli on of the fund in education, and $1.9 billion in other public assets. That
means we have not had to go to foreign lenders for more money. We have been able to
use the savings of New Zealanders who bought the shares to invest in New Zealand
assets. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The level of barrage I am getting from two or three members
on this side means they can take this as their final warning. If it continues at that
volume, I will be asking those members to leave the Chamber.
20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3447

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: H ow have dividends paid by mixed -ownership companies to the
Government increased since the part sale of those companies?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: At the time there was some suggestion the Government
would be giving up dividends if it sold down the shares, but I can inform the House that
the Government, as a 51 percent owner, is now receiving more dividends than it did
when it was, on average, a 100 percent owner of the companies. For instance, the
highest annual dividend rec eived from Genesis Energy at any time in the previous 10
years was $57 million. The average dividend was $32 million when we were the 100
percent owner over those 10 years. This year we will receive $76 million in dividends.
As a 51 percent owner, we will get more than twice the dividend we got on average
from Genesis Energy. We can apply that to more high -priority Government social
programmes.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: How will Budget 2015 continue the Government’s ongoing
programme to improve public services for New Zealanders while helping to support
more jobs and higher wages through careful fiscal management?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: In many ways that will be talked about in detail in the House
tomorrow, but it will be against the background of growth over the next 4 years forecast
to deliver more jobs through to 2019, in addition to the 194,000 jobs that have been
added to the economy since 2011. Wages are expected to continue increasing ahead of
the cost of living. Budget 2015 will be a  responsible Budget from a responsible
Government.
Budget 2015—Youth Unemployment
4. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Minister for Tertiary
Education, Skills and Employment : What plans does the Government have in the
Budget tomorrow to get the 146,000 officially unemployed New Zealanders, as
measured by the Labour Market Statistics, into work?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): The Government will continue to operate the same sensible economic
and fiscal policies that have delivered 194,000 jobs to New Zealanders in 4¼ years, and
23,000 more jobs than the 171,000 jobs forecast by Treasury in Budget 2011, with more
than one quarter to run. In fact, this Government and businesses around the country
have delivered job growth in 16 out of the  last 17 quarters, and I am confident that the
Budget tomorrow will project further job growth. I thank the member for his question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: What are the Government’s plans in tomorrow’s Budget
for Māori and Pacific yo uth, where unemployment under this National -led Government
has increased by over 40 percent for Māori youth—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Rubbish!

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: —and almost 50 percent for Pacific youth —no, no, I am
not dealing with your speciality: rubbish; I am talking facts.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not sure about the member’s figures, but I certainly
would agree with him that Māori and Pasifika youth unemployment is  too high. I agree
with him. We have got a number of measures under way alongside the Ministry of
Māori Development to improve that situation, including, of course, the Māori and
Pasifika Trades Training Initiative, which is a programme that is delivering great
opportunities for young Māori and Pasifika in the trades around New Zealand. And
there may or may not be more information about that in the Budget tomorrow.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How is his Government going to be able to claim  to be
working for New Zealanders when we have tens of thousands of youth who are
3448 Oral Questions  20 May 2015
currently unemployed, yet, his Government has approved over 47,200 international
student visas with work rights in our current financial year?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN J OYCE
items.text: The member may not be excited about international
education, and I am reasonably confident from all his past statements that he is not, but
international education creates for this country around $2.85 billion worth of value a
year and some 33,000 jo bs, and a relatively small number of international students
actually participate in the employment market. But I thank the member for his question
and say that international education is very important for New Zealand’s future.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I did not ask about
international education, did I?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Yes. [ Interruption] Order! The member will resume his seat. If he
wants to go back and look, he included in his question the  47,200 people here on
student visas. That is the part the Minister chose to address.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I specifically said
“student visas with work rights”—those are the critical words.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The answer has certainly addressed the question. If it is not to the
member’s satisfaction, then that may be so. The way forward is to ask concise
supplementary questions.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How will tomorrow ’s Budget reduce the rate of “neets” —
those not in education, employment, or training —among youth in Northland, where the
rate has now increased to one in five youths not in employment, education, or training,
since National became the Government?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: If I was the member I would be very, very careful about the
regional numbers for a small demographic. But, nevertheless, I agree with him that
those numbers are too high, and that is why the Government has a comprehensive
programme to develop economic opportunities that positively affect Northland —for
example, the New Zealand - Korea free -trade agreement and the Trans -Pacific
Partnership—and we would welcome, obviously, the member’s support in that regard.
[Interruption] He may scoff, but that is very important for the kiwifruit farmers and to
the meat farmers and dairy farmers of Northland. Also, we are encouraging tourism
investment, including, of course, the projected investment by the Chinese investor in the
Carrington R esort—and I look forward to the member endorsing that because I
understand that they plan to train up young Northland youth. And also, of course, there
is the Ngāpuhi settlement, and we look forward to the member’s positive report of that
as well.

items.speaker: Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My point of order is that
he is not answering the question. My real point is—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! [ Interruption] Order! The member,
when I rise to my feet,  should resume his seat immediately. That question, again, was
addressed. If the member wants a further supplementary question, then he should ask it.

items.speaker: Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It is not that the question
was not in some way addressed —we know what the rules are —but you heard a long
tirade and ramble that did not address the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! If the member knows what the rules
are, I suggest he has a look at them. If he can make his questions more concise, I can
help him get an answer that might satisfy him. Does the member have a further
supplementary question? Otherwise we will—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Yes, I do, as good as the last one. Why is the Government
not filling the 5,000 job vacancies in Christchurch with young trained Kiwi workers,
given that we have 76,000 youth who are unemployed and that we are now in our fifth
20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3449
year since the Christchurch earthquake —instead of getting all the ski lled people from
offshore?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The member just needs to come and get a bit of
information, because there is actually a lot going on in Christchurch, including, for
example, the $3K to Christchurch which gives people the opportunity to shift to
Christchurch. If the member wants to participate in that scheme, I am sure we could line
him up with the Ministry of Social Development and get him down to Christchurch so
he can wield a hammer. We are also doing a huge amount of tr ades training in
Christchurch. The Building and Construction Industry Training Organisation, for
example, has record numbers of trainees and, actually, we would welcome more young
New Zealanders to take the opportunity to head to Christchurch and, in fact,  to the
whole South Island, which currently has very low levels of unemployment.
Budget 2015—Return to Surplus
5. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does his Budget 2015 speech include the statement, “there will be a small
surplus this year and increasing surpluses forecast over time”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will just have to wait
one more sleep to find out.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Why should New Zealanders , tomorrow,  believe his making a
promise for a surplus for next year and forecast surpluses for the following years, given
that he made that exact promise last year and will break it tomorrow?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, I am quite confident that New Zealanders will make
up their own minds about that, regardless of what that member says. In fact, if that
member criticises the  Budget and our economic management, most of them will
conclude that we are probably doing the right thing.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that Treasury advised him that the surplus he will
promise tomorrow for next year is possible only if there is a significant rebound in
global dairy prices?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will just have to wait until tomorrow, but I
hope tomorrow he uses the term “fiscal crisis”, because—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am going to invite the member to ask that question again.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that Treasury advised him that the surplus he will
promise tomorrow for next year is possibl e only if there is a significant rebound in
global dairy prices?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will have to wait until tomorrow, but I hope he
uses the term “fiscal crisis” tomorrow.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! If the member is saying that question has not been
addressed, on this occasion, it has. He talked about the surplus that will be promised
tomorrow in his question. It has been addressed.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that Treasury advised him that a surplus for 2015 -16
is possible only with a significant rebound in global dairy prices?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will have to wait until tomorrow.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: No, no.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, he will have to wait until tomorrow.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. That is the third time I have
asked a straight question to the Minister—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! The member will resume his seat. That
is not the same question he has asked three times. On the second occasion he repeated
3450 Oral Questions  20 May 2015
the question he had asked the first time, and on that occasion I ruled that, because of the
way it was framed, that question had definitely been answered. Does the member have a
further supplementary question?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: So you are saying that—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am on my feet, and I am going to warn that member that if
he interjects like that again while I am on my feet, I will be asking him to leave the
Chamber.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Are you telling me that the
Minister addressed the question I just asked?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I am not. I am saying that when you rose and took a point of
order and said you had asked the same question three times, you are —[Interruption] I
have a very good mind to do it. The point I was making was that the member was wrong
with his f irst point of order, when he said he had asked the same question three times.
He had not. We are moving forward. I f the member wishes to ask —[Interruption] I am
not entertaining further questions on my —[Interruption] Order! I am not entertaining
any furthe r adjudication on that matter. If the member has further supplementary
questions, I will hear them.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am trying to be helpful, as an
independent observer.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will simply raise his point of order.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: The point of order, Mr Speaker, to assist you, is that he—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order, I hope, but it will be heard in
silence. It will be heard in silence.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I am not challenging you at all, but—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member simply raise his point of order.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I am trying to. The point I want to raise with you is that he did not
actually sa y those words. His words were “This is the third straight question I have
asked.”, not “I have asked the same question”—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member may not have heard me, but I said that as far as
I was concerned I had adjudicated on the matter and that was the end of the matter. The
member may not have heard that.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it correct that Treasury advised him that a surplus for 2015 -16
is possible only if there is a significant rebound in global dairy prices?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member will have to wait until tomorrow.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. How is that an answer
addressing that question? It is about advice he has received. He cannot tell me to wait
until tomorrow. Amazingly enough, Treasury do give him advice. He ignores it—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We have had a similar line of questions now on four
occasions. It is not the way I would have hoped the Minister would answer the question,
but—[Interruption] Order! Grant Robertson will leave the House. I warned the member
that—[Interruption] Order! The member will leave the Chamber.
Grant Robertson withdrew from the Chamber.

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The colleague Mr

items.speaker: Hon Member

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member now interjects and says that it was on four occasions.
As I have pointed out to the  House, those questions were different. In one he quite

Defence Force—White Paper and Public Engagement
6. MARK MITCHELL (National—Rodney) to the Minister of Defence : What is
the Government doing to engage the New Zealand public on the future of the Defence
Force?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I recently announced the
beginning of a public consultation process on the 2015 defence white paper. We are
asking the views of New Zealanders on the future capabilities of the New Zealand
Defence Force. A series of public meetings will be held around the country to better
inform the consultation process. The meeting schedule and the information on the
submissions process can be found at www.defence.govt.nz.

items.speaker: Mark Mitchell
items.text: Why is the Government undertaking the 2015 defence white paper?
20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3453

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The white paper, which is intended to be published
before the end of the year, will be a blueprint for how the Government plans to address
the security threat s, challenges, and opportunities facing New Zealand over a 25 -year
period. Recognising that matters affecting our security can change rapidly, it is my view
that a 5-yearly cycle for white papers is desirable. The white paper 2015, therefore, will
review and build on the 2010 white paper while outlining the roles and tasks that the
Defence Force should undertake in responding to challenges as well as the capabilities
and resources that it needs to carry out its roles and tasks effectively.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Is the Minister prepared to engage the public and Defence Force
families on the more immediate issue of his assessment of the risks posed to New
Zealand soldiers in Taji, just over 100 kilometres away from Ramadi, which has just
fallen to the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The Government has been very cautious about its
commitment to building partner capacity in Iraq, and therefore it is very concerned
always, and has been from the outset, about the sec urity of soldiers who are
participating in that programme at Taji. That will continue.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Again, that question, in my mind, was addressed. It is marginal as
to whether the question should be allowed in. The member cunningly used the words
about whether he will engage with the public, and on that basis I allowed it through.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: In engaging the public will he ensure, then, that soldiers deployed to
Taji for the non -combat role of training will not soon be engaged in a major fire fight
and attack?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNL EE
items.text: As we have said right from the start, it is not our
intention that New Zealand troops in Iraq for the training mission will be engaged in
front-line combat. What we have said is that there is a force protection—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: You’re teaching them how to retreat!

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: It is not the sort of matter that people should be joking
about, frankly, Mr Parker. The point I would make is that we have always said that we
would review New Zealand’s commitment depending on the circumstances that existed,
and, of course, that if they come under fire we would expect them to protect themselves.
Finance, Minister—Return to Surplus
7. JULIE ANNE GENTER (Green)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by
his statement that “the surplus target is important”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, I stand by the full statement,
which was that “The surplus target is important. It has imposed a discipline on us and
on Government agencies to work hard on achieving value for money and providing new
spending only where we can get better results.”

items.text: Is h e aware that in the last year, his public statements about
returning to surplus were at the lowest level since 2010, and does he accept that the
National Government reached peak surplus talk 3 years ago in May 2012?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I was not aware of that particular statistical artefact but I
can reassure the member that the amount of work and focus within the Government on
achieving better value for money is higher than ever.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Can he explain why  from 2012 onwards his public statements
about returning to surplus have decreased, first gradually and then suddenly by almost
50 percent from 2013 to 2014?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I can only surmise that it is because of the rapid progress th e
Government has made towards surplus, and I am gratified to see that the Greens are at
3454 Oral Questions  20 May 2015
least counting all my statements. I wish they would read them and take a bit more notice
of them.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Is he concerned that forward predictions of his public statements
about returning to surplus are tracking upwards for the current year, and therefore, if
historical trends continue, the likelihood of actually returning to surplus will decrease in
the near future?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, but I can say that the commentary by the Greens on the
surplus makes a lot more sense than the commentary by the Labour Party.

Forestry—Government Support
9. Dr JIAN YANG (National)  to the Minister of Science and Innovation : What
research is the Government undertaking to strengthen the forestry sector?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yesterday I
announced that the Government will invest $5 million ove r 7 years in a $10 million
research partnership to help increase the competitiveness of the forestry sector. This
research will focus on developing a broader range of high -value, better -performing
wood products from tree species such as eucalyptus, Douglas  fir, and cypresses, which
provides an alternative to our predominant tree species, radiata pine. The new
partnership is led by Future Forests Research, an industry -operated entity, in
collaboration with Scion, the University of Canterbury, and the New Zea land Drylands
Forests Initiative, and will operate on a dollar for dollar basis, matched by the industry.

items.speaker: Dr Jian Yang
items.text: Why is the Government investing more in forestry sector research
and development?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: This investment aims to strengthen the ties between
research organisations and the industry, building on our existing forestry strength and
moving up the value chain by developing high -value specialty wood products while
retaining a strong focus on sustain ability. It complements other research work we are
supporting in the forestry sector. [ Interruption] You would think they would ask a
question rather than just talk all afternoon. The Primary Growth Partnership project on
steep land harvesting is designed to increase the safety of forestry workers on steep and
sloping land, while reducing the cost of harvest by 25 percent. Forestry is New
Zealand’s third-largest export earner, behind dairy and meat. It contributes around $5
billion to our exports, and we ar e committed to growing that further with investments
such as this.

Negotiations): I am pleased to advise that the Government has purchased the property
where the Battle of Ōrākau took place. The battle, in which 300 Māori defenders faced
1,500 Crown troops, is considered by many to be the decisive battle of the New Zealand
Wars. Māori sustained heavy casualties and the Crown subsequently confiscated the
land. The property is going to be held in the land bank in the Office of Treaty
Settlements while the Government engages with relevant iwi about future possibilities
for the site.

items.speaker: Barbara Kuriger
items.text: Why was it important for the Government to purchase the Battle
of Ōrākau site?

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: The Government has been very keen to
purchase this important site for a number of years, as it is of great significance to
several iwi and to New Zealand’s history. The opportunity recently a rose for the
Government to carry out the purchase when the owners of the property offered to sell it.
The site contains the remains of Māori who were killed during the battle and buried
where they lay. It has been recorded by Heritage New Zealand as a wāhi tapu area, and
the Crown and iwi agree that only certain uses of the property are going to be
appropriate in the future.
Roading, Tauranga—Tauranga Central Corridor
12. CLAYTON MITCHELL (NZ First) to the Minister of Transport: What is the
Government doing about the Tauranga Central Corridor?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: A lot, and that is because we
committed to the Tauranga Central Corridor and are going to invest over $100 million
in the project. The member may be aware that enabling works have st arted, and
20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3459
construction of the Maungatapu-Hairini underpass will start a little later this year. If the
member is a really good boy, I might even invite him to the opening. If he is really,
really good, he might get a cucumber sandwich.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That will not help the order of this House.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. A lot of things are said
in this House, but those would be some of the most insulting words I have ever heard.
To refer to a member of Parliament —who has had a real man’s background, not like
his—as a boy is just unacceptable—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It certainly was not going to bring order to the House, and
that is why I asked the Minister to conclude his ans wer. If the member took offence at
it—

items.speaker: Clayton Mitchell
items.text: Yes, I did. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has taken offence at that remark. I require the
Minister to withdraw the remark.

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! If the member wishes to join his
colleague?

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Mr Speaker, my question is to you.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If it is a point of order, would you—

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: You are the last—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member simply raise his point of order
immediately.

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Why should the Opposition have to as k you to deal with that sort of
behaviour?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: What is—

items.speaker: Ron Mark
items.text: Why should we have to ask—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will sit down. [ Interruption] Order! If the
member would go back and study the Hansard, he will see that as soon as the remark
was made I told the Minister to cease. I was surprised that a member then took offence
at it, but if a member takes offence, the process is that I ask the Minister to withdraw.
That has been the process for as long as I have been here, and that is considerably
longer than Ron Mark.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is this a fresh point of order?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: It is a fresh point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Fresh point of order, the Hon Gerry Brownlee.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: From time to time things are said in the House tha t may be
offensive to members. There are other times when things are said in the House that are
so offensive to members that there is a consideration as to whether or not that matter
should be raised at all. I would suggest, Mr Speaker, that when you get b ack to your
office you have a look at the Twitter feeds, so that we could see that some of the
hypocrisy that is being offered by the New Zealand First Party today is a complete
disgrace.

items.speaker: Clayton Mitchell
items.text: Does the Minister acknowledge N ational’s commitment to create
a four-lane State highway—not a local road —to run from the Welcome Bay underpass
across the Turret Road bridge and along Fifteenth Avenue by 2015?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Of course, what we are doing is, in sub stance, keeping the
announcement. That is why we are spending over $100 million on this area. But it is a
staged project. That is why at the moment stages one and two —the early stages—worth
some $20 million of work, are occurring. That is why stage four—where the member, as
3460 Oral Questions  20 May 2015
I say, if he is lucky can have a cucumber sandwich —is about to occur and it is worth
some $68 million of underpass. Then, as required, we will look at the third stage.

items.speaker: Clayton Mitchell
items.text: What is the Minister doing to pr event the Fifteenth Avenue State
Highway 2A from becoming part of the local road network and putting half of the cost
of the upgrade on Tauranga ratepayers, against National’s original commitment?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: Whether it is a State highway or a local road, it is of some
significance to the agencies involved but, in a sense, from the Government’s perspective
it is neither here nor there. Unlike New Zealand First, we are in Government and we can
make these projects happen.

items.speaker: Clayton Mitchell
items.text: Does the Minister understand that for the Welcome Bay
underpass to be effective, the widening of Turret Road and Fifteenth Avenue needs to
happen at the same time?

items.speaker: Hon SIMON BRIDGES
items.text: I thank the member for his  opinion. I understand what is
required in relation to that underpass and project and also what is required in Tauranga.
That is why we have spent some $800 million in the last 3 years and achieved much
more in transport than the New Zealand First - Labour Government ever did.
Point of Order—Answers

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. Today has been a very interesting question time, and I am sure that there will
be some commentary that runs on from it. I am wondering whether you might consider
whether Speaker’s ruling 167/6 still applies, and sugge st that that may be something
that our opponents in the Opposition want to have a look at. It is a ruling delivered by
Margaret Wilson in 2007.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will certainly have a look at that.

items.speaker: RON MARK
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I would like to take
the opportunity to withdraw and apologise to the House for making a comment that
some people may have been offended by or that would have brought the House into
disrepute. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Speaking to
the Hon Gerry Brownlee’s point of order, the ruling to which he refers says: “A member
cannot require a specific or particular answer to a question. The Minister is just required
to address the question.” This is the very point we were making. We want an answer
that addresses the question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member ought to become more familiar with both the
Standing Orders and Speakers’ rulings. The Opposition cannot demand an answer that it
requires. My job is to judge whether the question was addressed. On this occa sion I did
so. That is the end of that matter. [ Interruption] Order! The member will resume his
seat. I just want to be clear: I have ruled on this matter. If the member is now
relitigating, that in itself brings this House into disorder. Has the member go t a fresh
point of order? If he has I will listen to it.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I was
addressing the Hon Gerry Brownlee’s point to you, which you have n ot ruled on. I did
not disagree with the Speaker’s ruling; I merely read it out and said our point was we
just wanted questions to be addressed.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That does not help the order of the House at all.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: I move, That the House take note
of miscellaneous business . It has been a somewhat fractious afternoon. We have had
pompous “gittery” in bucket loads coming from the other side, and we are in eager
20 May 2015 General Debate 3461
anticipation of what may be handed down tomorrow. And for goo d reason too because
when you look back at some of the promises, pledges, and foreshadowing that has come
from the Government, it is going to be a very interesting day indeed. For example, the
Prime Minister, John Key, when he was talking about the proposa l for a Government -
led building programme to ease the Auckland housing crisis —a proposal that we made
some time ago —what did he say? He said: “Oh, it’ll either fail miserably, deliver
dwellings that people don’t want to live in, or require massive taxpayer  subsidies.” And
what are we going to see tomorrow? A Government -led building programme to ease the
Auckland housing crisis. So we live in eager anticipation.
Then there was this about restrictions on foreign buyers of Auckland houses. What
did the Prime M inister say in April last year? He said: “Oh, I think that’s a bit of a red
herring. It’s not needed.” And what have we seen from the Government? We have seen
just that. Then there is this about child poverty. You see, we had Anne Tolley, the
Minister for Social Development, saying: “We are working on a comprehensive plan on
child poverty.” And in the days and weeks following the election,  the Prime Minister
himself said: “Child poverty will be our top priority.” And what do we see now? The
Government is back-pedalling rapidly and is backing out of doing anything about child
poverty. So we live in eager anticipation —we live in eager anticipation. I might add,
also, what the Prime Minister said just a couple of days ago about children in poverty.

items.speaker: He said
items.text: “Oh , children in poverty don’t have it so bad, because they get lots of
entitlements that better -off kids don’t get.” This is National’s attitude towards child
poverty.
I never thought I would say this but I have been inspired in my contribution to
today’s general debate by none other than Minister Nick Smith, who said yesterday that
Christmas is coming for Auckland homebuyers in the Budget. So I have prepared a little
contribution to today’s debate, and those of you who have grown up with Christmases
in New Zealand will know about the great Christmas carol rhyme, and so I now offer
my rendition. I say this:
’Twas the night before Budget, when all through the House,
The National backbenchers were keen for a stoush.
The promises were hung during the election with care,
Of course they would fill them; how could they not? They wouldn’t dare!
September 14 was a different time;
The backbenchers quite happy—some in their prime.
Nestled all snug in their leather armchairs,
John, Bill, and Steven washed away all their fears.
There had been promises of surpluses, of poverty relieved,
Of great fiscal wonders; or so they believed.
“They have got us this far,” the backbenchers said,
“What could possibly go wrong? We’re so far ahead!”
But Bill English knew, he just hid his fear,
That all their good words were just plain hot air.
It’s great that Mike Hosking and Paul Henry are glowing,
But nothing can mask an economy slowing.
“We have to do something! We have to be quick!”
Said John Key to his Cabinet that had run out of tricks.
“Ministers Bennett and Bridges and Tolley—
Forget Steven Joyce and his conventional folly.
Ministers Woodhouse, McCully, Crosby, and Textor,
3462 General Debate 20 May 2015
If there’s one thing that’s clear, you’ll all have to do better.
I need plans to help Auckland, to slow housing prices,
To help feed the kids, and fix other vices.
Where’s the plan for trains, trucks, and bikes?
My Facebook page’s tanking; I can’t get no likes.
And I’m sick of seeing Andy, the new man about town;
He never gets angry; we can’t bring him down!”

items.speaker: Bill English stepped forward in canonical mood

items.text: “Just stop there, John. I don’t mean to be rude.
You may not have noticed, but we have a crisis,
And it’s nothing to do with our troops fighting ISIS.
Exports are diving, dairy is down,
There isn’t much happening in any small town.
I know I’ve said the problem’s inflation,
But there’s something much bigger: John Banks’ compensation.
You’ve said don’t touch taxes, levies, and fees,
But how will we pay for this? It don’t grow on trees.”
And then the talk came to a stop with a shudder.
The Prime Minister knew, his heart now aflutter.
Up from the back came a great throaty roar;
Judith Collins appeared on Parliament’s floor!
“I’ve heard all your talk—me and Todd Muller.
All you’re known now is as a ponytail puller.
Out of the way, shove this in your gob;
I’m here to take over. It’s my turn in your job.”

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I think David
Cunliffe’s poetry on Harvard was significantly better. Poetry will do for Mr Little’s
career what it did for Mr Cunliffe’s career. Mr Little could not even get agreement on
Labour’s response to National’s housing tax policy on Sund ay, with half its caucus
saying it was a capital gains tax and the other half saying it was not. Tomorrow’s
Budget will be about further delivering on our plan for New Zealand. It is a pity there
was not a single idea or plan in Mr Little’s contribution.
The backdrop for this Budget is the best set of economic fundamentals that this
Parliament has seen in a generation. Economic growth at 3.5 percent is growing at a
faster rate than in Australia, the UK, the US, Japan, or Europe. Employment is up by
74,000 in the past year, with the unemployment rate down to 5.8 percent —less than in
Australia, less than in most countries in the OECD. Inflation is 0.1 percent in the last
year. That is the lowest rate in 17 years. Interest rates —I know they do not matter to the
members opposite; they actually matter to housing —are 5.5 percent. That is the lowest
in 40 years. When you look at education, when you look at health numbers, when you
look at crime, when you look at welfare, every one of them is headed in the right
direction. My challenge to members opposite is to tell me of a country in the world that
is doing better. New Zealanders know we are doing well. That is why a record number
of New Zealanders are not leaving; in fact, a record number of New Zealanders are
coming home.
I want to focus on the mantra from the Leader of the Opposition that National’s
programme is in tatters in respect of the economy because we did not quite make a
surplus this year. In fact, Mr Little said that this is the biggest political decept ion in a
20 May 2015 General Debate 3463
lifetime. Well, Mr Little must be very young. If this is Labour and the Greens’ big
attack on the Budget tomorrow, it is going to go down like a damp squib. Let me give
you the numbers.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: What, the Budget?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: Treasury forecast —no, your criticism. Last year we
forecast a surplus of $0.4 billion. The latest numbers are that it is likely to be a deficit of
about $0.6 billion. That is overspending of $70 billion. We will not know the final
number until October, but it is fair to say it will be about $1 billion or about a 1.5
percent difference from what was forecast. Well, if that is the greatest political
deception, let me just remind members opposite of one thing. The last time you were on
this side of the House, you promised the House a $1.3 billion surplus. And what did we
get? We actually got a $3.9 billion deficit, out by $5 billion. So if a $1 billion mistake or
variation is the biggest political deception ever, what is $5 billion —what is $5  billion?
In fact, I asked the Parliamentary Library how Budgets and actuals compare over the
last 20 years. Do you know what? Over the last 20 years the average variation has been
$2 billion. In fact, in the nine Budgets that Labour delivered, they were o n average out
by $2.5 billion, a record significantly worse than this Government’s. The truth is that
the record is this: an $18 billion deficit for 2010 halved to $9 billion, halved to $4
billion, down to $3 billion, and well and truly under $1 billion. I  compare that with the
Budget in Australia last week —a $40 billion deficit going further into the red for the
next 4 years. I know what side of the Tasman I would like to be on in respect of good
fiscal management.
Let me give you another number. Are memb ers opposite saying it was a broken
promise when National promised 171,000 jobs? We delivered 194,000 —194,000.
Forecasts are just that. This Government is well and truly, if you look at those numbers,
in great shape. I am going—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member’s time has expired. [Interruption] Order! If you
are going to table a document, just seek leave.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.role: Minister for Buil ding and Housing
items.text: I seek leave to table
a document prepared by Grant Cleland from the Parliamentary Library for Budgets over
the last 20 years, comparing that—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That has been described enough. I will put the leave. Leave
is sought to table that particular information. Is there any objection? There is.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I think it is time to ask, at this
time of the electoral cycle, what we look for in a Government. What do we look for in
the leader of a Government? I think the answer to those two questions must be integrity,
ethics and morals, trustworthiness, truthfulness, and sincerity. So the next question that
I would then ask this Parliament—[Interruption] Oh! They are responding before I even
get to it. That is kind of like they are admitting defeat before I even start. But I would
say that the next question must be: does this current Government and its leader , John
Key, have integrity? Do they have ethics and morals? Are they truthful? Are they
trustworthy? And are they sincere? [ Interruption] Thank you. Well, I think that it is fair
to say, after almost 7 years, that the National Government did start out with —those
members were keen, they were eager, they were cooperative, and they were very, very
excited after 9 years in Opposition. But 7 years later, on almost all of those fundamental
measures of good leadership and government that I have mentioned today, th is
Government is a failure —it is a failure. John Key now acts on the understanding of
what he can get away with, what can never be found out, and what he can cover up.
There is a mounting number of examples of deception, of trickery, of evasion and
duplicity, and of downright Tory arrogance.
3464 General Debate 20 May 2015
If you wanted to see Tory arrogance, you saw it today —you saw it in question time
today. It started with the Prime Minister, who did not answer a single question but
attacked every other party in this House that is not  in Government. It was then followed
by Steven Joyce, who is the most self -satisfied, smug member of the Government, and
Anne Tolley, who kept saying: “One more sleep, one more sleep.” when she would not
answer questions about the Budget that were not even  about the Budget but about what
she had done towards it. Then we had Simon Bridges, the cabin boy, who stood up and
insulted New Zealand First. And then the doozy of them all —the doozy of them all —
Tim Groser, who has been going around the world grossing o ut all the people we would
like to do trade with. He is the man headed for Washington. He is going to be our man
over there in a diplomatic role—what an embarrassment.
This Government made some pretty big solemn promises to New Zealand before the
last ele ction. Not just orally; it put them in pamphlets and stuffed them through just
about everybody’s letterbox in New Zealand. Then it sent letters —personally addressed
letters—paid for by the taxpayer and signed “Yours sincerely” by the Prime Minister,
and no w we are told that those promises are just mere suggestions, they are just
aspirational goals, and they are “nice -to-haves”. The latest one of all from the Prime

items.speaker: Minister was when he said
items.text: “They were never promises in the first place.” So the
promises that  were solemn promises are not promises now, according to the Prime
Minister. Well, there is a good word for that: it is chicanery. That is what it is —it is
chicanery. And that now describes the modus operandi of this Government.
Let us look at some of the  trickery and duplicity of this Government that New
Zealanders are experiencing. What did it promise around wages? It told us that they
would be increased by $7,000 per annum by 2017, and now the Prime Minister tells us
that it will be only half that. It p romised 150,000 new jobs; now it can deliver only half
of that promise, according to the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: It promised balanced books, Mr Smith. It promised
balanced books, and now we are going to have a $5 million to $6 million deficit. “Never
really mattered—didn’t really care if we had a deficit or not.” That is not what was said
last year—solemn promises to New Zealand. It promised that housing would be more
affordable. Well, what a big, fat fabrication that was. We have seen house price inflation
running at 14.6 percent per year and Auckland house prices rising by 63 percent under
this Government. The Prime Minister said: “There’s no crisis.” but this week he finally
said: “I think they are rising faster than is healthy.” He then said: “They have been
going up a little more rapidly than we would like.” So, finally, the Government knows
there is a problem and it is trying to put the cotton wool around it. This Government is
not being honest with New Zealanders. It does not show the moral fibre that it ought to
have as a Government. It has become tired, it has become arrogant, and it ought to leave
this Parliament.

items.speaker: Hon TODD McCLAY
items.text: Listening to that last intervention
from the Hon Annette King made me feel so very, very sorry for poor old David
Cunliffe. Did you see what happened at the last election? All the members of the Labour
Party on that side of the House deserted him as fast as they could. But when one looks
at the last poll published around the country, poor old David Cunliffe was polling higher
on that day as preferred Prime Minister —and the Labour Party was also polling high er
then than it is currently, after the last 6 months —and certainly polling higher than their
new leader, Andrew Little, is. Here is a prediction for you: very soon there will be a poll
around the preferred Prime Minister that will show that the true Leade r of the
Opposition is the Rt Hon Winston Peters, not Andrew Little, because Andrew Little is
going down and Winston Peters, on that side of the House, is going up.
20 May 2015 General Debate 3465
Do you know what? The reason for that is that the Labour Party has the shortest
memory of any political party in the history of this country. I want to read this out. It is
a statement that was made in this House not so long ago: “Much concern has been
expressed about overinvesting in housing and the impact of the tax system in
encouraging this.” It then goes on to say: “… I am mindful of the fact that under the
current law investing in housing for the purpose of making a capital gain, that is trading
in housing, is taxable. In order to underline the significance of this fact and to send a
clear signal to housing investors about the purport of the current law it has been agreed
between myself and the Commissioner of Inland Revenue that an additional $14.6
million [will be put in over 3 years to focus on housing tax compliance].” That was in
2007, under a Labour Government, and it was Michael Cullen who said that.
Well, in 2010, under exactly the same law this National Government gave the Inland
Revenue Department $33 million to look at property tax compliance. Over the last 5
years that has retur ned $258 million in additional tax. In 2013 we gave the department
another $33 million, and in the Budget tomorrow we will give an extra $29 million.
Over the next 5 years the Inland Revenue Department will have $62 million to go out
and focus on the current law, which has been in place since the 1970s, and it says that it
will return about $420 million on that.
We do believe that good tax law needs certain rules, and taxpayers as well as the
Inland Revenue Department need certainty. That is the reason tha t the Prime Minister
announced that under the Budget there will be a number of changes. The first is that
anybody who is purchasing a house in New Zealand other than their own home, their
principal place of residence, will need to provide an Inland Revenue  Department
number at the time of purchase. A foreigner, a non -tax resident, will have to give us
their tax information number from their own country. Secondly, the non -tax resident
will need to open a bank account in New Zealand before they can get an Inland Revenue
Department number, which means the full range of New Zealand’s anti - money-
laundering laws will apply to them.
I think it is reasonable that we know that anybody who wants to be involved in New
Zealand pays their fair share of tax and that th ey are coming here with good intent. We
are going to look to investigate and implement a withholding tax system so that those
non-tax residents, when they sell a property and are captured by the existing rules, will
have to pay that tax on the spot. The In land Revenue Department will have the money.
Non-tax residents will need to apply to get it back, in cases where they feel that the tax
is not due.
On top of this we want to provide greater certainty and clarity to the taxpayer. Within
the first 2 years, with the exception of your family home, your principal place of
residence, a home that you may have inherited or because of a marriage settlement,
there will be a brightline test that says if you have made a profit from a house that you
have purchased and have sold, you must pay tax on any gain. There will be a number of
rules that we will work out around that. Good tax law is consulted on, so we will be
consulting on that before it comes before the House.
The challenge in many parts of New Zealand and in Auckland is one of supply. We
need good tax rules so that those who should be paying tax are paying it, but the
challenge is one of supply. In the last year or so we have gone from 14,000 houses a
year being built, to 25,000 houses a year being built, and there will be 43,000 additional
houses able to be built under the special housing areas that Nick Smith has negotiated
with parts of the country.
The Government is focusing on supply. We are making sure that those who should
be paying tax are paying tax. We are making sure that the rules are clear and are giving
3466 General Debate 20 May 2015
the Inland Revenue Department $62 million over 5 years for property compliance, to
make sure that all those who should be paying tax are paying it. Thank you.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: Tomorrow on Budget day New
Zealand is going to witness yet again a further fanfare of fiction, fantasy, and fatalism,
seasoned by arrogance and smugness. The fiction again w ill be the surplus, the fantasy
again will be the rock star economy, and the fatalism again will be the inevitable decline
of our provinces under a Government obsessed with Auckland and massive
immigration.
Back in 2008 this bright young thing Mr Key said  that the next 10 years, to 2018,
must be—let me rephrase the words he said —“a decade of maximised opportunities”.
We were going to be aspirational because we were being led by somebody who was the
product of an American company called Merrill Lynch. You d o not hear much about
Merrill Lynch these days, do you? It was the fifth company to go belly up in the Wall
Street - generated financial crisis of greed and fraud, and then it was bailed out by the
American taxpayers. That is his background. There is not o ne fundamental political
principle—just do a deal and move on. Or, like that famous ad, just “spray and walk
away”. I tell you what, it is running thin. The man has lost his mojo.
In fact, he turned up, up north, and he was on 500 hoardings —500 hoardings—with
the slogan of all slogans: “Working for Northland”. Up there the people took one good,
hard look—the farmers, all the old supporters of National —and they said, like the Tui
ad: “Yeah, right! Where?”. There were the 72,000 jobs from the organiser of th e
campaign, Steven Joyce, the “Mr Fix -it”. They said: “So there’s 72,000 up here in the
north and you have created 172,000 in the country. That is a lot for Northland, is it not,
when all the other electorates share all the rest?”. Then they kind of talk t o people like
Mr Bishop who was up there, and my friend Alfred Ngaro, and Mark Mitchell. What a
sad case it was. It was so sad that I began feeling sorry for them; I really did. We knew,
and we said it 3 weeks out from the election, that they were going to  see a seismic shift.
People in the provinces are not going to take that bulldust any more. They want some
action. They want to see things happening.
You know, here we have got a two -tiered economy: Auckland versus provincial
neglect. As for the member fo r Christchurch Central, the only reason why her province
is surviving is because of an accident or disaster. If it was not for that, Christchurch
would be screaming at the bottom like the rest of New Zealand. Manufacturing is
declining against GDP. Exporting is declining against GDP. The Government debt is up
to nearly $70 billion, over seven times the Government debt of 2008. That which should
be up in New Zealand is down —manufacturing, exporting. That which is down —that
means productive exporting, the pro ductive part of the economy, and debt —is up. In
fact it is upside down, with the National Party. The people up north got the message.
Around the country, from Invercargill to Ōāmaru, Timaru, the Hawke’s Bay,
Gisborne, and Wanganui, we are going to take ou r message. There is one party that
understands the provinces and their economic background. What we understand more
than anybody else is this: it is you in the provinces who create this country’s real
wealth. So why are you down at the bottom of the income  stream? We are going to set
things right. We are going to go and tell them that they will not get a change in the
economic settings until they change their priority when voting and go out and vote for a
party that knows where all the hard work and manual work is. Half of the National
Party—you can tell by the look of them, this new breed that came in —thinks that
manual labour is the Prime Minister of Mexico. They have never done any physical
work and it shows in their attitude.
Mr Bishop has never done any physical work in his life; we know it. He gets up there
to Ruawai or up there to Dargaville, and the people there do not know what they are
20 May 2015 General Debate 3467
talking to. They say that this man cannot be from the party of Holyoake. He cannot be
from the party of Marshall a nd McKay and all those famous National Party guys and
women who did understand the nation and the condition of the provinces. Back then
people rightly voted for National, but not anymore. Up north they got the message.
They are getting it in Whangarei righ t now. When the head of the ANZ bank turned up
and said: “This is zombie town.”, what did Mr Reti say? Did he say it was an outrage?
No, he agreed. They have got a zombie member. But no longer.
Thank you, Mr Speaker. I would like to go on. Can I move a mo tion that I speak for
a bit longer? This is a very important speech.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.
Hon NI CKY WAGNER (Associate Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery): First, I would like to say how disappointed I am in the member Mr Peters
and his attitude to the people of Christchurch. Yes, the people of Christchurch have
been hit by a disaster, but we  have picked ourselves up and got on our feet. Our
province is flourishing, and it will continue to flourish.
As the Minister for Disability Issues, firstly, I would like to start by thanking the
New Zealand Sign Language interpreters who are working here  this week. They have
done a great job. Thank you very much.
Secondly, I would like to start to talk about the focus of Christchurch and Canterbury
on housing because absolutely Christchurch has been hit by a terrible disaster : 170,000
houses were damaged or destroyed, and 170,000 families have had to manage their way
through that. If you say it quickly, 170,000 does not sound that much, but that is the
equivalent of nearly six Palmerston Norths. Of those 170,000 homes, 10,500 were
destroyed and had to be demolished and rebuilt.
I am going to skip quickly through the resilience of the Christchurch people, the
emergency housing, the emergency repairs, the Canterbury Earthquake Temporary
Accommodation Service, the accommodation subsidies, the accommodation v illages,
the Earthquake Commission insurance repairs, and the consenting issues with the city
council, until we get to now —4 years later. We believe we are pretty close to being
back to the same number of houses that there were in Christchurch and Canterbu ry pre
the earthquakes. In 2014 alone 4,400 houses were built. But there are still pressures.
The first problem is that people are coming to Christchurch. People want to be a part
of our rebuild. We are a magnet for talent to Christchurch, and, of course,  that means
that those people have to find housing, so there has been increased pressure for housing
for workers.
Secondly, there is a problem with quality homes. We have got better -quality homes
in Christchurch. You might say that that is not a problem. It is absolutely not a problem
for the people who are living in them, but the rents and the costs of those houses ha ve
gone up. It means there is less choice for people who have a lower income, and that is a
real problem. So, to overcome that problem, Hous ing New Zealand, the city council,
and housing organisations have created new temporary housing options for the
vulnerable. We are working really hard to make sure that that all works. Housing New
Zealand is spending $1 billion. It has done 5,000 repairs, and it is building a new home
every day. These are fabulous new homes that are double -glazed and totally insulated.
There is no downside to that quality because people are still getting income -related
rents.
One of the best initiatives in terms of repairing houses has been the initiative we have
with Christchurch Prison, where prisoners are out there giving houses a new lease of life
and at the same time learning skills they can use when they come out of prison into the
construction industry in Christchurch, giving a new lease of life to them as well.
3468 General Debate 20 May 2015
Christchurch City Council is working well. Every week we are  seeing new houses
opening, and all its houses are accessible. I visited a block last week , and any one of us
would be really happy to live there.
The best difference in terms of supply is the housing accords. The Government is
working with the city council on four major sites . T here will be over 1,000 new
houses—1,000 new houses —and 20 to 30 percent of those houses will be affordable
houses. They ha ve already started on the Awatea site over in Hornby, the contract has
been let for Welles Street and Colombo Street in the centre city —and as a centre city
resident I am looking forward to those people moving in to our areas —and the
Riccarton racecourse site is under way. That 20 to 30 percent of affordable housing will
be available through the KiwiSaver HomeStart package , and that is a real opportunity
for people who want to get into their own houses, particularly young New Zealanders.
The policy has been  particularly tailored for Christchurch so we can allow  second-
chance buyers to get that KiwiSaver HomeStart package because of the earthquakes.
It is absolutely true that housing the people of Christchurch and Canterbury  has
been—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member’s time has expired.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: What an embarrassing last 90 minutes it has been for
the New Zealand Labour Party, the Opposition —the obstreperous Oppositio n: angry
Andy and angry Annette. It was an embarrassing last 90 minutes. They fell apart
completely during question time. We had Grant Robertson there, who threw his toys out
of the cot and was ejected from the Chamber. Mr Peters, on sort of road to Kawaka wa
experience, suddenly was a new convert to bringing refugees into New Zealand. Well,
he was back to his usual tricks in the general debate and in question time on a long -
winded rant about international students flooding New Zealand and bringing their ski lls
and expertise, and bringing their income and their wealth to our country. He was
straight back into it in the general debate, recycling jokes from the 1970s. That joke
about manual labour has been around since the 1970s, and that is the best that he ca n do
in 2015. It is embarrassing —absolutely embarrassing. It is no surprise his jokes come
from the 1970s because that is exactly where his economic policies come from. Then,
after Grant got thrown out, David Cunliffe got up to save the day. The new chief whip
of the Labour Party, David Cunliffe, got up with long tendentious points of order. He is
back. He is back, and we know he is back because the Leader of the Opposition —the
current Leader of the Opposition, the temporary Leader of the Opposition—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Who is it today?

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: It is Andrew Little, Mr Macindoe. Andrew Little decided to take a
leaf out of David Cunliffe’s book and repeat a poem during his general debate speech. It
was not a patch on “I am Harvard ”. It was not a patch on David Cunliffe’s magnum
opus from his time as a scholar at Harvard in the 1990s, but it was a pretty good effort.
It was reasonably amusing, but I have got to say it was embarrassing that that is the best
that the Opposition can do  1 day out from the Budget. We are 1 day out from Bill
English’s seventh Budget, and all that Andrew Little can come up with is some half -
rhyming poem. So it was a very embarrassing time.
Then we had old Ron Mark who was almost thrown out of the House for  a sweary
mouth. The obstreperous Opposition has had a very bad afternoon indeed. Clare Curran
was tweeting away about how we on this side of the House were glum. On the “Planet
Labour”, the parallel universe that Clare Curran seems to spend most of her li fe in, we
on the Government backbenches were glum. Nothing could be further from the truth.
This is a Government and this is a party that is in good heart. The reason for that, and
the reason why the obstreperous Opposition members over there are so frust rated, and
the reason why Grant was thrown out, and the reason why they are so angry over on that
20 May 2015 General Debate 3469
side of the House is that they know that tomorrow Bill English is going to deliver a
Budget that will show that New Zealand is heading in the right direction.  He will
deliver a Budget that shows we are growing at one of the fastest rates in the developed
world. He is going to deliver a Budget that shows that inflation is low, wages are rising
faster than inflation, and unemployment is down, and not only that —and this is very
important—he is going to deliver a Budget that shows New Zealand that this
Government is tackling some of the intractable social problems that have bedevilled us
for far too long.
This Government is tackling things like material deprivation. It is tackling the
housing affordability problem that we have in this country. It is tackling entrenched
welfare dependency. It is tackling the educational disparities that exist between Māori
and Pākehā, and Pasifika and Māori in this country, and it is implementing and
embedding in the Government books the social investment approach that my colleague
Anne Tolley, my colleague Paula Bennett, and Bill English have been working on for
the last 5 years.
Actually, you will not see much media commentary about that approach tomorrow
and you definitely will not see Jacinda Ardern or Carmel Sepuloni talk about it. You
will not see them talk about that social investment approach. For starters, the Labour
Party members do not understand it and to the extent that they do understand it they
