fundamentally disagree with the idea that will be at the heart of the Budget tomorrow.
This side of the House, the Government, is in good heart. The Opposition members
are frustrated and angry, and they are frustrated and angry for a good reason —because
this Budget is going to be an important marking point in New Zealand’s future and our
history. All they have are rants and anger over on that side of the House. What we ha ve
is a Budget that will continue to deliver for New Zealanders.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: I apologise in advance for my seriousness and lack of
personal abuse in this speech —it seems to be counter to others. If an e conomy is not
working for everyone, it is not working, and this economy is not working. We have
about a quarter of a million of our children living in poverty. We have between 60,000
and 100,000 children consistently going without nutritious meals, their o wn beds,
waterproof or warm clothing, shoes, access to transport, or the ability to go on school
trips or to get birthday and Christmas presents. We have more than one child a week
dying of preventable poverty-related diseases.
We have more beggars on the  streets than I can remember in my lifetime. We have
community workers having to access food banks at the places they work because they
believe in the importance of caring for others, even when this Government cuts the
funding for their services. We are he aring about people sleeping in their cars or on the
streets in Ashburton, in Hastings, in Auckland, in Invercargill, in Tauranga, in Kaitāia,
and in Wellington.
From one end of our abundant country to the other, people are on our streets
struggling. We have a capital city with the highest rates of depression in the country due
to the constant restructuring of our public services. We have distressed farmers worried
that they might lose their farms as they have been encouraged into untenable levels of
debt. We have wages for half of this country stagnating, even while ours as MPs
increase.
We have an entire generation abandoned. Those under 40 are burdened now with
massive student debts. They are increasingly having to face up to the fact that they may
never own a house, or may have to wait until their parents die in order to have a house,
and far too many are struggling to even find a warm, stable, affordable place to live. We
are seeing more people now with Bachelor’s degrees in the lowest income bracket —
more than we have ever seen before —and we have a generation facing, or trying to
3470 General Debate 20 May 2015
ignore, the looming emotional and financial burden of climate change due to a failure of
successive Governments to act.
National tells us that it is working for New Zealand. Na tional has lost touch with
everyday New Zealanders. It has chosen to build an economy that works only for New
Zealanders who already have a lot. The Budget is an expression of our collective
priorities as a country, or it should be. But it seems that we ar e going to be getting
another Budget that is ignoring the reality of all too many of us, and this makes me
worried for all of us because it costs to look the other way when someone else is
suffering.
I am sure everyone in this House knows that sick feelin g you get when you have hurt
someone. But, rather than fronting up to them and dealing with it, you ignore it, and of
course your relationship with that person suffers. We all know that; we have all done
that. If we do not feel a little bit sick when we are staring into the faces of those children
going without their own beds and going without a decent meal, then this is a disturbing
reality of ideology and the impact of it on us.
The Green Party is prepared to stand up for younger New Zealanders and all t hose
who do not have enough to get by, who are being let down by this National
Government. There is an alternative —in fact, there are many —and the Green Party has
real solutions to ensure our economy would work for all of us. For us, it is sensible
economics for a small country, but, much more than that, it is what we know is right.
An economy that is working for only a few is not an economy that is working.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is an honour to  take a call in this general debate.
First of all, it is my first time to speak since the passing away of our rangatira Ērima
Hēnare. He maumaharatanga ki te tino rangatira a Ērima Hēnare [ a recollection to the
great leader Ērima Hēnare]. Can I just acknowledge my respect for him. He was a great
leader. He was on a number of boards. One in particular that I know that Pita Paraone
will know is the Waitangi National Trust Board. He will be greatly missed because of
his leadership up in the far north.
I make mention of that leadership because leadership becomes critically important to
this country and it is what our communities look for. I know that the Rt Hon Winston
Peters talked about the far north and about a community looking for something
different, some thing new. Can I say that absolutely there was a sense of looking for
more opportunities up there, whether they be in employment, whether they be in
forestry, whether they be in roading. So they were looking for that. Can I also add to the
part of the pict ure that is not often talked about, which the Rt Hon Winston Peters has
not described, and that is the handshake, the deal that was done behind closed doors
with the Labour Party. Andrew Little was up there and what happened actually was the
fact that both  the Greens and Labour conceded. They conceded and so that was the
difference: a majority of 4,000, which made New Zealand First win in the end. It did
win. I will not take that away; it was a win.
But can I also say that when you do those deals —and Labour members are used to
that even though they talked about the deals that have been done on the National side.
Yet they know that Jeanette Fitzsimons in Coromandel —the deal was done there with
Labour voters. The gain was that Labour was able to stay in Gover nment. Or whether it
was with Jim Anderton and the Alliance —the deal was it was able to stay in
Government. However, in this case Labour has been the greatest loser because out of
this what has happened? Absolutely nothing. In fact, on day one after the el ection, when
asked about whether there would be some deals of working together, this is what the Rt
Hon Winston Peters said. He said there is no debt to be owed —there is no debt to be
owed. That was classic of Winston. That is actually what was said.
20 May 2015 General Debate 3471
But what the country is looking for, what the regions are looking for, is leadership.
When we look at this National Government tomorrow will be an important day, because
of the leadership of this Government and what it has been able to do. When we have the
polls that go out, what is the No. 1 issue that comes up? Constantly it is around the
economy. It is around the economy, it is around other issues —around housing,
education and health—but people ask whether we can fiscally manage ourselves in our
economy. We have shown with the leadership of the Rt Hon John Key and also the
Deputy Prime Minister, Bill English, that we have had steady, sensible finances that are
in order. In fact, do not take our word for it. Let us talk about what has come out of the
Dominion Post. This hurts the Opposition because now we have people like Shamubeel
Eaqub, for instance, who has turned round and said that people have talked about the
economy as a rock star economy, but instead on this side we have talked about a rock
solid econom y. Here is what he says: “Before the recession” —prior to that time,
obviously, when Labour was in Government —“we were … willing to borrow and
spend.” Is that not a classic example of the Labour Government: “borrow and spend.”?
“In comparison we’re being ve ry careful now.” In fact, he said that we are managing
our economy, and that in the long term it is an economy that is working ahead of other
economies in the world, for instance, other traditional powerhouses like Japan, like
United States, and even like Britain.
Again, we are seeing that confidence in the leadership financially pays a difference.
How does that make a difference to our communities at large? It makes a difference
because when we manage that economy well fiscally, we can do the things that are
important to our communities in regard to health, housing, and education. In fact, we
know that the total annual cost of new initiatives in the Government’s last six Budgets is
less than $2.9 billion. By comparison, the extra costs in the last six Budg ets of the
previous Government totalled $20 billion. That is the difference that we are making —
$2.9 billion versus $20 billion —we are managing successfully. However, despite the
fact that we are managing, we are reducing our costs, we are also not renegein g on the
things that are absolutely important to us.
Quickly, I want to talk about the KiwiSaver HomeStart package, which is making a
difference. That was launched on 15 April out of west Auckland —home of the west —
out at Henderson Baptist Church. Over the re, over 150 people came because they
wanted to hear about housing affordability. Here are the three things, the three changes
that are important: replacing the KiwiSaver FirstHome deposit subsidy with a grant,
doubling the support for buying a new home, a nd increasing the housing pricing limits.
So, for instance, for those who have been on the scheme for 3 years, it will be $3,000;
for 4 years, $6,000; and $8,000 if you have been on for 5 years. We will double that out
from $5,000 to $10,000 for a new home . We believe that is making a difference. The
second thing is that we are now able to enlarge the KiwiSaver FirstHome withdrawals,
and almost 95 percent of that can be used for your KiwiSaver HomeStart loans. I
think—and I know —that we are doing a great th ing to lead the country. We look
forward to the Budget tomorrow.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: What a difference 1 year
makes—what a difference. P ublic-private partnership s or  “PPP” used to mean
something different to the National Party. It was the holy grail of Government
intervention. Think Skycity gambling deals. Think Novopay streamlining. But they
were just a glimpse of a promised future holy land. When Government partners  with the
private sector, anything is possible —just ask the Inland Revenue Department. But do
not get me wrong. Labour is not averse to partnering with the private sector. We have
done it before and we will do it again. You just will not see the same kind of excited
dribbling every time the term is raised. But what a difference a year makes. In the
3472 General Debate 20 May 2015
National Party “PPP” has taken on quite a different meaning. Members around the
House have probably heard National Party backbenchers breathlessly whispering abo ut
“PPPs” in the corridors and in the select committees. The National Party’s “PPPs” are
on every backbencher’s list right now. Because of the National Party’s usual excitement
about privatising gains and socialising losses, I gave these hushed “PPP” whisp ers little
breach at first, but they persisted—they have persisted.
What is this new “PPP” the National backbenchers are so obsessed with? What is
this buzz around the beehive? I consider it must be some scandal, so I gave it some
thought. Could it be a new scandal around Pansy Wong about which we do not yet
know, after she used her parliamentary funding for her husband’s private business
trips—“TPPP” or travelling with partner for private profit, perhaps? It seemed unlikely.
Could it be a new scandal aro und Richard Worth —something about text messaging?
Rumours about piquant private pictures abound. Or was it a new revelation about Phil
Heatley and the publicly funded pinot payout? Still more rumours were doing the
rounds. “PPPs” were everywhere I looked —the National Party is full of gossip and
backstabbing these days; I can hear it coming from opposite now —but I easily
dismissed the next two rumours. That Aaron Gilmore was a pathetic piss -prick was
hardly news. Private purchases using public funds seemed t o fit the National Party
mantra, but Claudette “Credit Card” Hauiti did not seem to have the head to be at the
centre of so much recklessness, so I dismissed that straight away.

items.speaker: Then it dawned on me
items.text: maybe it was a reference to the Statler and Waldorf of the
National Party backbenchers. There they are over there. Perhaps their coup planning
was about to have its pay day. Maurice Williamson, the police-phoning politician, might
be involved. Maybe the “PPP” whispers related instead to the ascension of his be nch
mate, the original “PPP” —the private business Poo -Bah of Peking—but still, I was not
sure. What I found out, though, after extensive research, is this. Not everyone at home
will know it yet, but I can disclose to the public watching this debate today t hat when
the National Party members talk about “PPPs”, they are in fact talking about post -
ponytail polling. In the National caucus they have seen the “PPPs” —the post-ponytail
polls—and I can see it by looking across the House. They are lining up across the House
to replace John Key. His credibility has been dented once too often. The teflon is gone.
I hear them crying out that Judith would be better. It is coming from across the
House. Around the House they know that the internal squabbles eloquently capt ured in
every movement of Judith Collins’ nubile eyebrows is costing them. They know that the
public of New Zealand is losing trust in the empty promises of the Government, and
they recognise a Government that has lost touch, that looks tired, and that loo ks
arrogant. This is a Government riven by internal divisions —a Government that has
broken its economic promise of a surplus. It is a Government that is now hosing down
its promise to deliver wage rises to workers. It is a Government that is failing.
Now its focus has fallen on the internal “PPP”. What a difference 1 year makes.
Running into the last election, we saw a Government wading through a quagmire of
scandals. The dirty politics revelations showed that John Key’s office was intimately
involved in s mear campaigns and treachery. But John Key stood to one side and said:
“It has nothing to do with me. I couldn’t possibly know what was happening in my
office. I have no responsibility for it.” That is what he said then. He said that there is
nothing to se e here. But all of this has changed. Since the election, the dirty politics
revelations have proved themselves correct. The tactics—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have rung the bell , so the
member sits. I am calling Sarah Dowie.

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: It is an absolute pleasure to enter into
this debate and, frankly, it is quite joyous, because I am so p ositive about what this
20 May 2015 General Debate 3473
Government has achieved. I will pick up on Mr Chris Bishop’s point about Clare Curran
calling us glum. I am a very happy person because I am so positive about this
Government and the initiatives that we have put in place, the work t hat we are doing.
We are growing New Zealand’s economy, we are creating more jobs, we are supporting
our families—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Come on, paint that smile on, Sarah!

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: —it is beautiful, is it not? Wailing and gnashing of teeth, because
you love it. You love me speaking to you, especially about Invercargill. Brace
yourself—I am going to talk about Invercargill soon.
But first of all, I am going to talk more generally about what this wonderful
Government is doing for our  society. We are supporting our families and our children,
and, of course, with our housing policy, we are supporting the most vulnerable in our
society. If you look back to 2008, what did we have? A bleak future. It was so bleak; it
was almost like Mordor , looking into some dark, bleak clouds. The Labourites had
mismanaged the country’s finances, the economy was fragile —never mind going into a
global financial crisis. Saving for a rainy day, I know, is a foreign concept to that side of
the House. The econo my was in a desperate state, crime was at an all -time high,
schoolchildren were coming out of school with no qualifications, ill -equipped to enter
into life and to get a job, and unemployment was spiralling.
But now look at us. We are the envy of the OECD , the absolute envy. In fact,
Australians, our big brothers—our fiercest rivals—are putting their arms around us now
and saying “Hey, you’re kind of OK.” They want the Hon Bill English and the Rt Hon

items.speaker: John Key to stay. They say
items.text: “Help us out, please.” We ar e doing so well. Through
financial prudence, what have we done? We have grown this economy. We have created
194,000 jobs since 2011. And what is that doing? It is getting people into work, it is
creating wealth for our families, and they are doing well.
I want to talk especially about putting more money into our health budget —our free
doctors visits for children under 13 years of age. What a difference that makes. I am a
mother; I have got two. I have been a first -time mother. I know what it is like taking  a
child to the doctor and having to pay full fees. It is amazing that we can now take our
children to the doctor and get them seen to, making sure that they have a better quality
of life, and taking the burden off the parents to take them to the doctor to  get them seen
to.
But there is still work to be done. I mean, you hear from the Opposition benches that
we are out of ideas and that we are lazy. No, we are not. We are not resting on our
laurels—not at all. We are dynamic, but we also turn to pragmatic s olutions. We are not
afraid to look at our policies and tune them up and make changes for the betterment of
all New Zealanders.
One of those policies, of course, is our social housing policy. As the member for
Invercargill, I was thrilled when it was sele cted as one of the first regions for the
proposed transfer of Housing New Zealand  houses to community providers. It is a
sensible move. This is local issues being dealt with by local specialist knowledge,
providing local solutions for local people in need,  and that is better for the people in
need on the ground in Southland. We have about 360 tenants with medium to long term
support needs in Invercargill, and about 380 houses. This policy is about delivering
services that are key to the tenant —ensuring that social housing is fit for purpose and
the right design, size, and in the right place for those people in need. It is helping
tenants to independence and encouraging and developing a more diverse range of social
housing providers, which will breed innovation and responsiveness to those local tenant
needs. It does work.
3474 General Debate 20 May 2015
All we need to do is look at the UK model. For example, the Shepherds Bush
Housing Group in west London began with four flats in 1968 and now has over 5,000
properties under management. They offer a wide range of services, covering everything
from dealing with domestic violence, something that is really important—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Has the member read this before?

items.speaker: SARAH DOWIE
items.text: —absolutely, I have—employment assistance, budgeting advice,
health services, and more. Again, those are community focused, community solutions to
community issues. So I am thrilled, as the member for Invercargill, to endorse this
policy. I am thrilled with the way this Government is managing th is economy and
helping our people—all New Zealanders; families and children—to success.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: The truth is starting to catch up with
National Party members. It is s tarting to dawn on them that making outlandish claims
about good economic management means that the public actually expects good
economic management. As it all starts to come unravelled and it starts to become
abundantly clear that that is not what they ha ve been delivering, it is all catching up
with them. When Alfred Ngaro speaks about borrow -and-spend Governments, he does
not accept the irony that this Government has actually had the largest borrowing record
of any Government in New Zealand’s history.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: More than Muldoon’s?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Even more than Rob Muldoon’s. This Government has borrowed
more money than any other New Zealand Government.
He talked about borrow and spend in the context of a Labour Government. Well, let
us bring some facts into that as well. The Labour Government ran surpluses for 9
years—every year that it was in Government. In fact, not only did it not borrow but it
also paid back the debt it inherited from the previous National Government, an d it did
that whilst saving for the future through the New Zealand Superannuation Fund. Thank
you, Michael Cullen. As Bill English said, when he first became the finance Minister,
Michael Cullen and the last Labour Government saved for the rainy day that w as the
global financial crisis. This National Government squandered the whole lot. It
squandered it all. It has left the New Zealand economy completely in a basket case,
because the Government has wasted every opportunity that it has been given, and it is
all catching up with it.
The promises that John Key and the National Party made have not been kept, and it
is all catching up with them. What did John Key say? He said that it would be a
fundamental purpose of his Government to narrow the wage gap between us and
Australia, and to grow local wages in New Zealand. How has it done on that? The wage
gap with Australia is now bigger. It is bigger than it was when the National Party
became the Government. The wage gap has got bigger. That is a broken promise. He
said: “I am not interested in selling assets; I’m all about building assets.” That is what
John Key said. Has the Government kept its promise? No, it has not. Assets have been
sold off right, left, and centre.

items.speaker: This is a direct quote from John Key
items.text: “We woul d prefer that we were a more equal
society with less inequality.” And yet the inequality gap in New Zealand has continued
to get bigger and bigger under this National Government. That is broken promise No. —
I am up to about 4 now, I think, but we will keep going because there are plenty more.
“I expect high standards from my Ministers.” —that accounts for broken promises Nos.
5 to 87. “I expect high standards from my Ministers.” Broken promises Nos. 5 to 87 are
accounted for in that. But, of course, John Key cannot keep that promise when he will
not lead by example. He also said: “My style is to be open and transparent.” Well, that
is broken promises Nos. 87 to 163 from John Key, because he certainly has not been
open and transparent. We have had plenty of lea ks from the National Government —the
20 May 2015 General Debate 3475
things that it did not want us to know about —and it has been abundantly clear that open
and transparent he has not been.
Let us talk about some of the other promises: “National is not going to be raising
GST.” One of the first things it did was put GST up —another broken promise from the

items.speaker: National Government. Some of its more recent promises
items.text: free doctors’ visits for the
under-13s and free prescriptions for the under -13s—except not all of them; only about
90 percent of them . It did not tell the public about that. So there are still 10 percent of
kids who do not qualify for that.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: More than that.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: And probably more than that —another broken promise by the
National Government.
Then, of course, it promised to lift wages. It said that average wages will move from
$55,000 to $62,000 under the National Government. Bill English is already saying that
that is not going to happen. He is already admitting that that is yet another broken
promise by the National Party. I have lost count already. We are up to 200 and
something, I think, broken promises by the National Party. “Over the next 2 years we
expect to see about 150,000 jobs created.”, the National Party promised. Not one single
forecast from any economist or from Treasury has indicated that that is going to be
delivered.
And, of course, then we have got the big promise. It promised New Zealanders not
that it was going to deliver a surplus but that it had already done s o. It told New
Zealanders that it had already done so, and now not only is it not going to deliver a
surplus this year but there is also real doubt about whether it will deliver one next year.
Bill English was very cagey when asked about Treasury’s telling  him that it would have
to rely on a recovery in milk prices to deliver the surplus next year. He would not
answer questions because he knows that it cannot deliver—another broken promise.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 19 May.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Yet another day in paradise. Is it
not wonderful to be here having listened to the general debate and knowing that the
taxpayer dollar is so well spent listening to us debate? Some of it, of course, was errant
nonsense, but there you go. It is a democracy , and if those members want to spend their
time wasting it —great. We are back to Radio New Zealand and radio generally. We
have already established that every year we have been giving, as a Government, $25
million to Radio New Zealand.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: How much? How much?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: $25 million. That is a wonderful amount of money, is it
not? And that compares very favourably with all the other money that we give to radio
stations in New Zealand. That is because we give them not a cent —zero, zip, nothing.
So Radio New Zealand does really well. For that, of course, Radio New Zealand does
not have to go cap in hand to advertisers and does not have to justify itself, other than to
select committees. That is a price that  we pay as taxpayers, because, actually, Radio
New Zealand has a charter and it has to produce certain things that may not be
commercially efficient and probably would not survive the commercial rule being run
over it. But are we not lucky that we live in a society where not only do we have Radio
New Zealand but we have so much more choice? If we do not want to hear the dulcet
3476 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
tones of Checkpoint, we can, in fact, listen instead to that fabulous person on Newstalk
ZB, Larry Williams, or we could listen inst ead in the morning to the fabulous Paul
Henry, someone whom I listen to quite a lot now, and I know that my friend Annette
King does too. That is the sort of thing. We have choice. Is that not wonderful?
But I would also say that we need to be very aware —and I am sure that the people in
the industry are —that there are very interesting times ahead for the industry. As we
have been hearing in the debate, so much in terms of technological change is happening.
It is so fast. Multimedia solutions are now being trialled and used, and we can see that
with the Radio Live Paul Henry show. We can also see it with others as well. I think
that is one of the things. We are going to see a lot of consolidation in the industry and a
lot of new and innovative ways of doing things. Radio New Zealand is well placed, and
I am really pleased with the progress it has made in the last 6 and a bit years.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call I understand is a s plit
call. Gareth Hughes—5 minutes.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora , Mr Assistant Speaker . Ngā mihi nui ki a
koutou. Kia ora. Following on from the contribution by Ms Collins, I am sure that there
are a few National Cabinet Ministers who would like to hear the end of those dulcet
tones on Checkpoint, given what we have seen over the years.
I want to touch on a theme. This is my third term of Parliament, and something I
have noticed is that, inexorably, when the Clerk reads out the new legislation being
introduced at the beginning of Parliament, the numbers are massively down. It has been
an awfully long time since we have seen any new ideas, any new legislation, and here is
a classic example. The Radio N ew Zealand Amendment Bill is something that has been
referred from the review of a committee from 2006 and it did not get around to being
issued to a select committee until 2009, and here is the Government, with nothing else
pressing on the legislative age nda, finally getting around to this bill, 6 years later. It is
finally getting around to looking at this bill. That tells you a few things.
If public broadcasting was a priority, this bill could have been knocked off many,
many years ago. It is an uncontr oversial bill. This bill simply enshrines in statute the
charter for Radio New Zealand, which is something that all parties in this Parliament
agree on. It also says something about the Government’s priorities, because the only
public broadcasting change, except for a massive funding freeze to the sector, is, in fact,
an uncontroversial bill doing something that should have come about in the mid -2000s.
It is setting up, finally, the charter for Radio New Zealand.
It is not controversial. We are talking abo ut a charter that talks about Radio New
Zealand being “independent and commercial -free”—which it is at the moment —and
having freedom of thought and expression, fostering a sense of national identity,
providing independent, freely accessible news, and enric hing our broadcasting
environment. It is all good stuff, which none of the 165 submissions could be opposed
to. But I do want to talk about something Ms Collins said. In her contribution, she
talked about nothing being available for other broadcasters, whi ch highlighted,
somehow, the Government’s exceedingly high generosity in funding public
broadcasting—or Radio New Zealand —in New Zealand. One word: it is MediaWorks.
We saw a fantastically huge bailout for MediaWorks and its stable of commercial radio
stations from this Government.
Let us look at the facts. In the last year of the previous Labour Government, KPMG
produced a report saying that Radio New Zealand was suffering from a funding shortfall
in 2007. It recommended a $6.7 million urgent reinjection.  What have we seen since
then, since the National Government was elected in 2008? Zero. It has seen an absolute
funding freeze across that period, which has been an effective funding cut to the only
public broadcaster in this country —that is, Radio New Zea land. Television One  and
20 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3477
TV2, of course, are not public broadcasters. Māori Television serves a different
service—an important service. We have seen a 9 percent funding cut in real terms.
This is something that needs to be addressed because it is importan t for all those
reasons that we are passing into law now to foster that sense of national identity —to
have that freely available, independent news and to hear those Kiwi voices. I would not
call the $25 million exceedingly generous. This is half, on a per capita basis, of what the
Australians fund for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation and a third what the Brits
do when it comes to the BBC. We are a laggard when it comes to public broadcasting.

items.speaker: So I challenge the Government
items.text: if it is serious, it shoul d put its money where its
mouth is tomorrow. This is part of the foundation for a strong civic society, a
foundation for our democracy. That is why the Greens are supporting public
broadcasting and it is why we need a public television broadcaster. Really,  the question
is for the Government to put its money where its mouth is.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Chris Hipkins—5 minutes.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I am very happy to take a call on the
Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill. My last contribution was so good. I am very
happy to take a call on this bill. My cold is catching up with me, so you will have to
forgive me if my voice is not perhaps quite as booming as it was in my last contribution.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Have a glass of water.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I have had lots of water, so I will be fine. I am very strongly in
favour of this bill, and it is good to see that it is finally going to progress through the
House. I think it is disappointing that it has taken such a long period of time to get it
through the House. Of course, the Radio New Zealand Act requires that the Radio New
Zealand charter is reviewed every 5 years. So the fact that this is based on a review that
happened nearly 10 years ago means that we are probably a couple of reviews behind,
and hopefully there will be further amendments required in due course.
I think one of the things that we have to keep in mind is that technological change is
happening really rapidly in this area. Just reading through the charter that is attached to
this bill, it is important to note the really strong emphasis that is placed on broadcasting
within that. And yet the lines between broadcasting and other forms of technology are
becoming so blurred now that there will inevitably need to be further change and further
evolution in this area. Actually, Radio New Zealand, in my strong view, should not
necessarily be about public, non -commercial broadcast content but public non -
commercial content and making sure that that is widely available, and that will be
through a variety of different mediums, including online content. Radio New Zealand is
increasingly doing more work in that area, and I think that that is a very welcome thing.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Programmes about throats?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: P rogrammes about colds, sore throats, and all those sorts of
things would be useful.
I think that Judith Collins was wrong when she said that commercial broadcasters in
New Zealand do not get one cent of Government subsidy. That is not true. As Gareth
Hughes has just pointed out, MediaWorks has done pretty well out of the current
Government. And she mentioned a few high -profile broadcasters in her contribution,
including Paul Henry, Mike Hosking, and others. I want to say that I think that is
absolutely fine. I think there is a legitimate place in the New Zealand media for those
voices just as there is a legitimate place for the John Campbells and others.
I think that really what we should be aiming for in New Zealand is a wide diversity
of views and opinio ns within the New Zealand media. But the niche, if you like, that
Radio New Zealand fills within that is that it can do more in -depth fact checking, more
in-depth investigative journalism, which the commercial broadcasters and commercial
media outlets are struggling to do, not because they do not want to do it, not because the
3478 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
journalists working for those organisations are not very, very good journalists —they
are—but simply because they are far more resource constrained. If the commercial
media environment  cannot fund that level of investigative journalism, inquiry, and
diverse debate, then we do need as a society to ensure that it is publicly available in
some other form. Radio New Zealand, in the radio sphere, has certainly been a bastion
of that.
I have heard people on the other side of the House refer to Radio New Zealand as a
bastion of left -wing propaganda. Radio New Zealand deals with facts, and it is one of
the organisations that do a lot of fact checking. If dealing in facts makes it left wing,
then, yes, I guess it will have to wear that particular label, but I do not believe that it has
any bias politically. I think what it does do—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I do not believe that Radio New Zealand is polit ically biased at
all. I think it strives very, very hard not to be politically biased, but there are some
journalists out there who make no bones about their political bias, and that is fine if they
are open and upfront about it. I think Radio New Zealand tries very carefully to not do
that, as the State broadcaster. I think we have a lot less bias in Radio New Zealand, for
example, than we do in Television New Zealand, where Mike Hosking’s editorials are
very biased. But he is upfront about that, and that is OK, but I think there is a need to
balance that by ensuring that an equally compelling alternative view is put forward, and
I do not think Television New Zealand does that very well. I think it lets New Zealand
down as the nation’s television broadcaste r in not providing that diversity, something I
know that Radio New Zealand strives very, very hard to provide.
I am very supportive of this bill. I am also very supportive of the Government taking
the foot off Radio New Zealand’s throat in terms of the fu nding constraints it has been
under. Overall, this is a good piece of legislation.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: It is a pleasure to take a call on this important bill. I
think members will agree that ther e is consensus across the House that the bill is
sensible. Members opposite have, I think, fairly raised some concern about the length of
time it has taken to pass this bill. Of course, the bill was first introduced, I think, in
2009. Yes, indeed; its firs t reading was on 4 June, and it was referred to the Commerce
Committee.
I think that members opposite cry crocodile tears when it comes to complaints about
the length of time it takes to pass bills. Members in general may be interested to learn
the names of a number of bills that were on the Order Paper in 2008 when National took
office. We had, of course, the Education (Establishment of Universities) Amendment
Bill. It was first introduced in 2006. There was no progress under Labour. We had the
Oaths Modernisation Bill and the Rail Network Bill, and there was a real doozy, the
Conservation (Protection of Trout as a Non -commercial Species) Amendment Bill. It
was first introduced in 1998 under the last National Government, and it made no
progress in 9 years under the Labour Government

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: Nine long years.

items.speaker: CHRIS BISHOP
items.text: Nine long years —thank you very much, Mr Hudson. So I think
that those members cry crocodile tears about it. But regardless of the time it has taken to
get to this point, it is an important bill that we are progressing.
I also want to make a few points in rebuttal to Clare Curran’s speech last night. I
was—privileged is slightly the wrong word. I was present in the Chamber to hear her
contribution to the de bate last night. There were a few odd remarks that I want to pick
up on in rebuttal. The first thing is to point out that the major thrust of some of the
criticism in the first part of her speech seems to be based on a speech that Tony Ryall
gave in 1993, presumably as a Government backbencher, about Radio New Zealand,
20 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3479
and one quote he had given in 1993. It seems to be drawing a slightly long bow to
criticise current Government policy in 2015 based on a comment from a member, who
is actually no longer a mem ber of Parliament, when he was a Government backbencher
in the previous National Government. So I think that Clare clearly was struggling with
her material if she had to go right back in the archives to 1993. I suggest to the Labour
Party research unit, wh ich is clearly listening to this contribution to the debate, that it
needs to do its homework better.
The second thing I want to mention about Ms Curran’s contribution is her comments
about the Television New Zealand charter. The Labour Party is very prou d of the famed
Television New Zealand (TVNZ) charter. The reality is that the TVNZ charter was a
debacle. TVNZ turned up at the Commerce Committee in 2007, and, in response to a
question about its commitment to Māori broadcasting, said that the Police Ten 7 show
was an example of its commitment to Māori broadcasting —Police Ten 7. That is how it
got away with fulfilling its mandate under the charter. It got given free money by Steve
Maharey and the other Min isters of Broadcasting under Labour to basically reclassify
existing commercial programmes like Police Ten 7  and say that that  was its
commitment to public service broadcasting.
Actually, the National Government took an enlightened policy to the 2008 election.
We said that rather than give TVNZ $15 million of free money, let us unshackle it from
its dual mandate, let us let it do what it wants to do anyway—be commercial—and let
us give that $15 million to New Zealand On Air, which will be medium -neutral as to
where that money g oes. In other words, New Zealand On Air  would select the
programmes. A programme could be on TV3, it could be on TVNZ, or it could be on a
variety of other platforms . I ncreasingly in the modern world , it is actually through
digital, and New Zealand On Air has now got a digital media fund, which is a world
first. It was an enlightened policy , and we think it has actually made for much better
delivery. It has unshackled TVNZ from that mandate.
The other mistake Clare Curran made was to say that National ha s made TVNZ
commercial. Actually, that was done by the fourth Labour Government in 1989 when it
deregulated the broadcasting sector and allowed TV3 to enter the market. In fact, you
could arguably say that TVNZ has always been commercial because only 1 year after
the inception of television in New Zealand in the 1960s, we had ads on television. Clare
Curran suggested in a tweet last night that one of the problems with television in New
Zealand is that we ha ve ads during prime time —ads during prime time . So th e Labour
Party broadcasting policy at the next election is going to be very interesting. It will be
interesting to see the Labour Party’s  commitment to the abolition of advertisements on
TVNZ during prime time. That will be a slightly odd policy , but it will be in keeping
with its general modus operandi when it comes to policies , which is that it has got no
idea how to pay for things and it has  no idea about the actual policies it is  trying to
pursue. So we are looking forward to that broadcasting policy.
This is an important bill. Radio New Zealand make s an important contribution to the
life of this nation. It is something that I and many New Zealanders listen to.  In 2014
Radio New Zealand’s live cumulative audience was 484,000. Increasingly, it is moving
into the online space. In 2013 -14 there were 3.5 million podcasts downloaded. I have
got many friends around the world, and I know that many of them like to download the
Radio New Zealand podcasts of Morning Report , Nine to Noon , and Checkpoint and
listen to them when they wake up in the morning in the United Kingdom or America or
wherever they are, and keep up with the news from New Zealand, because it is a very
good source of information and the podcasts are well produced.
Increasingly, the Wireless, whi ch is the youth -oriented website that Radio New
Zealand has set up, has grown in popularity , as well. I have had a couple of friends who
3480 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
have worked for that website, and it does produce good content. One of the things
people used to talk about back in the  1990s was a youth radio network —that New
Zealand needed a triple j, like Australia has, which would be an advertisement -free
radio station. I know that Neil Finn, the musician, and a few other people were very,
very keen on a youth radio network.
Actually, to be fair, I used to be an advocate for a youth radio network, as well. I was
once a youth parliamentarian, and I advocated for a youth radio network in my question,
in the Youth Parliament ’s question time, to the Minister of Broadcasting, Maria n
Hobbs. Despite the fact that it was apparently Labour Government policy at the time,
she gave me the brush-off.
People used to talk about having a youth radio network , but I think that now, people
would generally agree that the way technology has evolve d, for the Government to fund
a dedicated commercial youth radio frequency would probably be a retrograde step , and
that, actually, the way of the future is something like the Wireless website, something
like the youth-oriented website that is associated with Radio New Zealand. Actually, the
Wireless was a finalist in the category of best site in the Canon Media Awards of 2014,
and Radio New Zealand continues to do well at the New Zealand Radio Awards, as
well. That is no surprise, because, as I said before , it fulfils an important role in the
cultural and social life of this nation.
With that in mind, it is important that we amend the Radio New Zealand Act 1995
because we need to update the Act and make it clear that the revised charter text makes
for a st ronger statement about its role as the public broadcaster  and makes sure it is
more accessible to the general public. There is also an update requirement for a 5-yearly
charter review.
This is an important bill. Radio New Zealand continues to play an impo rtant role in
the cultural and social life of this nation. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: Tēnā rā koe e te Māngai o te
Whare. I a mātou e kōrero an a mō tēnei mea te reo irirangi, e hiahia ana ahau ki te tū ki
te mihi atu ki tērā o ngā whānau kei roto i a Mangamuka. I tērā Mane kua kaingatia tō
rātou teihana irirangi e te ahi. Arā, ko tērā teihana reo irirangi, ko Tautoko FM. I te
Mane kua pahure ake nei, i ahau e haere ana ki te wāhi rererangi o Kerikeri, ka pahure
ahau i taua teihana. Kīhai i pau te ono hāora i muri atu kua kāpurangia e te ahi. Nā reira,
ka tuku atu ahau i ōku mihimihi ki tērā whānau nā rātou i whakapau i ō rātou kaha ki te
hāpai i Te Reo Māori, i ngā take Māori, ki a Cyril Chapman mā, ngā mihi aroha atu ki a
rātou.
[Thank you indeed, Mr Speaker. While we are speaking about this radio thing, I want
to rise and acknowledge one of the families living in Mangamuka. Last Monday their
radio station, Tautoko FM, was consumed by fire. As I was travelling to the aerodrome
of Kerikeri this Monday just gone I went past that station. Not quite 6 hours afterwards
and fire razed it. So I want to extend my sympathies to that family who worked hard t o
elevate the Māori language and Māori matters, to Cyril Chapman and them, loving
concerns to them.]
Just while we are speaking about the Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill, I want to
acknowledge Mangamuka and the whanau who, on Monday, had their iwi radio station
burnt to the ground. On Monday afternoon I passed over Mangamuka Bridge, and Radio
Tautoko was on the left. It was not some 6 hours later that a fire razed the whole station
to the ground. I just want to extend my thoughts to the whanau there at Tautoko FM—in
particular, to Cyril Chapman, a man who has been involved in running that station  for a
number of decades, and I believe that they have made the commitment to have their
station up and running again as soon as possible. I think it is important just to
20 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3481
acknowledge Tautoko FM and the whanau there. For a number of decades, Mangamuka
has done such a great job in uplifting our Reo and our culture.
In 1996 Christopher Phillips, an American, lamented the fact that a nytime he turned
on the media, he was dissatisfied with the way people engaged in supposed intellectual
discourse. More often than not, he said, he heard browbeating and one -upmanship.
There was intellectual snootiness. People were using knowledge as a clo ak and shield,
rather than using it to diffuse enlightenment. And he said that democracy hinges on an
enlightened citizenry. These days the content of many commercially driven radio
stations tends to be more infotainment than information. They tend to be g oing for the
30-second sound bite, and in some cases it is not even a 30 -second sound bite; it is a 3
to 5 -second sound bite. Citizens of New Zealand are becoming deprived of real,
meaningful broadcasting, where opinions and information are disseminated an d where
people can hear people, politicians, sportspeople, and other members of the community
putting forward their points of view. That is why this bill, through which the Radio New
Zealand charter is going to be amended, is a great bill.
I would like to refer to a couple of points in new section 8 of the Charter, the
“Purpose”, in particular the point that says: “Freedom of thought and expression are
foundations of democratic society and the public radio company as a public service
broadcaster plays an es sential role in exercising these freedoms.” Another point in the
“Purpose” says: “The public radio company provides reliable, independent, and freely
accessible news and information.” Those purposes I can only commend. The charter’s
“Delivery” says: “In achieving its purpose, the public radio company must endeavour to
provide services of the highest quality which —(b) inform, entertain, and enlighten the
people of New Zealand:”, and that endorses the quotation from Christopher Phillips in
1996. It also says,  under the “Delivery”, that Radio New Zealand needs to “(d) foster
critical thought, and informed and wide -ranging debate:” We are often bereft of wide -
ranging debate in broadcasting. We have heard that a number of people whose opinions
are often politically clouded are just out there, and we do not actually get to hear wide -
ranging debate; we just get to hear certain reporters’ jaundiced views of the world.
I would just like to go to the first reading of this bill and throw a bouquet to Jonathan
Young. I like what he had to say. He said: “this charter not only speaks to the necessity
of those with political or commercial interests not exerting their influence in appropriate
ways, but also, just as important, places on broadcasters the serious responsibility  to
maintain their editorial independence and integrity in the execution of their
responsibilities and duties.” He also said: “Radio New Zealand does not make the news,
but reports it; does not create opinions, but accurately reflects the views and opinion s of
New Zealanders in a legitimate and appropriate way.” But I would just like to contrast
that with the then - Minister of Broadcasting, the Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman, and his
silly contribution, which said: “This bill languished under the last administrat ion,”. It is
funny how your words can come back to haunt you, because if this bill languished, in
his opinion, under the previous Labour administration, then what do we call 7 years’
sitting on the Order Paper gathering dust if that is not languishing? He said: “whereas
this Government” —his Government —“is committed to fulfilling its legislative
responsibilities.”
This makes it sound like there was a sense of urgency around this bill. We know that
after 7 years, that was definitely not the case. “This should  have been done, but the
previous Government just never got around to doing it. This is an unfair situation for
Radio New Zealand,”—well, if it was unfair 7 years ago, imagine what the situation is
like for Radio New Zealand right now. I mean, this charter  was meant to be amended
every 5 years. It was meant to be amended in around 2010. It has now been 10 years
since it was amended, and this is a Government that is saying it is doing all it can. The
3482 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
previous Minister of Broadcasting —this is, again, the Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman—said
the previous Labour Minister of Broadcasting had other priorities. Well, the Minister of
Broadcasting in the last Labour Government probably did have other priorities. He was
a hard-working Minister.
“It is highly desirable that t he related legislative process be concluded as soon as
possible”. Well, let me tell you, if 7 years is this Government’s idea of “as soon as
possible”, then we wonder whether the Budget surplus is also going to come to fruition
as soon as possible, or, in terms of this bill, go through the rest of the stages —the
Committee stage and the third reading. Are we just going to have to wait until
tomorrow? As my colleague Phil Twyford says, every time this Government says that it
is going to do something, it is al ways: “We’re on the cusp. We’re on the cusp of
something great.” Well, maybe we are just on the cusp of this bill being passed. “It is
highly desirable that the related legislative process be concluded as soon as possible to
ensure that Radio New Zealand c an operate with an up -to-date and clear public service
mandate.”
Another member who is a Minister now, Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, in a similar vein said:
“This bill is an example of the Labour Party resting on its laurels and not getting
legislation through this House. It is a brave move to take on this legislation and move it
quickly through the House.” Seven years, in anybody’s opinion, is not moving quickly.
We have concerns about the budget freeze for Radio New Zealand, because the
honourable Minister back i n 2009 had all these plans and everything was going to
happen. He wanted to do this; he wanted to do that. And then the Government froze the
budget, which we know, through inflation and over time, is essentially a budget cut for
Radio New Zealand. We hope that in tomorrow’s Budget, after one more sleep, we will
find out that Radio New Zealand is actually going to get some more money in its coffers
so that it can fulfil its charter. Kia ora.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Thank you for allowing me to speak
on the second reading of the Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill. It is a well -
established fact that Radio New Zealand delivers quality content to its listeners. I am a
big fan of radio, and normally whenever I am travelling I prefer to listen to the radio
rather than to any other media. The technology is changing, but, still, I am a big fan of
radio. The four radio stations that I normally switch between are: Radio New Zealand,
Newstalk ZB, BBC, and Radio Tarana. When I came to New Zealand in 2001, Radio
Tarana was the only Indian radio channel, available for a few hours in the day, which
kept us connected to our homeland. I appreciate that, having gone from strength to
strength, Radio Tarana is now a 24 -hour Indian radio channel, and it has a very wide
audience. I congratulate that team.
Radio New Zealand is one of those stations that deliver an unbiased viewpoint, and I
normally listen to this radio station from time to time. It ha s got a long history. It was
established as a public broadcaster in 1925, and at that time the funding was given
through the radio licences —25 shillings out of each licence issue d at that time. Then it
continued and, as the demand grew, the company was est ablished in 1931 when the
Government appointed the New Zealand Broadcasting Board. It was dependent upon
the licence fee. In 1936 the Government established the New Zealand Broadcasting
Service as a Government department, which soon added fully commercial radio stations
also. After the war, the New Zealand Broadcasting Service’s Government department
status was ended in 1962, and the Government established the New Zealand
Broadcasting Corporation. During the next 30 years the system was changed numerous
times, but public, non-commercial radio service remained its integral part.
Given the changing technology, there are some other facts that are very relevant
today that I would like to share with this House. In 2014 Radio New Zealand’s live
20 May 2015 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 3483
accumulative audience for its National and Concert audience was 484,000. In 2013 -14
3.5 million podcasts were downloaded. In 2013 -14 Radio New Zealand’s homepage
reached 21 million viewings. In 2014 unique users of the website grew by over 50
percent. In 2013, again, on a re gular basis Radio New Zealand’s mobile app grew by
almost 62 percent. I am sharing this with the House because the technology is changing.
Nowadays youngsters prefer using different media from the normal radio. I inherited
this habit of listening to the ra dio from my father, who used to listen to the radio all the
time. At that time there were no satellite televisions and there was not much
broadcasting on television. I remember that the last news broadcast used to be at 12
o’clock, midnight. He used to lis ten to that before going to bed. I inherited that habit of
listening to the radio from him.
It is because of the quality of its programmes that Radio New Zealand remains the
preferred radio station. Radio New Zealand provides content that some of the priva te
broadcasters may not be able to do due to their commercial realities. In contrast, Radio
New Zealand delivers its content independently. By way of this bill, we want to ensure
that Radio New Zealand continues to deliver quality, unbiased content to its listeners.
Furthermore, by way of legislation, we also want to ensure that new media and
technologies that Radio New Zealand intends to implement are also allowed to deliver
quality and unbiased programmes.
Some of the previous speakers mentioned that the budget has been frozen and no
additional money has been given to Radio New Zealand. But I want to say that I
appreciate the Radio New Zealand team, the technicians, and the leadership for using
what they are given. They manage their programmes very well. I  remember at one of
the briefings that we had from Radio New Zealand at the Commerce Committee, they
mentioned that the technology that has been developed at Radio New Zealand helped
them to go further and use that technology within the budget so that they  can improve
the quality of the programmes.
This, once again, shows the National -led Government’s commitment to delivering
better public services. I take this opportunity to congratulate the honourable Minister
Amy Adams on taking the initiative of progres sing this bill. We have time and again
shown how serious we are towards our commitment to improving public services in all
areas, big or small.
The current legislation is focused towards simplifying Radio New Zealand’s charter.
It makes a strong statement on the purpose of Radio New Zealand and how its charter
will deliver for the benefit of all New Zealanders. The charter was prepared after public
consultation and was well deliberated on by the select committee. The committee
received over 165 submissions.  The committee also considered the existing charter and
the legislation. After thorough analysis of all aspects, the bill we are debating today was
introduced to the House in 2009. All this work has meant that we have legislation that
ensures futuristic thinking and the best results for the public of New Zealand.
Based on the review, we now have a clause that caters to the new and emerging
technologies in the media space. The world of technology is ever -evolving, and now
everywhere we see more and new media  in use. The other day while watching the New
Zealand - South Africa Cricket World Cup semi -final, I saw a drone flying over Eden
Park, covering the entire match from an eagle’s -eye view. We thought that drones were
limited only to defence technology —in this case, it was for New Zealand radio. This
clause will ensure that the broadcaster takes advantage of the most effective means of
delivery and provides the best user experience.
Furthermore, the charter recognises that New Zealand is now a very multicultu ral
society. Keeping this in mind, the charter states that the diverse forms of cultural
programming, including but not limited to drama, comedy, literature, and the
3484 Radio New Zealand Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
performing arts, need to form an essential part of Radio New Zealand’s programming. I
remember when I once asked the Radio New Zealand officials what their thoughts were
about the diverse communities and the diaspora of New Zealand. They mentioned that
they are planning to have in the near future, as communities are getting diverse,
traditional programmes available, like in Hindi, Mandarin, and Cantonese. I hope the
day is not far away when the technology will allow Radio New Zealand to have such
programmes to be broadcast from its platforms.
Of course, the modern -day era requires that there be a balance between providing
social content and the ability of the organisation to earn commercial revenue from its
operations. Amongst its various social obligations, Radio New Zealand remains our go -
to station in case of any civil defence emergencies. The  legislation permits Radio New
Zealand to be able to market its products and services such as broadcasting and media
services.
Bill read a second time.

sections.heading: Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill

items.text: Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.role: Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage
items.text: I move, That
the Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill be now read a second time . Kua
hinga te tōtara o Te Wao -Nui-a-Tāne. Ka tangi a Ngāti Hine, ka tangi te motu. Ko te
poutokomanawa o Te Reo kua wahangū. A tree has fallen in the great forest of Tāne.
Ngāti Hine mourns and the nation mourns with them. A mainstay of the Māori language
has been silenced. I begin by acknowled ging the passing of Ērima Hēnare, the widely
respected and beloved Ngāti Hine leader, who, among his many roles, was a member of
the Waitangi National Trust board, and who made an excellent contribution to that
board.
This bill amends the Waitangi National Trust Board Act 1932. Its principal purpose
is to make changes to the membership of the trust board and to provide fixed terms of
appointment for board members. In doing so, it will provide a new framework for the
ongoing relationship between the Government and the board. The responsibility of
caring for the birthplace of our nation, the place where the Treaty of Waitangi was first
signed, is a significant task. It is one that the Waitangi National Trust Board has
discharged since the Waitangi estate was gifted to the nation in 1932 by Lord and Lady
Bledisloe.
The Waitangi National Trust Board’s aspirations extend beyond maintaining the
Treaty House and its grounds, to making sure New Zealanders can learn about their
history and understand the historical and contemporary role of the Treaty of Waitangi.
The board is doing this partly through a major development programme to build a new
museum and education centre at the Treaty grounds. Work on the new museum is
progressing well, and when completed, hopefully by Waitangi Day next year, it will
further enrich the visitor experience and enable the unique story of the development of
our nation to be told in a more detailed and accessible way.
I am sure that such developments  would have been very much approved of by Lord
and Lady Bledisloe, whose gift of the Treaty grounds and its surrounding estate to New
Zealanders has enabled the constitutional and heritage values embodied in the site to be
shared with current and future ge nerations. In this spirit, it is essential that the
organisation responsible for one of our most significant historical sites has a suitable
governance structure to support its aims and aspirations for the future while also staying
true to the original intent of the board when it was formed.
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3485
The purpose of the Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill is to create a
clear separation between the Government and the board while also setting up a new
framework for positive relations between the board and th e Crown. This bill is
deliberately narrow in its focus. It specifically removes the Governor -General, the
Prime Minister, and two Government Ministers from ex officio positions on the board.
It addresses the real or perceived potential conflict that could arise under the current
structure by virtue of such ex officio members being on the board while also having a
constitutional role.
Clause 6 inserts new section 4A, which establishes a statutory Crown representatives
group, comprising the Prime Minister, t he Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, and
the Minister for Māori Development. This group will provide a clear link between the
board and the Government and will encourage open and positive dialogue. The bill
allows for the Governor -General to be an h onorary patron of the Waitangi National
Trust, should he or she so choose. The bill also provides for two members of Parliament
to be appointed to the board. New section 4B, in clause 6, requires one new full board
member to be nominated by the Prime Minis ter and one to be nominated by the Leader
of the Opposition. Creating these two new positions ensures ongoing Government and
parliamentary input into the work of the board and a direct link to the elected
representatives of New Zealand.
The bill restricts the length of time a board member can serve. It creates 3 -year terms
for most board members, who will then be eligible to serve for up to three terms —that
is, 9 years in total. The two members of Parliament being added to the board will serve
for the dura tion of the parliamentary term in which they are appointed, unless they
become Ministers or leave Parliament first.
The Māori Affairs Committee received three written submissions. The committee has
recommended an amendment to the bill to increase the repr esentation of Māori families
on the board so that each of the four families currently represented on the board would
have its own member. At present there is only one representative for four Māori
families. The committee recommended this amendment in respo nse to a submission
from one of the families. The amendment has been included in the bill as clause 3A,
which amends section 2 of the Act.
In recent years the board has standardised appointment processes for new board
members. It has taken steps to make these appointments transparent, through advertising
and disseminating widely the call for nominations. I would expect that the appointment
of additional Māori family representatives to be in accordance with this rigorous
selection process.
Although I under stand the committee’s reasons for recommending the amendment
concerning representation of Māori families, it raises questions about whether the
current basis of representation on the board should be reconsidered more broadly. I am
therefore initiating a wi der review of the Waitangi National Trust, with the aim of
ensuring the best possible governance and management of the Waitangi estate.
The review will also respond to issues raised by the board in its submission on the
bill. Although supporting the intent of the bill, the board asked for changes to its powers
and to penalties for offences and by -law breaches under the Act. These matters are
outside the narrow focus of the current bill but will be considered as part of the wider
review. Generally speaking,  it is my intention that the review will look at the role,
composition, and powers of the board; the appointment process and criteria for board
members; how best to provide for iwi Māori involvement in the governance of the trust;
offences and by-laws on the Waitangi estate; and the financial sustainability of the trust.
By establishing a framework for continued positive relationships between the board and
3486 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
the Government, I believe the bill will create the necessary conditions for a wider
review of the trust to take place.
I wish to thank the chair and members of the Māori Affairs Committee for
consideration of submissions during the select committee process. I am pleased to note
that there is broad, cross -party support for the bill, and I am confident that the bill will
provide for a positive and cooperative relationship between the Government and the
board. I look forward to progressing the bill through the House.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: E tika ana me tāpiri taku
mihi ki tērā rangatira rongonui, tērā tōtara a Ērima, nō reira, e te rangatira moe mai, moe
mai rā.
[It is fitting that I add my tribute to that well -known leader and tōtara, Ērima; so to
you, revered one, sleep, rest there.]
I would like to also support the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage’s
acknowledgment and recognition of the former board member the late Ērima Hēnare
and his contribution not only to the Waitangi National Trust Board but also  in other
fields as a contribution to New Zealand’s history. Nō reira e te rangatira, e kore e mutu
ngā mihi ki a koe [Consequently, my tributes to you, esteemed one, will never end].
The Minister has covered much of the consideration of the Māori Affairs Committee,
but I thought it would be useful to share some of the considerations of the select
committee when we made the changes that were referred to. Much of the history with
regard to the gift of lands and the establishment of the trust board was leaned  upon to
consider the submission request, certainly of Arapeta Hamilton, and the
recommendation that thought be given to equity of representation of family members. I
want to draw the attention of the House to Vernon Reed’s history and recollection of the
Bledisloe gift because that is the basis upon which we thought it would be only fair to
consider the addition of Māori family members of those stated.
For those who are history buffs, I would call on your own thoughts surrounding the
way in which members were added to this particular board. Indeed, in a brief way,
Henry Williams and Tāmati Waka Nene were the first named representatives on this
board, and then Edward Gibbon Wakefield was added, and then that fell to identified
representatives Hone Heke, Mai hi Kāwiti, and Pōmare to be included. What was not
factored into the process was that for the four Māori whānau, one representative actually
had to give voice to those interests, whereas for the other whānau, each family member
was able to have a represent ative of their own. I have heard the Minister say that a
transparent process should occur for the selection of those members, and I am sure that
the current convention of those four Māori whānau to select their representation has
some process to it. Far be  it from me to try to articulate that, but the point should be
made that there would be —certainly within those family members —an agreed way to
be able to select their particular member.
Of more interest and note, I think, in our deliberations was the subm ission from the
board. The board appeared keen in its submission to ensure that the future thinking
about the way in which the Waitangi National Trust Board conducts its business and
affairs were within the frame of modernising the scope and power. So we w elcome—
certainly as a select committee —the indication from the Minister that there will be a
review. In fact, when the Minister appeared before the select committee to answer some
of the questions that we had in our own minds around clarity for the review,  we were
heartened to know that a broad review would take place, that there would be
consultation with the board, and that it would be in quite a defined time frame, although
no reference was made to urgency on the legislative timetable. We know how these
things work, Minister. So that was a very comforting kind of response. However, that
said, we did continue to believe that it was within the scope of the bill to include
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3487
representation of the Māori members, and that is how we have reported back on this
particular bill.
We also believe that some of the powers that were identified by the board’s
submission were useful to raise in this House as well. The board wanted practical
things: powers to manage and protect the trust’s assets into the future. That would  be a
part of the modernisation process. It stated that it was important to consider the scope of
the trust to be able to borrow, to remove some of the lease restrictions that were on it,
and to include further provisions relating to the management and uti lisation of the
forestry block in the Waitangi endowment land. For my part, in reading the submission
and trying to understand the current operating limitations, perhaps, of the board, I
thought that these were all very genuine, useful suggestions and they could be picked up
in the review that the Minister has committed to.
One of the things that the board raised in its submission was the ability to increase
penalties for offences and breaches of by -laws. I did not, kind of, pursue a question line
along this frame, but it seemed to me that if it had asked for it, it might wel l be
something to consider going forward.
We did ask the question, as we considered the two particular land blocks that are
associated with the trust —firstly, the forestry block and then the endowment block —as
to whether any of these two pockets of land w ere subject to Treaty settlements. In
relation to the forestry block, we were informed —and officials had this contained in
their advice—that this is solely private land and it would not be subject to settlement.
However, there is a potential for the endowm ent block being subject to settlement
because it is actually owned by the Crown.
Can I say for my part, given that the original Bledisloe gift was for the benefit of
New Zealand, the Bledisloes have done our country a great service to ensure that the
document that defines our country, the Treaty of Waitangi, and the place for where
those celebrations can occur should be something that we can continue to support in the
spirit of what the Treaty represents for this country. It would be a sad day if the trans fer
of the endowment was handled in a transactional manner that did not take account of the
significance of Waitangi as the place where our founding document was signed. So I
place that on the table. Maybe it is something that will be debated at some later time and
in another type of debate.
Can I say that we are really privileged at the Māori Affairs Committee to have the
kinds of conversations and debates that require us to pursue with some diligence the
issues that would in other select committees divid e a committee —divide the views of
committee members on a number of things —but that did not happen in this particular
instance. Where we felt that there was some tension around expanding the membership
in front of a review, we took time to consider what we were trying to achieve here. Can
I say, in the spirit of our committee, that we have basically landed on the fact that it is
about equity of representation. Yes, perhaps the board is a large board. Yes, perhaps it
could make decisions round the table somew hat lengthy. However, the spirit of the
decision making at this particular board, I would hasten to say, is probably a little bit
different to that of some other boards.
On that note, in relation to the decision around shortening the time of service of th e
members on the board to a maximum of three terms, we had some further discussion on
this, and this may also come up in the review. Certainly, in relation to the membership
of the Māori members, where mana is recognised and where the contribution of servi ce
is recognised, often it is a lifetime appointment and nothing an individual can do can get
them away from that. So although in this particular change to the bill there is a
stipulation of a 3-year maximum term, I would much rather think that in the revi ew this
may be one of the issues that will be revisited, based on how representation over time
3488 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
has conducted itself in the best interests of the people, of Māori, but certainly in the
spirit of the Waitangi National Trust Board to ensure that our overall i nterests as a
country can be represented on this particular board.
I am looking forward to the opening of the new centre. I am looking forward to
continuing to see young people go to Waitangi as a part of their national education
programme about the histo ry of our country, just as I enjoy going to Anzac ceremonies
and seeing that particular day celebrated in the way that can make us proud as New
Zealanders. Kia ora tātou. We support the bill.

items.speaker: NUK KORAKO
items.text: E mihi atu ki a koe e te Mana Whakawā, ā, huri noa i
te Whare, ka mihi. Before I begin I too would like to acknowledge the passing of Ērima
Hēnare and in particular his service on the Waitangi National Trust Board since 2007.
Nō reira, e te raka tira o Te Tai Tokerau, haere atu rā. E haere atu rā ki te pao o te
whakawairua. E takoto mai, takoto mai, takoto mai. Nō reira, e te rakatira, okioki i roto i
rakimārie. Nō reira, moe mai, moe mai. E te whanau pani, ā, ki a koe Peeni, ka nuinui te
mihi, ka nuinui te aroha. Kia kaha, kia māia, ā, kia manawanui.
[Therefore, farewell to you , revered one of Northland. Depart as the ditty of
spirituality resonates. Lie down, lay down , and lie there ; rest in peace. So close your
eyes and sleep. To you the bereav ed family and to yo u particularly, Peeni, many, many
condolences and empathy to you. Be strong, brave, and resolute.]
I am proud to stand as a member of this House, and as the chair of the Māori Affairs
Committee, for the second reading of the Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment
Bill. I tautoko the previous speakers, who have done a sterling job of giving a very good
overview of the bill to date. I want to keep it high level, but I want to talk about two
important things that were covered by the Māori Affairs Committee, and also
acknowledge the wider review that will pick up a lot of what the previous speaker
highlighted.
Many consider the first Waitangi Day to be 6 February 1932, although Waitangi Day
was not celebrated annually for another 15 years after that, and even then there were no
Māori present. So 1932 is a special year in Waitangi history. It was on that day  that the
then Governor-General Lord Bledisloe gifted the former home of James Busby, where
the Treaty was signed, to the nation. The house and surrounding grounds were dedicated
as a public reserve and placed under the guardianship of the Waitangi Nationa l Trust
Board.
We have come a long way since 1932. Waitangi Day is now widely recognised as
our national day —the day that marks the birth of our nation. The historic Treaty
grounds now play a central role in our annual celebrations. If Waitangi Day marks the
birth of our nation, then the Treaty grounds are indeed its birthplace. As such, it is
appropriate that we stand here today, in this House, having recently marked the 175 th
year since the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi, to consider a bill that updat es and
modernises the arrangements for guardianship of this great taoka, this national treasure.
That was 79 years ago.
The Waitangi National Trust Board was legally established by the passing of the
Waitangi National Trust Board Act 1932. The Act appoint ed two types of members to
the board. Under the original Act, the trust deed, there are seven members representing
the following groups: the family of Archdeacon Henry Williams, the families of Hone
Heke, Maihi Kāwiti, Tāmati Waka Nene, and Pōmare, Māori l iving on the North
Auckland peninsula, Māori living in the rest of the North Island, Pākehā living in the
Bay of Islands, Māori and Pākehā living in Te Wai Pounamu —the South Island —the
