family of Edward Gibbon Wakefield, and the eighth member is to be a pro minent
person in the life of this country Aotearoa. In addition, there are four ex officio
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3489
members: the Prime Minister, the Minister of Conservation, the Minister for Māori
Development, and the Governor-General if he or she chooses.
This bill is the resul t of a review of the Waitangi National Trust Board Act 1932
undertaken by the Ministry for Culture and Heritage between 2006 and 2008. That
review concluded that there is a risk of an actual or perceived conflict of interest
between the constitutional roles of members of the executive and the roles they serve on
the trust board. So that is the first point, particularly, about part of the make -up of the
board and the roles. It would not be good enough to just remove the Governor -General
and Ministers as this  would sever an important link, a very important link, between the
trust board and the Crown. Instead, the Prime Minister, the Minister for Māori
Development, and the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage will make up a Crown
representative group. This g roup will ensure continued communication between the
trust board and the Government. In addition, the Governor-General may choose to be an
honorary patron of the Waitangi National Trust and this preserves the historic link
between the Treaty grounds and th e Governor-General, stretching back to the original
donation by Lord and Lady Bledisloe.
To replace the ex officio members on the board, two members of Parliament will be
appointed. One will be chosen by the Prime Minister and the other by the Leader of t he
Opposition. Of course, members of Parliament can also be members of the board in
representative roles, and I acknowledge Pita Paraone for his work as chair of the
Waitangi National Trust Board.
The bill, as it was sent to us on the Māori Affairs Commit tee, also introduced terms
of 3 years for board members, with a limit of 3 years to be served by each. This was the
second point particularly around tenure. This provision will also be applied to current
members of the board. The current term of each member will effectively end on the next
3-year anniversary of their appointment. If on that date they would have served for 9 or
more years on the board, they will be eligible for one further term. It was suggested to
us by the Ministry for Culture and Heritage  that we amend the legislation to prevent
current members from serving an additional 3 -year term. We did consider this change.
However, we decided that the transitional provisions in the bill as originally proposed
do strike a sensible balance between comp lete retrospective application of the three -
term limit and allowing current members to serve a further 9 years.
I come now to the significant amendment that was highlighted by our Minister,
which we on the Māori Affairs Committee have recommended. We rece ived a
submission from Arapeta Hamilton, who pointed out the disparity between Pākehā and
Māori members on the board. There are seven families represented on the trust board.
The families of James Busby, Edward Gibbon Wakefield, and Archdeacon Henry
Williams are represented by one member each —three members in total for these three
Pākehā families. The families of Hone Heke, Maihi Kāwiti, Tāmati Waka Nene, and
Pōmare are represented by one member for all four families. Of course the member
currently in that role is Pita Paraone. Although he is the chair, and some may suggest he
is as good as three other people, there is an obvious disparity in the representation
between Māori and Pākehā.
This sort of disparity in Pākehā and Māori representation may have been a normal
thing in 1932, but it certainly would not be accepted if such a trust board were
established today. Members of the Māori Affairs Committee took the view that this
situation is serious, it is unfair, and it should be addressed soon. The Ministry for
Culture and Heritage suggested that this representation would be best considered as part
of a planned wider review of the role and composition of the board. The  Hon Maggie
Barry has been clear in her commitment to hold such a review. We are grateful to her
for engaging with the committee and for providing us with the details of what the
3490 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
review will cover. Given the wide-ranging nature of the planned review, the Minister, of
course, could not be specific about when any changes resulting from the review would
come before this House to be passed.
Given the seriousness of the inequity that we believe currently exists in the make -up
of the trust board and the uncertai nty as to when the proposed review process would
make changes to the structure, there was a strong feeling within our committee that we
should take the opportunity we currently have to correct this anomaly. For that reason
we have recommended that when Pit a Paraone’s current term comes to an end, his
position is replaced by four positions that represent those Māori families.
We acknowledge that this change is not perfect. We do acknowledge this. It will
increase the size of the Waitangi National Trust Board to a size that some would suggest
will make it even less effective. And we acknowledge that this may mean that members
representing these families serve on the board for a short period only before changes
resulting from the review change the make -up of th e board yet again. That is really
crucial. Finally, I thank my committee, the Māori Affairs Committee, and the Minister
for all of the hard work that we have done to get the bill to the second reading. I
commend this bill to the House. Kia ora.

items.speaker: PEENI HENARE
items.text: Reo Māori e te Māngai o te
Whare. Ā, kupu mauri ora ki te whei Ao, ki te Ao Mārama, tihewa mauri ora! Tā te mea
ko tēnei he wā tuatahi ka kōrero ahau ki roto i tēnei Whare mai i te matenga o tōku
pāpā, e hiahia ana ahau ki te poroporoaki atu ki a ia, me te mihi anō ki tēnei Whare i
whakatuara mai i tēnei ngoikore ki roto i ngā wiki kua pahure ake nei. Nō reira, e taku
nohoanga, titiro ki te awatea taku taumata tiro ake ki te Ao Mārama. E tangi ana tēnei ki
a koe e Pāpā, me ngā tapuwae kua horahia mai ki runga i te nukuroa, e kīa nei te kōrero
o tō pāpā, a karani pāpā, e kore e mōnehunehu te pū mahara, te momo rangatira i
whakawhiti i te nukuroa o Te Moana-Nui-a-Kiwa, kāti ake ko ā ratou tapuwae ki runga i
te mata o te whenua, he taonga, he tapu, he taonga, he tapu. Kāti te tangi ki a Pāpā! Ka
tāpiri atu, ko ngā hunga wairua o tēnā, o tēnā e hui tahi nei, kotahi tonu te kōrero mō
rātau, haere mai, haere!
I tēnei tāima ka tahuri atu ahau ki te hunga ora. Koutou e ōku hoa mahi, koutou i
tukuna mai ō koutou roimata, ō koutou hūpe ki runga i a pāpā, nā, i tōna matenga, i tōna
takotoranga ki runga i te marae o Ōtīria, ki runga anō hoki i te marae o Mōtatau, ki roto
i te wiki kua pahure ake nei; koutou katoa mai i tēnei taha o te W hare ki tērā taha. E
mihi atu ana ahau ki a koutou mō tō koutou rau aroha ki tēnei tō koutou hoa mahi, tēnā
koutou, tēnā koutou, tēnā tātau katoa. E te Māngai o te Whare, ka tahuri atu ahau ki
tēnei take nunui rawa atu, e mea nei, ko tēnei take e kikini nei i te whatumanawa o tēnei
e kōrero ana.
[In the Māori language , Mr Deputy Speaker, a statement in regard to life in a
changing world and one of enlightenment—behold I speak! Because this is the first time
since the death of my father for me to address this House, I want to make a farewell
tribute to him and acknowledge this House for the support it gave me for this
listlessness during the immediate past weeks. Therefore , my encampment, I look t o the
broad daylight as the summit of my look ing up at the world of enlightenment. I am in
grief for you, Dad, and for the footprints spread out before me over the great distance .
As your father,  Grandad, quipped, the memory of the type of leader that cros sed the
great distance of the Pacific Ocean will never diminish , but, enough, their footprints
upon the face of the Earth are treasured and sacred, treasured and sacred. Enough of
the grieving for Dad! Put together all the spirits that belong to each and e very one of us
assembled here, and there is only one thing to say to them: welcome, farewell!
At this point in time I will turn to the living. To you my colleagues, you who
collectively shed your tears and mucus upon  Dad when he died, when he lay in state
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3491
upon the courtyards of Ōtīria and Mōtatau in the week just past —all of you, from this
side of the House to the other side —I acknowledge you collectively for your
extraordinary compassion to this colleague of yours . Thank you, thank you , and thank
you to all of us. Mr Deputy Speaker, I turn now to this matter of immense significance,
with the comment that it is one that nips at the seat of the emotions of the one speaking.]
At this time I want to turn to this particular amendment bill, the Waitangi National
Trust Board Amendment Bill, a bill that is close to my heart. I want to start by reading
just a very brief passage in a letter from Sir Apirana Ngata to Sir Peter Buck, who
talked about, and was, of course, instrumental, in the establishment of the Waitan gi
National Trust Board and, of course, its centenary celebration in 1940. He says here:
“You have already heard the news of the death of Taite and Tau.” —in that respect he
was referring to my great grandfather, not my cousin —“To mention the politicians first.
Their ideas will be carried on by many younger men whatever be their political
allegiance. I found the north at the Waitangi centennial celebrations very sound and
intent on carrying out the policies Tau gave his life for.” I wanted to read that as a start,
first, around the historical landscape, of course, of this particular taonga known as
Waitangi. We know, of course, as mentioned, it was the signing place. We know of the
house of Busby. We also know too of the great gift of the Bledisloe family to this
nation.
What is not mentioned is at the centenary celebrations, the opening of Te Whare
Rūnanga, a carved meeting house stands alongside the Busby house. On the inside of
that house there is a small but very poignant saying and that saying goes: “Ko au anō
tētahi i reira.” —I too was there then. What that refers to is the failure at the time of
recognising the Māori input in the conversation around the Treaty of Waitangi. Te
Whare Rūnanga went a long way to give Māori voice on the Waitangi national gro unds
and it is an important part of the history. It is also important to remember that at that
time in 1940, it was also the place where Apirana Ngata, and indeed the nation, sent off
the 28 th Māori Battalion to World War II. Why I cover this historical la ndscape is to
paint a picture of just how important this place is to the country. My fear in painting that
historical landscape is that in an attempt to create a more business style or model in the
running of the Waitangi national grounds I fear that this shift detracts from the historical
significance of the Waitangi land.
I want to, before I continue, say that we do support this and I do want to commend
the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage on her desire to review this piece of
legislation, because it is outdated. One of those examples is, of course, as mentioned in
the bill, the travel reimbursement where once it was reimbursed only to those who came
by railway. This one is a very good positive step to make sure that those people such as
my father, who actually spent most of his time in Wellington, do not have to catch the
train to Waitangi. So it is important that these types of developments in the bill’s history
carry us on into the future. We also welcome —and I support the kōrero in the House —
the broader review of the Waitangi National Trust. We are encouraged by a lot of its
functions at the moment spreading the word and the history of our country to our young
people, because if there is one thing that my father was passionate about, it was young
people. As much as he was a storehouse of knowledge for Māori, and, in particular, for
the people of Te Tai Tokerau, he always had one eye on the future and it is important
that we share the story of our nation with as many of our young people, be they Mā ori
or non-Māori, as possible.
I want to get back to the membership now. Of the 83 years of the trust, I want to
point out that for 65 years of that my family have been involved. The first member you
will see on the history provided by Parliamentary Servi ce is Tau Hēnare, my great
grandfather, who was on the board. Upon his untimely death in 1940 my grandfather Sir
3492 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
James Hēnare took over on the board and, as far as I know, has served the longest
time—49 years —on the Waitangi National Trust Board before his  untimely death in
1989. In more recent times, of course, there was my father, who has been mentioned,
from 2007 to 2015 upon his untimely death. I had a bit of a chuckle to myself when I
consider my whanaunga the member Pita Paraone who serves currently o n the trust. It
was mentioned to me at my father’s funeral how perhaps the trust is the departure
lounge and there is a word of caution in there for those who wish to take up a role on
the Waitangi National Trust. So kia tūpato e te pāpā—be careful!
But t he reason I draw out my family whakapapa with the trust —I also want to
mention Sir Tumu te Heuheu who was involved —is that it joins on to what my
esteemed colleague the Hon Nanaia Mahuta was talking about, which is the mana of the
positions. It is the mana  of those positions that carries the history of this country. Sir
Tumu te Heuheu’s tupuna Iwikau te Heuheu at the time of the Declaration of
Independence in 1835 and, of course, the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840 was
resident in the Bay of Islands. So it is only fitting that Sir Tumu te Heuheu continues his
role on the Waitangi National Trust.
It is amazing how fast 10 minutes disappears on you, so I do not want to labour too
much more about the particular bill other than to say that we support it and I want to
finish on a couple of notes for the future. We know that there is a case for developing
the Waitangi National Trust and its capacity. One of the dreams of my father, and
indeed the people of Te Tai Tokerau, was that the actual document of Te Tiriti o
Waitangi, which is currently held in Archives New Zealand here in Wellington, be
returned to the sacred lands in which they were signed. We know that the trust is
looking at building its capacity to hold such a precious taonga because we know t hat it
is precious and it is important that it is looked after appropriately. It is our dream to see
that returned to the land of Waitangi.
We also have another dream in the north that other sites of significance gain just as
much mana and conversation in  this House. Coming up in January is the
commemoration of 170 years since the battle of Ruapekapeka, the final battle in Te Tai
Tokerau. It is one of four significant battles in the north —as well as the signing of the
Treaty of Waitangi. If we are serious about our history and about acknowledging the
birthplace of this nation at Waitangi, it is important that we do it warts and all. Nō reira,
e te Mana Whakawā, kāti. Ki a tātau, tēnā koutou katoa.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: It is indeed a privilege and a
pleasure to be able to speak on the Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill. It
has been really interesting listening to the contributions from around the House. I
always think, and often say to people, that apart from the fabulous work we do in select
committees—I see my colleague Catherine Delahunty agreeing with me —it is actually
on Waitangi legislation and Treaty of Waitangi settlement legislation, and everythin g to
do with Waitangi, where this House generally comes together without any acrimony and
genuinely and generally tries to come to solutions to bring about justice for those who
make claims but also for everyone, really. I think it is something that we gen erally do
very well.
So when I have been listening to some of the reasons that are being given around
why we need to update and amend this bill, I thought that they all sounded very sensible
to me. Quite clearly, things have moved on from when the trust b oard was originally set
up and it is important to have the families who feel the greatest commitment and
obligations to the trust board represented separately, although I note that our colleague
Pita Paraone apparently does the job of four people —I am sure he does. But I think it is
important.
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3493
I think too that this is a bill that actually has constitutional significance, perhaps not
in the black -letter law way but certainly within the general sense of it. The Treaty of
Waitangi is something that is not solely important to Māori and it is not solely important
to the Crown; it is actually of significance to all people who wish to be New Zealanders
and who are New Zealanders. When I look at my own whakapapa, and I am not going
to run it all out for you today, although I would be happy to do so at any stage should
anyone want it—

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: Ha, ha! Feel free to do it.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Oh, Ms Delahunty, you are just too kind. But I can say
that I have no other home than New Zealand. I am like many New Zealanders. No other
country can call me theirs, and probably no other country would, and I would call no
other country home. My family has been in New Zealand in various parts of the
country. My ancestors whom I have found so far were first recorded in New Zealand  in
1841, a Captain Walker of Nelson —you see, this gene of wanting to be in charge is
something you just cannot get past. He was a ship’s captain, but a whole lot of the
family came in through the years. There is no other home. That is not unusual in New
Zealand, although pretty much I am quite unusual for Pākehā for having been here for
so long, as a family.
I grew up in the Waikato. I grew up in a situation where my parents grew up, in the
King Country—born there, grew up there. We are not people who are fazed by cultures
other than Pākehā - New Zealand culture. Having said that, lots of New Zealanders now
do not have that background and do in fact want to engage in, and want to know more
about not only the Treaty of Waitangi and New Zealand and New Zealan d’s
constitutional history but also where we are now and where we want to be going. It is
important that these new New Zealanders are able to feel part of our team, our team
New Zealand or team Aotearoa, whatever —our clan, where we are loyal first and
foremost and, pretty much, only to our country.
So I wonder whether or not this trust board change —and I hope it will —will help to
settle some of the issues that we routinely, and unfortunately, see at Waitangi on
Waitangi Day each year. I actually am one of the many New Zealanders who have felt
somewhat distressed by some of the behaviour that has been displayed particularly at Te
Tii Marae when guests have been humiliated or abused. I know that that is not
Waitangi. I know that that is a small group—we probably all know who they are—

items.speaker: Catherine Delahunty
items.text: I’m one of them.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: —who wish to —oh yes, Catherine Delahunty is one of
them. A dear old mate, Catherine. But actually for a lot of New Zealanders, p articularly
new New Zealanders, it is really intimidating and it sets up quite a barrier to wanting to
get engaged more. It sets up also for New Zealanders like myself a bit of a barrier to
wanting to be involved and hoping to be welcomed. So I like to hop e that all these sorts
of things that we do are the sorts of things that will mean that the attitude and the
behaviours will improve and be more welcoming.
I know that there have certainly been instances in the past where people have felt,
quite rightly so, that they should be able to protest on things, and of course you can. But
I just have this plea about this. I know that this particular board works very hard to
maintain what is a treasure for our nation, given, as we have said, to the nation by Lord
and Lady Bledisloe. You know, this is a tremendous gift that they did not have to make,
but they did it out of a commitment to New Zealand and an understanding of the
importance of Waitangi, and also the Treaty of Waitangi, to us as New Zealanders. So I
say that it would be lovely to have Waitangi Day being celebrated all around the
country, but particularly at Waitangi, and always understanding that things are never
going to be perfect—nobody is ever going to be happy with everything. One of the great
3494 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
things in New Zealand is that we are always trying to do better and I think that is where
we want to be able to give some credit where it is due.
There has been a tremendous amount that has been done wrong  over the years,
actually, which we as a country are now  addressing. This particular Government, since
we have been in office, just over 6 years, has signed 46 deeds of settlement. As at
February this year there have been 72 deeds of settlement signed —so it is not just this
Government but the previous Government as well—and 43 of those deeds of settlement
have been enacted in legislation. This is a huge effort by quite a lot of people, actually,
and it is something where both those representatives of the Crown —in other words, the
rest of New Zealand—and the Māori involved in this as claimants should be very proud
of the effort that has gone in and the goodwill. By the end of 2017 we would like to, if
possible, have all deeds of settlement signed, but that is actually very much dependent
on both sides being willing. Obviously, iwi need to be able, and willing, to sign as well.
You cannot force approval or agreement; people have to want to do it.
So these are really good things that we can point to. Point out to me anywhere else in
the world where we have that sort  of coming together and that sort of commitment to
righting the wrongs of the past —point to any other country that has that history. That
goes back not just because we are all fabulous people here in Kiwi land; it actually goes
back to the very essence and  the wording of the Treaty of Waitangi and what it was all
about. No other country that I can think of that was colonised in the 19 th century by
Britain, or any other country, ever actually ended up with a document such as the Treaty
of Waitangi; no other country. And that is something we should be very, very grateful
for. It enabled settlement in New Zealand of people other than the indigenous Māori
population. It also enabled a protection of rights and a conferring of rights as well, and a
protection that we should be very proud of.
No matter what we do in this area, there is always going to be someone to complain.
That is the nature of democracy; it is a fabulous thing. There is nothing wrong with
complaining—I have done a bit myself. But I would say tha t when we come to these
bills, we do a great job. I would like to acknowledge the chair of the Māori Affairs
Committee and all the members for the hard work that they have put into this and also
the Minister for bringing this bill to the House.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: Kei te mihi ki a koutou. May I begin by also
acknowledging the very untimely and sad passing of an extraordinary man. Ērima
Hēnare had a lifetime —a far too brief lifetime —of service to his  hapū, to Tai Tokerau,
and, indeed, to all of New Zealand, in the tradition of that family, I must say. It was an
honour, genuinely, to be present at Mōtatau for his final farewell. The atmosphere, the
speeches, and the very presence that was at that place  reflected something of the man
himself. I think we can be assured that our colleague Peeni Henare, in his time in this
House, and, indeed, outside this House, will continue to add mana to the name he bears.
Kia ora.
I would like, first, to reflect on the fact that the wide and genuine support for this bill
is a reflection on the good work of the Māori Affairs Committee. It seems to me that
that committee has ways of its own of getting things done. It works in mysterious ways
on occasion, but it seems to generate good work and get good outcomes, and this bill is,
I think, a good example of that.
I admit, I must say, that I was initially sceptical when I saw the first draft of this bill
because the first thing that struck me about it was that it has the Gov ernment and senior
politicians giving away power and authority, and that is completely counter -intuitive to
anybody who has been in politics for any length of time. But indeed, that is, in a sense,
what is happening with this bill. It is reallocating respo nsibility and authority for the
management of that unique place —for Waitangi —and I do think it is a move for the
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3495
good. As I say, my initial scepticism was laid to rest, and it does indeed seem a genuine
attempt to update a governance and management structu re that was in need of some
work and in need of some attention. I think that what has come out is something that
will serve us well, acknowledging, of course, there is to be a further review —and that is
a good thing, too—just to see that we do get this right.
It is difficult to overstate the importance of Waitangi —the house, the grounds, and
the area around it—to this country, not least of all culturally. It is the site of the signing
of the document that gives this Government —of which we are all part —legitimacy and
that gives the Crown its legitimacy in this country. We must continue to return to that —
that it is absolutely fundamental; it is a living document that is as valid today as it was
in 1840, when it was first signed. I must confess that even to th is day, when I meet New
Zealanders who have never visited Waitangi, it always comes as a surprise, but, OK, for
some people it is a long way from home. My own memories of it go back to when I was
sort of 4 or 5, and I am privileged to still live nearby, so  I am a regular visitor. It is
extraordinarily important culturally, politically, constitutionally, and, dare I say it, the
site also has some significant economic importance for Northland, particularly.
It is important that the governance and management structure is right so that we
maintain the quality of the experience for the people who do visit that place, and it is
important that we seek to enhance that experience not only because of the fact that it is
literally the place where our nation, Aotearoa New Zealand, began but because it is a
site of historical significance. I think we need to do our very best to ensure that it retains
the value and qualities that ensure that people go there, remember the experience, reflect
on it, and tell others about it.
Indeed, as an aside, I think that we are nowhere near exploiting the potential of the
wider heritage of Northland and of the sites —and some have been mentioned —of
Waitangi, Russell, Paihia, Mangungu, Waimate, Kerikeri, the mission house, and, dare I
say it, Clendon House. The more that people become aware and start to join the dots
about the extraordinary stories of those remarkable people, both Pākehā and Māori,
actually, who made this remarkable agreement, and who lived through those times in
the late 18th century through to the 19 th century and did some extraordinary things —I
think to some extent, all history is social history. I think we are very fortunate in New
Zealand that we still have the artefacts like the homes and the furnishings and, indeed,
the very close relationships. A generation or two back, we can look to people who were
actually there on the day in Waitangi, and that is something to be treasured, I think, and
to be shared not only with each other, with New Zealanders, but with others wh o come
here to find out what this—to some people—remote country is all about.
That is slightly an aside, but I have to say that I think the bill has advanced the
management and governance, potentially, of the place. We are particularly pleased, of
course—and the point has been mentioned already —that embedded in this bill is a
commitment to having a presence on the board of the descendants of Hone Heke, Maihi
Kāwiti, Tāmati Waka Nene, and, of course, Pōmare. At one point it seemed as though
that inclusion m ight need to await the review, which could have delayed it for some
time. So I am particularly pleased that, as I say, the interesting machinations of the
select committee have ensured that that commitment is embedded in this bill at this
point, and I do hope that the bill goes through without further delay. I see no reason why
it should not. It is a good document, it will achieve some good things, and we certainly
look forward to the work that we hope the board will do in future to continue to add
value, t o enhance that place, and to get the visitor centre there. To have the original
document there would be extraordinary and that would be a wonderful thing, so we
hope that this is as successful as we all hope it will be. Kia ora.
3496 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015

items.speaker: PITA PARAONE
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker, arā, tēnā tātou e te
Whare nei. Ēngari, i mua i te haere tonu o waku kōrero mō te kaupapa nei, i te hono au
ki tēnā ō koutou i tū ake i mua i a au ki te mihi i tōku whanaung a, ahakoa, e horekau
ahau e hiahia ana ki te ’hakahē i tā koutou kōrero. E karanga atu ana ki a ia, he
rangatira. Horekau he raru ki tēnā ēngari, ki a mātou i roto o Ngāti Hine, he pono he
pononga a te iwi. Nā reira, e Ērima, haere, hoki atu. Hoki atu koe ki ngā kōiwi o ō tāua
mātua tūpuna. Kua pau kē ngā mamaetanga o tēnei ao kei runga i a koe. Kei runga ngā
taumahatanga kei a mātou i muri nei, nā reira, e kara, te pononga o te iwi, haere, hoki
atu. E tātou mā, ka hoki mai ki a tātou, ki te kaupapa i mua i  a tātou i te rā nei. Ka nui te
hari, te koa o te ngākau i kite atu i tēnei kaupapa i puta mai i te Whare nei. Nā reira, tēnā
koutou.]
[Acknowledgments to you, Mr Deputy Speaker, and to us of this House. But before I
continue with my address in regard to this policy, I join members who stood up before
me to pay a tribute to my relative, despite the fact I have no desire to contradict the
view made by them. I want to assure them  that my relative is regarded highly. There is
not an issue with that but within us in Ngāti Hine; he is astute and a servant of the tribe.
Therefore to you, Ērima, farewell and go back. Return to the skeletal forms of our
ancestral forefathers, yours and mine. The pains of this world that were upon you are
spent. The burdens are now upon us, the ones left behind, so to you, dear friend and
servant of the people, farewell, return. I come back to us and to the policy before us
today. There is much joy and delight in the heart to see this policy emerging from this
House here. Thank you all.]
First of all, I would like to acknowledge the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage
and the fine gesture she made after making her presentation, joining our chairman of the
Māori Affairs Committee, which is really an example of the collegiality tha t members
of the Māori Affairs Committee share with one another, albeit that we sit on opposite
sides of this House. When we are considering matters that come before the Māori
Affairs Committee, there is that collegiality, which, obviously, because other p eople
have made comment, may not necessarily be exercised in other select committees. So I
want to acknowledge the Minister for that.
I also want to acknowledge the Minister for her commitment in seeing this bill
through in a timely manner, taking on boar d the commitment to carry out a wider
review of the Waitangi National Trust Board Act and of the machinations of the board.
For me, I felt that a lot of the concerns that the board had were already known to the
officials, and I know that a number of member s of the board felt that those issues and
those concerns could have been added to this bill. However, I take the Minister on her
word, and notwithstanding the comments made by the honourable member from
Waikato-Tainui about her reference to the legislative  programme, I feel confident that
the concerns we expressed in the Māori Affairs Committee process will certainly be
addressed in the wider review.
Waitangi is being described as the most significant historical place in our country,
and it is a privilege of mine to be, first of all, a member of the trust board responsible
for the maintenance and care of the estate and also to chair it. I know that my
membership of the board may have caused some disquiet, some concern, with other
members of the House, but I  want to reassure both them and this House that in order to
retain that sense of integrity to ensure that there would be no accusation of conflict of
interest or patch protection, I did not participate in casting votes in terms of the
decisions made by the select committee, and I also stood down as chairman of the board
during the discussions with the board and with officials, concerning this bill. I am
pleased to be able to report that to the House.
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3497
I want to say that the board has a very important respon sibility. In recent years it has
adopted the position that its responsibility should be confined not just to the care and
maintenance of the estate but to ensuring that the history of Waitangi is shared amongst
our fellow New Zealanders and, as the member from the Green Party David Clendon
alluded to, the number of New Zealanders who have not visited Waitangi. I suppose
there are various reasons for that, and the honourable member Judith Collins made
reference to it. As I hear such comments I feel a little bit annoyed—I am not annoyed at
her—about the assumption that that part of Waitangi is allied to the Treaty grounds. In
fact, those of us from the north know that it is almost like two separate worlds, two
different planets. However, that is the perception  that many of our fellow citizens have
of Waitangi.
This bill looks not only at the structure of the membership of the board but also at
increasing the representation of those Māori families. I must say that it has been a real
privilege and a pleasure to represent the families of those four tupuna. I want to make
this comment. In terms of the particular family that I descend from —and this is a
question that has always bothered me —Maihi Kāwiti is one of the sons of Te Ruki
Kāwiti, of Ruapekapeka war fame. M aihi’s part in history was that every time his
fellow tribesmen cut down the flagstaff, he promptly put it up. Maihi is the son of Te
Ruki, and one has to ask the question of why you would put the son ahead of the father.
To this day, no one has been able to tell me why. Perhaps there have been a confusion
in terms of the descent, because when the original Act was discussed in the second and
third readings, Sir Apirana Ngata referred to Te Riri Kāwiti as the grandson of Maihi. In
fact, he was the son. So I do not know.
I just want to confirm that New Zealand First will certainly be supporting this bill.
We look forward to the Committee stage, and I cannot see too many difficulties during
that process. We certainly look forward to seeing it enacted. Although  I personally will
be affected, it is something that I certainly support.
As a closing remark, I just want to tell those who are already lining up to become
members of the board that we do not pay a fee. I just want to say that the admission cost
that we have imposed on visitors has caused some disquiet amongst our fellow citizens.
I am anticipating that during the wider review of the Act, some consideration will be
given to an annual gratuity from the Government to the board, along the lines of Te
Papa. Nā reira i roto i aua ’hakaaro, tēnā koutou, tēnā koutou, kia ora mai anō tātou.
[So with those thoughts in mind I acknowledge and salute us and you collectively,
thank you.]

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Deputy Speaker. Before I start my
korero, I too want to pay respects on the passing of our Ngāti Hine rangatira Ērima
Hēnare, and I wish also to pass on my aroha to you, Peeni, and to your whānau. Kia ora.
The other person I would like to acknowledge is the Hon Maggie Barry, our Minister
for Arts, Culture and Heritage, who is shepherding this bill, the Waitangi National Trust
Board Amendment Bill, through the House. It is a very important bill. Even though it is
quite narrowly focused, it is important in the history of this country.
The purpose of the bill is to make changes to the Waitangi National Trust Board
membership, and that is why it has such a narrow focus. Before I talk about that focus
and the membership and the kōrero we had at the Māori Affairs Committee, I just want
to take us on a little trip down through the annals of history, because without the history
we would not be here discussing this bill today.
The background to this bill is that the property, the house, was owned by the Busby
whānau. During the 19 th century and at the beginning of the 20 th century the land and
the building kind of changed hands a bit. In 1932, as we have heard, a former member
of Parliament, Vernon Reed, had a passion that the Treaty House and the grounds it was
3498 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
on were a historic place and needed to be nurtured. That is why he invited the then
Governor-General, Lord Bledisloe, and  Lady Bledisloe to come and have a look at the
grounds and the Treaty House, to encourage them to make sure that that house was
going to be preserved.
Lord and Lady Bledisloe obviously did more than that, as we have heard from
previous speakers. They boug ht the grounds. Lord Bledisloe also invested £1,000 into
the Waitangi restoration fund to start the process for restoring the Treaty House itself.
The Government of the day also added another £500 to that restoration fund. So the first
form of restoration started back in 1932. It was also the time when the 1932 Act began.
I stand here as a mokopuna of this land, and I am absolutely grateful and thankful to the
Bledisloe whānau for their contributions, for gifting the Treaty House and the grounds
to this nation.
Anyway, as I was saying, the 1932 Act —the Waitangi National Trust Board Act —
gave statutory effect to the Waitangi National Trust deed and it also established the trust
board. The Bledisloes did this in the time of the Great Depression. Our country wa s
going through the Great Depression. There was high unemployment, and this was a way
for the Bledisloe whānau to be able to help people by giving them employment in the
restoration of that house. It was also another way that Lord Bledisloe could settle up  the
relationship between Pākehā and Māori.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: JOANNE HAYES
items.text: I have just a little more of the historical facts about what
happened on the Treaty grounds. In 1834 the Confederation of the United Tribes of
Aotearoa first raised their flag on the lawn of the Treaty House. It was very historic. As
we all know, 6 years later, in 1840, the Treaty of Waitangi was first signed, although
only a few days later the biggest signing was held across at Te Mangungu Ma rae. I was
privileged to be at their 100 -year celebration this year with the Minister, the Hon
Maggie Barry.
The Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill modernises the governance of
the board members of the trust. I just want to acknowledge our New Z ealand First
member Pita Paraone. I just want to say that it is a very humble thing for him to step
away from the discussions at the select committee. I know he was bursting to actually
get involved in those discussions but the gentleman that he is, he sat  back. Also he went
off the trust board so he did not have many conflicts of interest there. I just want to say
that I was pleased to hear from him that the trust members were supporting this very
important bill. That is not to say that the membership disc ussion within the select
committee was not debated very vigorously. I just want to thank the chair and my co -
members of the Māori Affairs Committee for the debate, and I thank the members of the
Parliamentary Counsel Office who came in with their report an d listened to our
discussions around membership. We have heard from other members in the House
about that membership.
I just want to reiterate that the current membership of the trust board has four ex
officio members including the Governor -General, the P rime Minister, the Minister of
Conservation, and the Minister for Māori Development, and we are starting to look at
how that is going to pan out, which I will talk about a bit later. There are family
representations from Archdeacon Henry Williams, Edward G ibbon Wakefield, and
James Busby, as well as a family member —I think it is Pita Paraone at the moment —
representing the whānau of Hone Heke, Maihi Kawiti, Tāmati Waka Nene, and the
Pomare families. There is a representative of the Māori people north of Auck land
peninsula—which I think was the position that the rangatira Ērima Hēnare held on the
trust board before he passed away —a Māori or Pākehā representative living in the
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3499
South Island, a Māori representative south of Auckland, and a prominent person who
has experience, either a historian or an archaeologist. So those are the current members
of the board.
What we are proposing is, as the Minister outlined in her speech, that the Governor -
General and the Ministers will be removed as ex officio members on the  board. The
Governor-General will became an honorary patron of the trust, and the Prime Minister,
the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, and the Minister for Māori Development
will form the Crown representative group. Hopefully, this will foster good  relations and
share information with the board. The two members of Parliament, one representing the
Government and one representing the Opposition, will be appointed as full members of
the board. By removing these ex officio positions on the board we remo ve the risk of
conflicts between constitutional roles and other roles of the trustees.
As I said before, the bill creates a clear separation between the Government and the
board while providing a means to ensure a positive working relationship through the
Governor-General’s patronage of the trust, the creation of the Crown representative
group, and the appointment of two members of Parliament as members of the trust.
Currently there is no statutory tenure limit for the board members on the trust. The bill
proposes that we implement a limited tenure of no more than 9 years, although our
select committee did debate the fact that current members, once the bill is implemented,
may have a further 3-year term in their positions on the board.
In closing, I note that this is a narrowly focused bill. It is a bill that, from what I have
heard in the House, is supported by everybody in the House. It incorporates the
Waitangi National Trust Board, which, as we know, administers the Waitangi grounds
and associated lands. It gives more power to that trust to be able to do things that it had
not been able to do in the past. I look forward to what is planned through the Waitangi
National Trust. I also look forward to the modernisation of the legislation, and its
fruition. Thank you very much. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Catherine Delahunty—a 5-minute call.

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Tēnā koutou e te Whare. I would just like
to start with a mihi to the Ngāti Hine and te whānau pani o Ērima Hēnare. Moe mai e
rangatira—an acknowledgment to Peeni Henare as the son of that very, very honourable
whakapapa, and that we mourn today the loss of his papa.
I would also like to acknowledge that we have the chair of the Waitangi National
Trust with us as well, Pita Paraone, and also everyone here from Te Tai Tokerau. There
are layers and layers of history associated with Te Tiriti o Waitangi and, therefore, wi th
the Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill. Although it belongs to all of us, it
is guarded the most fiercely, in my experience, by those of the north. Having spent
every Waitangi Day at Waitangi for the last 15 years except for 1, I have had a re al
education in the passion of Te Tai Tokerau not only for the national trust and for the
marae but also for the other sites of significance that have been referred to tonight: the
lower marae, Te Rau Rangatira; the places where He Wakaputanga o te Rangati ratanga
o Nu Tireni was signed in 1835; and all of the different aspects of the history. There are
many complex layers, and in speaking about them we need to acknowledge that there
are people here in this Parliament who descend directly on both the Pākehā side and the
Māori side, as does my colleague David Clendon, and others who have much greater
whakapapa relationship with the site that we are talking about tonight.
I had a brief experience on the select committee working on the bill and I would like
to acknowledge the select committee. As always, I found the Māori Affairs Committee
a really welcoming and positive place to come into. At the time —and when I left after
my short sojourn —there was quite a lot of debate going on on the issues of equitable
representation. So it is very pleasing to see that once again the Māori Affairs Committee
3500 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
has found a pathway before there is a major review, which we also support, and that the
Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, the Hon Maggie Barry, came and discussed
very graciously with that committee. There has been a pathway for some immediate
resolution as well.
Our concern—for some of us at that time—was really the statement that is in the bill,
which I am going to quote from, which is where the Māori Affairs Com mittee say: “We
considered the view put to us in the submission from Arapeta Hamilton that the current
makeup of the Board is unfair, as there is a disparity between the representation of
Pākehā families, which is one for each of three families, and of Māo ri families, where
there is just one member representing four …”. Given that this is about Te Tiriti o
Waitangi, there is a clear call to action in that statement if Te Tiriti o Waitangi is to be
honoured. It is not a Māori treaty; it is a treaty that give s my culture status in this
country, if my culture honours it —otherwise we are here as settlers and colonists rather
than as citizens. It is really, really important that the national trust board and this law
reflects that equitable issue of representation . If Te Tiriti o Waitangi and the documents
that preceded the building of our nationhood are about anything, they are about
recognising two sides of the story and that there is not going to be a dominant culture.
There is going to be tino rangatiratanga —this is the dream; we are not there yet —but
also there is going to be honourable kāwanatanga.
This bill is a really positive step forward in that regard, in that the select committee
members listened to the submitters and they were able to find a way before  the broader
review to recognise those issues of equity and participation, which are essential.
Although there were arguments and debates at the time —again, I would acknowledge
those from the Parliamentary Counsel Office, because they also did play a posit ive role.
They did come and say that this was within the scope of this bill, and that it was
possible to do this at this time, because we were trying to do what was logical as well as
what was right. I think that, thanks to all parties, what has been logic al as well as what
is right has been achieved in this process.
There is much more I could say about te Tiriti. I can never resist speaking on te
Tiriti, because I am so passionate that Pākehā recognise Waitangi, passionate that
Pākehā recognise that this place—and not just Waitangi itself but the whole of the area
where our history has taken place around that document and around He Wakaputanga o
te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni —is recognised by all of us as a basis for our nation. And
that it is not a matter of taking out the story; it is a matter of learning the true history,
the painful history, and the right history, rather than the sanitised history that is
sometimes told not only about what happens at Waitangi on the day —which is often,
actually, complete ly misinterpreted by the media —but also about what this place is
really all about to us. The Greens support any step forward that is based on equity and
on the articles of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, so we are proud to support the bill. Kia ora.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Mana  Whakawā.
Tuatahi kei te hiahia au ki te tautoko i ngā mihi kua mihia i tēnei pō ki tērā o ngā
tohunga, o ngā rangatira kua hinga i tērā wiki. Ko koe tēn ā e Ērima. Kua haere atu koe
ki ngā ringa mahana o te Atua, ki te taha o ō tūpuna, tō pāpā, ngā rangatira o Ngāti
Hine, ngā rangatira i whakarite nei i tēnei whenua mō tātau katoa i roto i te Tiriti, āe.
Anō nā, kai te hiahia au ki te tautoko i ngā mihi ku a mihia ki tērā o tana tama a Peeni. I
tū ia ki te kōrero i te pō nei, ā, kua kite au i te mamae, i te taumahatanga kai runga tonu i
a ia. Kai raro tonu a ia i te kapua pōuri, me tana whānau, ā, te whānau pani. Nā reira, ki
a koutou o Ngāti Hine, āe, kua n garo tēnei rangatira. Kua ara mai tētahi hei whai i ōna
tapuwae, ā, tēnei te mihi atu ki a koutou o Ngāti Hine, o Ngāpuhi, te wāhi o te
tīmatatanga, te whānautanga o tēnei whenua ki Waitangi.
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3501
[Thank you, Mr Speaker. First I want to endorse the tributes accorded this evening to
that one of the skilled and revered ones who collapsed last week. I am referring to you,
Ērima. You have gone to the warmth of God’s arms, to be with your ancestors, your
father, the esteemed ones of Ngāti Hine, and the noble ones wh o arranged in the Treaty
that this country be for all of us —yes! I also want to support the tributes accorded by
Peeni, that one of his sons. He stood to speak this evening and I could see that the pain
and burden is still upon him. He and his family, the bereaved family, are still under a
cloud of remorse. Therefore to you of Ngāti Hine, yes, this leader is gone. Someone will
rise up and follow in his footsteps, and I commend you of Ngāti Hine and Ngāpuhi, the
starting place and birthplace of this country at Waitangi.]
Kia ora. I want to add my voice to the kōrero tonight about Waitangi and its
importance and its relevance to this country. When I travelled to Waitangi this year, the
first time as an MP, with the Government, my mother actually scolded me, an d said:
“Where are you going to be? I need you here in Carterton because we are going to
celebrate Waitangi here in Carterton with our whanau as we have done in Masterton,
Wairarapa, for years.” I said: “Well, actually, Mum, I will be a few steps behind th e
Prime Minister at Waitangi, trying not to get hit with any flying projectiles.”
And so it was that I travelled there, to the birthplace of this nation—and that is how it
was described by all who were there. All who were in attendance described Waitangi as
the birthplace. And yet, when I got off the plane, having not been to Waitangi since I
was a girl, I looked for the sign that would show me the way —and there was none.
There was a sign that said Paihia—or Paihea? Pai?

items.speaker: Kelvin Davis
items.text: Paihia.

items.speaker: MARAMA FOX
items.text: Paihia. Right. Well, I did not know where that was. I had to get
out my Google map on my phone to find my way because there is no signage pointing
out the most historic place of our nation, the birthplace of our nation, where a
partnership was formed. And so I think that needs to be addressed.
But today we address the partnership that is the Māori trust board —the Waitangi
National Trust Board, not the Māori trust board just on its own, but as a partnership of
Māori and Pākehā com ing together. Yes, for me the biggest thing in doing this was to
address the representation and make sure that it was equitable. Everybody has talked
about it. We had four families being represented by one representative on the Māori
side, and three families each being represented by three representatives.
Yes, there is going to be a review. I want to acknowledge the Hon Maggie Barry who
worked with us and briefed us on the important matters of the Waitangi National Trust
Board so that we could ensure that there was equitable representation. She listened and
she made the amendments, and now we have an equitable process going forward. Yes,
the review may, in time, change that. But we felt that we could not let another day go
on, another week go on, another year go on while the review took place, where a glaring
inequity would continue. I want to acknowledge the members of the Māori Affairs
Committee, who worked together to ensure that not one more minute would go by with
that inequity continuing.
I also want to acknowledge our member on the Māori Affairs Commi ttee, Pita
Paraone, who, as everybody has stated, has worked tirelessly in this area. And though
there may be some issues about representation going forward about who in those
families will come forward to row this waka together, I am sure that we need to put our
faith in the people, that democracy will out, that they will continue to uphold the mana
of this place as the birthplace of our nation, and do the wonderful job that has been done
to this point to ensure that those grounds, that area, continue to t hrive and represent our
nation as a sparkling example, as they do at this time. Kia ora e te Mana Whakawā. I
commend this bill to the House.
3502 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
SIMON O ’CONNOR (National —Tāmaki): I am very pleased to take a call this
evening to speak in the second reading of this bill, the Waitangi National Trust Board
Amendment Bill. I am very conscious, as I stand here tonight, that I have not sat on the
Māori Affairs Committee, but I have been very fortunate to discuss this legislation with
an excellent caucus —or, rather, the likes of Nuk Korako, the chair of the committee,
and Maggie Barry, the Minister sponsoring this bill, have been very wholesome and
fulsome with us as a caucus in their disc ussions around what is happening. And so,
again, I am particularly pleased to stand along with others tonight to speak to this bill.
Like others, I would like to acknowledge the passing of Ērima Hēnare, a man who
has stood very tall, proud, and loud in the  Māori and, of course, New Zealand
community for many actions, particularly around Te Reo and the maintenance and
promotion of that—and, of course, his role, which has been acknowledged here tonight
many times, sitting as a member of the current Waitangi b oard. I acknowledge, too, his
son, Peeni Hēnare. Outside of Parliament, he and I have known each other for a good
amount of time. I have mentioned that, before, we worked together at the Ministry of
Social Development, and although we might find ourselves on opposite sides of the
House, good conversation can continue, with memories past and, I think, a common
bond to serve our country as best we can in the future.
In doing so, I acknowledge again the Minister and the work that has gone into this
legislation. I acknowledge the members of the select committee. I am conscious that
where this started is not necessarily where it ended or was intended to end, so a lot of
discussion has gone on, and debate —fraught at times, I am sure. But it has reached a
place now that members are happy with, if I am hearing the debate tonight correctly.
Within that is the intention for a review by the Minister as well, and we will touch on
that a little bit later. So this is a step in the right direction.
Waitangi is a place that  sits very strongly in our national consciousness for a variety
of reasons, but, of course, first and foremost it is part of our national identity—a point in
time that has defined and, arguably, began to define New Zealand’s identity. For me
personally, being someone born and raised in the north, Waitangi is a place we would
visit every year, not necessarily on 6 February, but it was a place that we would go to
frequently. The place has much history and tradition, not just around the Treaty itself
but also as a place where many early settlers came. I know this, certainly from my own
side of the Catholic community, which was well -connected into the Hokianga, where
Bishop Pompallier is buried. And, of course, across in Russell you have the Marist
fathers, whom I was very connected with. It is a place where I find myself at home. It is
a place where more recently National Party members found themselves at home, when
we went up there for our conference. And I have to say, not only the locals but also the
weather performed exceedingly well.
I do want to note that the Treaty of Waitangi and the place of Waitangi itself is larger
than just one place. I am reminded of this because a few months back I was very pleased
to join Ngāti Paoa  at Karaka Bay in Glendowie in my  electorate, where they
acknowledged the 175th anniversary of their signing of the Treaty. Although the seminal
moment may have occurred up in Waitangi with the conversations and signings there,
the Treaty then began to go around the country to be signed. As far as I am able to say,
for Ngāti Paoa , the signing at Karaka Bay —within the electorate of Tāmaki , as it is
now—is the really important moment for them. I have to say  that it was an incredible
honour and privilege to be invited to join them and to be o ut on their waka on the
Waitematā Harbour. It was an absolute thrill, and also very educational, I have to say, to
be able to sit through the hours of the talk and speeches.  I just mention th is because
Waitangi may be a singular place , but with the Treaty and its signing, for all of us as
New Zealanders it moves beyond just one place.
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3503
Important, we do look towards Waitangi itself to symbolise that, and so this bill is
about updating the structure of governance. Under the original Act and trust deed , there
are eight representative members. One comes from the family of Archdeacon Henry
Williams. I, in fact , met his, I think, great, great —oh, I have forgotten exactly. I met a
guy called Bill Ludbrook. Sorry, Bill, that I have forgotten the exact connection, but
Bill Ludbrook joined me at Karaka Bay representing the Williams family. It was, again,
an incredibly powerful moment , as, obviously, the descendants of Ngāti Paoa were
there. And here was this descendant of Archdeacon Henry Williams sharing the story as
had been passed on to him. Again, it was a remarkably powerful moment.
The fa milies of Hone Heke, Maihi Kāw iti, Tāmati Waka Nene, and Pōmare are
represented by Pita Paraone, who is currently sitting  for the New Zealand First Party.
Pita, I do not know how you balance one family, let alone four, but kudos to you, sir. I
think we will come back to that as well because one of the discussions that have come
through the debate tonight is around inequities. There is a representative for Māori
living on the North Auckland peninsula, Māori living in the rest of the North Island,
Pākehā living in the Bay of Islands, the family of Edward Gibbon Wakefield, and No. 8
is a prominent person in the life of our country, and that is the Sir Don McKinnon at the
moment. I thin k it is good to mention his name and acknowledge his work. When we
talk of a prominent New Zealander, it is the calibre of Sir Don that we are talking about.
There are four members ex officio, those being the Prime Minister, the Minister of
Conservation, the Minister for Māori Development, and, of course, His Excellency the
Governor-General, or whomever he or she chooses. With the review of the Act, changes
are being suggested. Important, the likes of the Governor -General and Ministers will be
removed from these ex officio positions. They will continue to be able to engage. I
understand the Governor-General is able to be the patron—is that right?

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Yes.
SIMON O’CONNOR: I think that is really important. The Governor -General is a
very visible expression of our Sovereign, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth. That
connection with Māori and with this country is incredibly important. So I am pleased to
see that although he is no longer represented, his representative ex officio mainta ins a
place.
The new board will also see the Ministers step away. In some ways, that could
remove any perceived conflicts of interest or confusion. Instead, what we are going to
see are two members of Parliament nominated. I am not going to make a pitch fo r that
role—I am not sure you really want me talking much more beyond the 10 minutes of
tonight—but one of those will be put forward by the Government and one by the Leader
of the Opposition. I note here, in some notes that I have put down, that the bill, by
removing the Governor -General and the Ministers, removes the risk of, as I say,
conflicts between their constitutional roles and those of trustees. It also removes the risk
of legal and reputational issues for the Crown. I think one of the really key el ements
here is for this new board, as they talk in legal terms, to be treated as a natural person. In
other words, the trust board, moving forward, once this bill goes through its third
reading, should be allowed to, basically, borrow money, pay it off as it sees fit, and
make the decisions that we as individuals, or as natural persons, are able to do. I think
that is very positive.
The last issue —because I am conscious that the bell has rung —is ultimately there
are—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: Let’s have more.

items.speaker: Joanne Hayes
items.text: Keep going.
SIMON O’CONNOR: Really? Do we want to move an extension of time?

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: More on the royal family.
3504 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
SIMON O’CONNOR: Well, we could ask them to come down bu t I am not sure
they necessarily always will. But, actually, they play a critical part.
One of the major elements has been that of inequity. The Treaty is based on
partnership and working together. At the moment, we have four individuals of Pākehā
descent—as important as it is—being represented, and then we have four Māori families
represented by one person. Regardless of whom that is, it is still one for four and four
for four —not really the way to go. So what this bill is doing is bringing about an
opportunity for more Māori representation. I think that is incredibly positive. I would
say to that, harkening back to what I discussed at Karaka Bay, that, obviously, Waitangi
is a place for all of New Zealand, and the Treaty is something that was experienced i n
multiple places in New Zealand by multiple families —Pākehā and Māori. Personally, I
would like to see that diversity of representation go much broader than just the
geography of Waitangi and the place of Waitangi itself.
I understand the Minister is goin g to be conducting a review. I also understand she
came before the Māori Affairs Committee, which I think is fantastic, and had a lengthy
discussion with members outlining what she is interested in doing. I trust and hope that
the select committee itself e ngaged with its expectations too, which will inform that
review going forward. I think this Government is very proud of its work around matters
to do with the Treaty. It would be remiss of me—primarily because he is in the House—
not to acknowledge the Hon Chris Finlayson for the work that he continues to do around
Treaty settlements. Again I think—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: It is tragic to have to interrupt the member; however, his
time has expired.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: Tēnā ra koe, Mr Speaker. Kei te
hiahia ahau ki te tāpiri i ōku mihi maioha ki runga i wērā kua utaina atu ki runga i tērā o
ngā mātua o Ngāti Hine, arā, a Ērima Hēnare, te pāpā o tō mātou hoa a Peeni. Nā reira,
e te pāpā Ērima, moe atu rā.
[Thank you indeed, Mr Speaker. I want to add my affectionate regards to those cast
upon Ērima Hēnare , one of Ngāti Hine’s parents , and dad of our colleague Peeni ; so
sleep on, father Ērima.]
Initially, I would like to take umbrage at the comments from Marama Fox, who said
that she was going to be at Waitangi this year for the first time instead of being in
Carterton and was concerned that, walking a couple of feet behind the Prime Minister,
she might be pelted with something. On behalf of all Ngāpuhi, I would like to say that I
am taking umbrage at that. Anybody who has worked with Ngāpuhi, such as the Hon
Chris Finlayson, will know we are a calm, dignified, rational iwi who will always resort
to diplomacy to resolve any of our issues. To suggest there will be trouble amongst
Ngāpuhi is just ludicrous.
I would like to go straight to the issue around the four tūpuna Māori. I am not on the
Māori Affairs Committee, but it just so happened that on the day that I was subbing in
for somebody, Arapeta Hamilton submitted saying that it was unfair that the four Māori
families had one representative and other families had a representative each. Arapeta’s
mother and my father are first cousins . L ike Peeni Henare, we have Pōmare, who is
mentioned in this bill, as our great -great-great-great-grandfather. We are direct
descendants.
He was a contemporary of Kāwiti. I have to say that I agree with what Pita Paraone
said earlier whe n he wondered why Maihi Kāwiti is the representative ancestor of the
Kāwiti family when Te Ruki was his father . By having Maihi instead of Te Ruki, you
are sort of omitting the father. I think it would be better to have Te Ruki and
acknowledge Maihi Kāwiti as part of that whānau.
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3505
Then we have the Hone Heke whānau. As we know, Hone Heke was the first
signatory of the Treaty. I will come back to that. We also have the Tāmati Waka Nene
whānau, whose father Tapua was one of the first people to go out and greet Captain
Cook when he arrived i n Whangaroa , not far from the Cavalli Islands , where Dover
Samuels does a lot of fishing. Going back to Hone Heke being the first signatory of the
Treaty, my tupuna Pōmare, who is included in this bill, signed the Treaty on 17
February, not 6 February. He was a bit miffed that his name might be under a name that
he considered inferior to his, so he and a few others signed on top. So if you actually
look at the signatories of the Treaty of Waitangi, the third name down is Pōmare of
Ngāti Manu, which is our hapū.
There are two Pōmares. I really want to correct history because you see a lot of
books that often get the names mixed up. The first Pōmare was born Whiria. Books
often say that his name was Whētoi, but Whētoi was actually his nephew. When Whiria
died—he met his Waterloo down in Nanaia Mahuta’s neck of the woods, on the Waipā
River. To commemorate him, his nephew Whētoi took his name and became Pōmare.
“Pōmare” is actually a Tahitian name. When some European captain came over, he
brought with him a couple of Tahitian translators, interpreters, because the languages in
those days were pretty similar. The Tahitian actually said “The king of Tahiti is our
King Pōmare.” My ancestor Whiria, the first person who became Pōmare here, said
“Well, if it’s good en ough for the king of Tahiti to be named Pōmare, I’ll take that
name.” That is how he became Pōmare. Anyway, he died in about 1826, and Whētoi,
his nephew, took the name Pōmare.
He is the signatory to the Treaty of Waitangi. An interesting —well, I find it
interesting—fact is that his son Hare married a woman called Hāriata from Te Ahuahu
and around Ōhaeāwai, and they went over to England as part of a group that I think was
a concert party, and had an audience with Queen Victoria. Hāriata at that time was
pregnant. Queen Victoria said to her: “If that baby is a girl, name her after me, Victoria.
If it’s a boy, name him after my husband.” —who was Albert Victor, the consort. So she
had the baby, and he was the first Māori to be born in England. He was a boy, so he was
named Albert Victor Pōmare. Queen Victoria said she wanted to be his godmother , so
she became his godmother. She presented him with some clothes —a christening gown,
which we still have possession of somewhere. I t might be in a museum, but I have
handled it. It is still there . There was also a gold goblet ; a knife, fork, and spoon ; and
other gifts. Queen Victoria paid for his tuition at St Stephen’s School. In later life he
joined the Royal Navy, and we believe that after that he may have been shipwre cked in
America and, strangely enough, mistaken for a runaway slave . W e are not quite sure
where Albert Victor Pōmare went. We lost track of him after that.
The name Albert Victor or Arapeta Wikita is a name that runs through our family —
the P ōmare family —to the extent that Albert Victor Hamilton or Arapeta Wikita
Hamilton was the relation of mine who submitted  on the bill , saying it was unfair that
the Māori families had only one representative. I entirely endorse his sentiment. It is
only right that the Māori whānau have the same level of representation as the non-Māori
whānau.
Whētoi Pōmare signed the Treaty of Waitangi. He is a signatory to what I have often
referred to in this House as the bridge between the Māori and the Pākehā New Zealand
that we kno w today . That  is sort of ironic because my mother’s father —my Pākehā
grandfather—actually physically built the bridge from Te Tii Marae over to the other
side of the Waitangi River. I believe that t hat bridge might have been opened on the
same date in 1934  that the first Waitangi Day was held. I recall seeing as a child a
number of black and white photos that my mother had in a photo album of the huge
crowds at Waitangi on that day in 1934. It is interesting that my Pākehā grandfather
3506 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
literally built a brid ge and my Māori great -great-great-great-grandfather metaphorically
built the bridge that is the Treaty of Waitangi.
We have heard the history about the Treaty grounds and how it basically fell into
neglect after the Treaty was signed. It was in the 1880s that Mrs Busby, I think it was,
sold it off. There were some Māori chiefs who wanted to have a ceremonial whare built
there, and the Government of the day declined that. Eventually we had a ceremonial
wharenui built there , and it was opened in 1940 to comm emorate the centenary. As
somebody who grew up in the Bay of Islands, I spent a lot of time around the Treaty
grounds—not so much because I was visiting it but because the golf course is next door.
There is a hole that runs up the hill , and I have got a terrible hook shot and had to climb
over the fence a number of times to go and retrieve balls. The Waitangi Treaty
grounds—I grew up with it. I have visited it a number of times.
It is a big part of New Zealand. I take what people say, though. Waitangi is becoming
greater than just the geographical area of Waitangi now. The whole meaning of
Waitangi and the Treaty of Waitangi spreads out to the Cartertons of the world and all
around New Zealand. We support this bill, and we look forward to it becoming law. Kia
ora.

items.speaker: ANDREW BAYLY
items.text: It is a pleasure to be speaking on the
Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill. But before I do so I just want to
acknowledge Mr Pita Paraone as the re presentative of iwi family on the board and as
chair of the board, and I also pass on my condolences to Mr Peeni Henare, of course, in
his time of need and acknowledge the great contribution that his father made to the
trust.
As New Zealanders we all reco gnise the importance of Waitangi, given its historical
significance and because it is embedded in our national heritage. It is a site where our
bicultural nationhood actually began. Its heritage status is actually unquestioned. For me
personally, it also i s a place of great meaning. The Baylys have farmed alongside
Waitangi trust land for many, many years. In fact, my brother and sister-in-law currently
lease some of the trust land where you often see my brother’s Angus heifers grazing. As
such, I have been a regular visitor to Waitangi over many, many years.
There is nothing like the hot summers of the north and the colours of the sea in the
harbour. When you look across the harbour and think about the strange, quaint place of
Russell back in the early 184 0s and how it was described as a den of iniquity of the
Pacific, it is a hard thing to envisage. Named after the British aristocracy, the charm of
the settlement today is a far cry from that infamy. The local population was attracted to
a mixture of desert ers from ships, escaped convicts from Botany Bay in Australia,
brothels, grog sellers, whalers, and traders —all growing fat on all the incomers to that
area. Nowadays there is little hint of that sordid past.
What I like is how the Waitangi National Trust  actually defines Waitangi. It is “a
place for all New Zealanders, a place of accord for all peoples. A place standing central
to our history as a nation and at the centre of growth of our nation.” The trust’s vision
for Waitangi for 2020 is to be a place of relevance to all New Zealanders, to be New
Zealand’s most important historical place, to be an important tourism destination, to
operate in a sustainable long -term organisation, and to be a model for bicultural
development.
After the signing of the Tre aty in 1840, the Busby family continued to own the land
and property, and the house fell into disrepair. It was not until 1932 that the Governor -
General, Lord Bledisloe, and his wife visited the Bay of Islands and agreed to acquire
the 1,000 acres plus the  house, with a view to gifting it to the nation. This historic spot,
the Treaty House and that land, was formally handed over to New Zealand on 6
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3507
February 1934, commencing a tradition of what is now known, obviously, as Waitangi
Day.
The deed of the Waitan gi National Trust, drawn up in 1932, sets out the objectives
for the Waitangi Treaty Grounds. The first board comprised the Bledisloes —as the
donors—the Prime Minister, Ministers, representatives from certain Māori families, and
representatives from the Bu sby, Williams, and Wakefield families. The latter family —
the Wakefields—I have got to say, I am related to through my mother’s family.
The board today continues to include descendants from all the families involved
those 83 years ago, but with the passage of time it is obviously now important to look at
how the structure of that trust is established and to set it on a new course that is
modernised and relevant to its current purpose. The trust is currently self -funded and
carries out the work of maintainin g the Treaty grounds without creating a cost to the
people of New Zealand.
The original Act, the Waitangi National Trust Board Act 1932, has been examined in
detail by the Māori Affairs Committee, and unanimously recommended that the
amendment bill should be passed, with a list of amendments. This Government seeks to
strengthen the financial viability and governance structure of the trust. So it is done,
really, with the purpose that all New Zealanders and visitors alike continue to benefit
from this histo rical site, and there is nothing better than to be at Waitangi at dawn for
the service or to watch the changing of the guard and the raising of the flag on those
hallowed grounds.
This amendment bill addresses the representation on the trust. At present t he board
has two sets of representatives: one being ex officio members —the Prime Minister, the
Minister of Conservation and the Minister for Māori Development, as well as the
Governor-General—and the second group being the representatives of the families o f
the Pākehā and Māori individuals who were prominent in New Zealand’s colonial past.
In the case of the second group, there is obviously a current disparity between the
representatives of the Pākehā families, where there is one member for each family, an d
the representative for the Māori families, being one member only. The Māori Affairs
Committee’s deliberations recommend that each of the four Māori families has its own
representative. Although this will increase the number on the trust board, it is a lo gical
outcome.
The other step change in this bill concerns the ex officio members —namely, the
removal of the Governor -General and Ministers from the position on the board. If the
Governor-General so wishes, he or she may become an honorary patron of the t rust.
Thirdly, forming a group of Crown representatives to continue to maintain the
communication and sharing of information with the board was recommended. This
group is going to consist of the Prime Minister, the Minister for Arts, Culture and
Heritage, and the Minister for Māori Development. Two additional MPs are going to be
appointed to the board, one from the Government and one from the Opposition.
The removal of the Governor-General and the Ministers from the ex officio positions
clarifies their roles and removes any ambiguity over their constitutional role versus their
roles as trustees. A clear separation between the Government and the board will,
therefore, exist while at the same time ensuring that positive work continues to exist on
that board.
Consideration is also being given to the maximum term of board members. They will
be limited to 9 years, being three terms of 3 years. At the moment there is no such
constraint, and there is a transitional measure that allows any person currently getting
close to a 9 -year term to roll that over for an initial 3 -year term. That will help in a
transitional sense to ensure ongoing representation during this period of change.
3508 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015
I also just want to highlight the fact that this Government is absolutely focused on
settling grievances. Under the Hon Chris Finlayson, we have signed 46 deeds of
settlement since 2008, and as at February this year 72 deeds of settlement have been
signed, and 43 of these have been passed into legislation. These represent over two -
thirds of the land area of New Zealand and nearly half of all of the settlements that we
expect to settle. And, of course, we have set ourselves a target that by 2017 all willing
and able iwi will have deeds of settlement in place.
This Government places much im portance on settling grievances, and also what we
are doing with this bill is putting in place a modern framework that will help to continue
that process. I want to particularly acknowledge the work of the Māori Affairs
Committee, and also the Minister for  Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations, in supporting
this bill.
Bill read a second time.

sections.heading: Organised Crime And Anti-Corruption Legislation Bill

items.text: Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon AMY ADAMS
