items.text: I move, That the Organised Crime and
Anti-corruption Legislation Bill be now read a second time . This bill reflects the
Government’s ongoing commitment to combat organised crime and corruption both i n
New Zealand and globally. Can I take this opportunity to thank the Law and Order
Committee for its work on the bill. I understand the committee received 20 submissions
and has recommended that the bill proceed with a number of amendments, mostly of a
minor and technical nature.
This bill addresses a serious issue faced by societies around the globe. Organised
crime is a corrupting influence worldwide, undermining public safety, economic
development, good governance, and national security. New Zealand has  robust legal
frameworks to combat organised crime and corruption and high levels of international
engagement in responding to these threats. However, we are not immune to organised
criminal activities such as money -laundering, identity theft, people -trafficking, and a
range of conduct that constitutes bribery and corruption. This bill tackles such conduct
in a number of ways. It enhances New Zealand’s ability to collaborate with international
efforts to disrupt organised crime and ensures that law enforcem ent agencies are able to
quickly and effectively respond to new challenges. Measures in the bill will also
increase New Zealand’s compliance with a number of international agreements.
One of New Zealand’s core assets internationally is its reputation as o ne of the least
corrupt countries in the world. However, we can never afford to be complacent. This
bill will send a strong signal that New Zealand values having, and is committed to
maintaining, corruption -free institutions. This is vital for maintaining New Zealand’s
reputation as a reliable trading partner and enhancing our influence in international fora.
The 2011 all-of-Government response to organised crime outlined a range of measures
that this Government had introduced to target and disrupt organise d crime. However,
we also recognised that more work could be done and identified a range of areas for
improvement. This bill implements many of these reforms by making a number of key
changes.
I will begin by outlining two important amendments to the mone y-laundering
offences under the Crimes Act. Firstly, the bill removes the requirement that the
proceeds of money -laundering be generated from offending punishable by 5 years’
imprisonment or more. This requirement places the police in the position of havin g to
establish that the proceeds of crime are generated solely from such offences. This
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3509
burden is both difficult to meet and inconsistent with the reality of these crimes, as the
proceeds are often intermingled and arise from a range of criminal activities.
The second change simply clarifies that the prosecution need not prove that a
defendant had intent to conceal the proceeds of crime, although this may result from the
money-laundering transaction. This is a return to early case law on the money -
laundering offence, which held that intent to conceal was not an element of the offence.
More recent decisions, however, have required the prosecution to prove that element,
creating unnecessary hurdles to successful prosecution. Removing this requirement will
help deter those who exploit the current limitations and responds to the concerns raised
by the Financial Action Task Force, which sets the international best practice for
combating money-laundering.
In addition, the bill introduces new reporting requirement s under the Anti -Money
Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act for two high -risk classes of
transactions that we know criminals use to launder money and finance terrorism. Under
the new requirements, financial institutions will need to report international wire
transactions of over $1,000 and all physical cash transactions of $10,000 or more to the
financial intelligence unit within the police. This amendment will improve our ability to
detect and investigate money -laundering and align New Zeal and with international best
practice for combating money -laundering. The fact that the banks are already required
to collect identity information from their customers means that the public should not
notice any change as a result of these new requirements.
The bill also addresses the issue of identity theft. Identity theft and the misuse of
personal information is estimated to impact over 190,000 New Zealanders each year,
and this bill deals with gaps in New Zealand’s identity crime framework by adding new
offences of selling or distributing unlawfully obtained identity information, and of
making or possessing goods intended to facilitate identity crimes, such as credit -card
skimming devices. By addressing the gaps in our identity crime framework, we will
ensure that a full range of identity crimes can be prosecuted.
Other important amendments in the bill expressly provide police with the power to
share personal information, including fingerprint information, with their international
counterparts. This amendment will allow implementation of the Agreement on
Enhancing Cooperation in Preventing and Combating Crime with the United States. The
Law and Order Committee has recommended inserting a new requirement in this part of
the bill for the Commissioner of  Police to consult with the Privacy Commissioner
before entering into international information -sharing agreements. This was already a
requirement in accordance with a Cabinet decision. However, including the consultation
in the bill will ensure that the o versight role performed by the Privacy Commissioner is
more transparent. In addition, the bill makes an amendment to allow information stored
in the DNA Databank to be provided to assist criminal investigations and prosecutions
overseas, subject to the Att orney-General’s authorisation. I have great confidence in
New Zealand’s law enforcement agencies, which have a successful history of
prosecutions against those who engage in organised criminal activities. The measures I
have outlined will further enhance i nternational law enforcement cooperation and
capability.
A range of amendments in the bill will also strengthen New Zealand’s ability to
combat bribery and corruption. These will enable the Government to ratify the United
Nations Convention Against Corrup tion, which is the first global instrument to address
corruption in both the public and private spheres. Although New Zealand already
broadly complies with the convention, the bill contains a number of legislative
amendments that are required before we can  formally ratify it. These changes include
increasing the penalties for private sector bribery and corruption offences under the
3510 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
Secret Commissions Act 1910 to bring them into line with public sector bribery and
general fraud offences.
The bill also create s new offences to address gaps in our anti -corruption framework.
The new offences criminalise the acceptance of a bribe from a foreign public official
and the acceptance of a bribe in return for using one’s influence over an official. Other
amendments in t he bill will enhance compliance with the OECD Convention on
Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions.
The foreign bribery offence is amended to ensure that it applies to bribery in relation to
the provision of international aid and clarifies the circumstances in which a company is
liable for foreign bribery. The Law and Order Committee recommended a further
amendment to make specified fines available as sanctions for foreign bribery, in
addition to a term of impri sonment. The amended penalties reflect the serious nature of
foreign bribery and send a very clear message that those who engage in corrupt
behaviour will be meaningfully held to account.
A final amendment to the foreign bribery offence addresses the exis ting exception
for small payments made to foreign public officials for the sole purpose of expediting a
service to which the payer is already entitled, commonly known as facilitation
payments. It is important to note that this exception has been part of ou r law for many
years and is important to ensure that New Zealanders acting in good faith are not
unintentionally criminalised. However, the bill tightens this already narrow exception,
such that it will not now apply to payments that provide an undue mater ial advantage to
the payer or an undue disadvantage to anyone else. This maintains compliance with the
UN convention, which requires parties to criminalise payments that provide the
recipient with an undue advantage. This measure, combined with a new requi rement for
companies to record such payments in their books, will ensure that the exception is not
open to abuse. I note that this is consistent with the treatment of such facilitation
payments in Australia, in the US, and in South Korea, and with operatio nal practice in
the UK.
Let me conclude by outlining three final sets of reforms in the bill. The bill extends
the Crimes Act offence of people -trafficking to ensure it applies to trafficking within
New Zealand and not just in or out of the country. The r evised section also expands the
trafficking offence to include the movement of a person for exploitative purpose —for
example, prostitution or slavery. These amendments enhance our compliance with the
UN anti -trafficking protocol, bringing us into line with  best practice. The bill also
amends the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act to allow foreign restraining orders to be
registered without notice and enable the court to extend the registration of these orders
more than once if necessary. A further amendment r ecommended by the select
committee ensures that extensions are not limited to extradition cases. Finally, the Law
and Order Committee recommended a minor amendment to the Extradition Act to
ensure that the police are able to take identity information from those arrested under that
Act in relation to offences committed overseas.
Collectively, the amendments in the bill will ensure that New Zealand has a robust
legislative framework that complies with best practice. The bill will ensure that those
engaging in organised or corrupt criminal activities will be subject to the full force of
the law by removing current limitations in domestic law and enhancing New Zealand’s
ability to internationally cooperate. I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to speak on the Organised Crime
and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill. It is a bill that has been some time coming. It was
first brought to this House by Judith Collins when she was the Minister of Justice. We
were told that it would be ready in 2013, but it came to us in 2014. Needless to say, this
is an area that, of course, is crucial to all parties in this House. It is, I guess, important to
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3511
us as a nation that we continue to uphold our standing in the international community
for doing our bit in this area. It does require cooperation and collaboration if it is going
to function properly. Labour, for instance, recognised that when it set up the Organised
and Financial Crime Agency within the police in, I believe, 2008.
But it is not just about reputational issues abroad. Obviously, making sure that we
keep our own house in order is incredibly important. I just wanted to use these
introductory comments as an opportunity to point  out that the Serious Fraud Office is
one of the best mechanisms that we have to make sure that we maintain our own
domestic high standards when it comes to fraud, bribery, and corruption. That is an
organisation that has, in the past few Budgets now, soug ht additional funding to do its
job. It warned the Government, for instance, of its concern that there might be
additional issues around corruption as a result of the massive amount of infrastructural
rebuild occurring in Christchurch. That was a bid that was declined. Instead, it was just
left simply to do presentations around the importance of being vigilant around
corruption in Canterbury. Equally, it has warned that it is not able to prosecute as many
cases as potentially it would like to. It is somethi ng I thought prudent to raise —that we
do need to make sure that we keep our own house in order, even though we are
primarily discussing today our international obligations in implementing this legislation.
Transparency International is one organisation th at does a very good job of keeping
in check where New Zealand sits relative to other countries. We have a branch that
operates in New Zealand, but it is part of a wider reporting regime that takes into
account what kinds of mechanisms New Zealand is implem enting to make sure we
remain a transparent, corruption -free country. We have fared very well in the past. We
had a slight slip in the last measure. We are at No. 2. No one wants to celebrate coming
second. Denmark pipped us at the post. In part, I believe it has been flagged that the fact
that we have not quite implemented some of these obligations has been part of the
reason why. That is because this is an omnibus bill. It implements proposals including
around the all -of-Government response to organised c rime, which it started back in
But it also aims to improve New Zealand’s ability to cooperate with international
partners. It ratifies the United Nations Convention Against Corruption, it implements
the US and New Zealand Agreement on Enhancing Coop eration in Preventing and
Combating Crime, and also enhances New Zealand’s compliance with a number of
other international conventions, including the OECD Convention on Combating Bribery
of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions, w hich I think is
something that Transparency International is particularly interested in.
There were 20 submissions to this bill. One of the ones, though, and the area that I
want to focus on the most —because there are a number of really important points
raised—does sit around a point that the Minister touched on, and that was the
facilitation payments exception that exists in this law. Labour overall is supporting this
bill; I should point that out. But we do have some reservations around the fact that we
do still have a facilitation payments exception in this bill.
I thought making reference to a bit of the background on this and also to the
submissions that were made against it would be useful for the House. New Zealand’s
foreign bribery offence contains, as the Minister said, a very narrow exception for small
payments to be made to foreign public officials for the sole or primary purpose of
ensuring or expediting the performance of a “routine Government action”. These are
not, for instance, the kinds of things that you might pay as part of tariffs or as part of
customs duty or anything like that. These are direct payments to Government officials
or public officials to help facilitate and expedite a particular activity.
3512 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
I think we should be very clear tha t in making this payment, you are expediting
yourself over and above someone else who has not made that payment. I think that is
clear in the way it is described. The exception, though, states that for such a payment to
be lawful in New Zealand law, it mus t be small. I would be interested to hear from
members of the committee whether or not there was a discussion over what the
definition of “small” was. Was it relative to what the payment was being made for? Was
it sized in any way? Will you make a bigger e xception around what “small” is
depending on the size of the country or the activity? It must be small for an action
within the scope of the official’s ordinary duties —so, obviously, if you are paying a
port inspector, it has to be around port issues —and n ot involve a decision about
awarding new business or continuing existing business. So it is about facilitating
business that would otherwise occur.
Examples of facilitation payments include “small payments relating to the grant of a
permit or licence, the  provision of utility services, or loading or unloading cargo.”
Again, it would be really useful for the House if members —I believe that the Hon Phil
Goff was on the Law and Order Committee; perhaps he could share with us some of the
examples that might ha ve been raised at the committee, because I do think that it is a
fine line. It is a fine line, and who is making the judgment over what is routine, what is
“small”, and where you decide there is a difference between —[Interruption] Either
Jonathan Young has  a contribution that he will hopefully make in the House or he is
talking to himself; I am not sure. But hopefully at some point he might make a
contribution, and talk me through some of ways that were discussed by the committee.
There were a number of submissions—I believe three—that were quite explicit about
this point in the bill and had concerns about it, including, I believe, the Human Rights
Commission and Transparency International New Zealand. Apparently, these
submissions were fairly similar in th e concerns that they raised. Their points were
these—and I think they are good points, so I want to reiterate them and highlight them
in this House. Their points were that such payments are bribes, regardless of their size.
If they are not something that i s applied universally and equally to all applicants, then
how is it not considered a bribe? The conventions that we are party to do not distinguish
between facilitation payments and bribes, and therefore there was a concern that by
having this exception we  might actually fall foul of the conventions we are trying to
make sure that we are ratifying in this law. Also, thirdly, the OECD and the Asia -
Pacific Economic Cooperation also encourage businesses to eliminate the use of such
payments.
I noticed that the Minister in her speech said that these kinds of payments exist in
comparable countries to us —she referenced Australia and the United States. They do
not exist in the UK. It has explicitly ruled out being able to use exemptions like these —
obviously, for good reason. In the response from the ministry, it has said that it does not
believe the exception is likely to fall foul of the conventions. How do we know? Were
we able to seek advice beyond our ministry officials on whether or not we wou ld
actually fall foul of those conventions by having this exception? The ministry also
raised that in the UK they have made the point that they are unlikely to prosecute for
small payments. It is a very big difference to say you are not going to prosecute small
payments versus creating an exemption in law that explicitly says you can do it. One is
much more permissive than the other.
So I do think that there are still considerable questions to be answered about this part
of the bill, which really does let down what is otherwise, I think, a very useful bill, and
one that we should all be supporting, not only for our international reputation but also to
make sure we spread best practice domestically as well. Thank you.
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3513

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Thank you, Mr Deputy Speaker, for
the opportunity to speak during the second reading of the Organised Crime and Anti -
corruption Legislation Bill. First of all, I would like to commend the Minister of Justice,
the Hon Amy Adams, for progressing this bill. Even though our country has robust
domestic law arrangements and enforcement and has low levels of corruption, we still
need to keep working on becoming more immune from domestic and tra nsnationally
generated organised crime. I would also like to thank the members of the Law and
Order Committee and the officials who guided us through this process. The committee
received 20 written submissions and heard 11 orally. There were changes recomm ended
to the bill that appear to be accepted by all the members.
The previous speaker, Jacinda Ardern, raised the issue of facilitation payments, an
issue that came up during the discussion of this bill. It was debated at length, and the
members of the Op position also agreed that if we do not have this provision, then we
are taking away opportunities from New Zealand businesses that are dealing in those
areas. These are minor payments, and it has been particularly worded so that a
facilitation payment is n ot included as a bribe in this bill, because these payments are
very small in nature for an action that is within the scope of an official’s ordinary duties
and that does not involve a decision about awarding new business or continuing existing
business. One of the examples that was given during the select committee was that in
some countries to move a file from one desk to another desk sometimes you have to
give some facilitation payment to officials. That is not a huge amount. It is token money
that is pa id and it makes the work easy for businesses to deal with such situations. If
they do not pay, then those files keep sitting on the first desk and do not move to the
next level.
So that was the reason, and we had a very good discussion and Opposition memb ers
also participated in this. The member who was speaking before me was not present at
the select committee. She does not have any idea of what discussions we had at the
select committee, so I want to clarify that and let her know that this discussion too k
place, and all the members agreed that we do not want to put New Zealand businesses at
a disadvantage, and we want to make sure that they are on a level playing field.
Another issue that came up, which was also discussed at length, was the
commencement date of the bill. Originally, it was proposed that the bill should be
implemented on 1 January 2016, but the banks and the New Zealand Bankers’
Association came and suggested that it would be very hard on them to implement the
software upgrade so that the provisions in this bill could be implemented. I think it was
a very reasonable call. The committee considered that, and the commencement date was
moved to 12 months after the date of assent of the Governor-General. These are some of
the issues that were raised during the select committee.
Another issue that I would like to touch on, discussed at the select committee and
raised by the banks, was that individual names in prescribed transaction reports should
be removed. It was proposed that the name of the e mployee from the bank who had
conducted that transaction should be made public or known to the police. But banks
were very hesitant about this clause, and they did not agree to it. This was amended. We
made a change and removed the requirement that the ind ividual employee be named in
the prescribed transaction report. This information is not necessary for intelligence
purposes, and can be requested by the New Zealand Police if necessary. If there is a
reason for it, then the police can ask the bank for the name of the person who has
completed that transaction.
Another issue that I would like to discuss today is some of the issues that were raised
by the Privacy Commissioner during their submission and considered in the select
committee. A special provision,  as the Minister mentioned, was omitted during the
3514 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
process, but it had already been discussed in Cabinet that the Commissioner of Police,
before entering any agreement with international agencies or renewing the existing
agreement, has to have a discussion  with the Privacy Commissioner so that they are
satisfied with the provisions of the agreement. This is all because we want to keep it
transparent. This Government is working so that we have world -class laws and
transparent laws available so that there is ease of doing business.
There were requests for certain types of transactions to be exempted from the
prescribed transaction reporting requirement and to extend the maximum time of the
period of submission of such reports and the date of commencement. The re is
uncertainty as to which reporting entities involved in international wire transfers will be
required to make a prescribed transaction report. Also, there were concerns that the
penalty for failing to report prescribed transactions was too high.
One of the major priorities of this National -led Government is to make communities
safer for New Zealanders. We are working hard to prevent people from becoming
involved in organised crime. This bill aims to strengthen the law to combat organised
crime and cor ruption. We are committed to being part of tackling this global problem
and protecting the country from threats posed by international and domestic criminal
networks. Once again, I would like to mention a few points about how this bill will
achieve our pur poses. It implements a proposal containing an all -of-Government
response to organised crime, which was reported in August 2011 when the Government
released an all -of-Government response to organised crime. It was realised that, even
though New Zealand has got a strong legislative framework in practice to obstruct
organised crime, a number of amendments are required to address gaps in the law that
are reflected in this omnibus bill. The bill will ensure that law enforcement agencies are
able to quickly and effectively respond to new challenges.
We all want to maintain New Zealand’s reputation as a fair and transparent country.
People from more than 200 different ethnicities live in New Zealand, and our country
ensures that everyone is treated fairly. This bi ll will improve New Zealand’s ability to
cooperate with international partners to disrupt organised crime and enhance New
Zealand’s compliance with a number of international conventions, including the OECD
Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business
Transactions and the United Nations Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish
Trafficking in Persons, Especially Women and Children.
One of the significant challenges for us is to reduce the use of cannabis and
methamphetamines, which leads to physical as well as mental ill health. I would like to
acknowledge the New Zealand Police for helping us in tackling this problem through
their recent implementation of the Organised Crime Strategy and the Methamphetamine
Control Strategy, in coordination with the Customs Service. Apart from reducing drug -
related harm, especially to vulnerable populations like youth, we are also focusing on
issues like robberies, theft, and fraud. This will help in raising awareness, especia lly in
young ones, of the potential harm that these drugs could cause. We want to be able to
reduce people’s desire for illegal and illegally sourced goods and services that further
increase the risk involved with offending. The penalty for bribery and cor ruption types
of offences under the Secret Commissions Act 1910 will increase from a maximum of 2
years’ imprisonment to a maximum of 7 years’ imprisonment. I commend this bill to the
House.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: The Labour Party will be supporting this
piece of legislation, but we are not entirely happy with every aspect of it, and I want to
differ with the chair of our Law and Order Committee in terms of the view of the
Labour Party on facilitation payments.
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3515
I raised a number of questions, particularly when Transparency International was
appearing before the select committee, because I believed that Transparency
International, the Human Rights Commission, and the Victoria Univer sity of
Wellington School of Government all made a very valid point when they said that it is
impossible to distinguish where a facilitation payment ends and a bribe begins. A bribe
does not have to be a big bribe to be a bribe. A small bribe is still a br ibe. If I was to
offer a Customs Service official in New Zealand money to speed up the transaction that
I was trying to get into the country, I would be committing a crime in this country. Why
is it a crime in this country to do that but if I am working ov erseas somewhere in South-
east Asia and I offer that payment, somehow it is not a crime? If it is a crime in New
Zealand, then it is a crime internationally.
I think that what Transparency International said made a lot of sense. It pointed out
that there a re countries that have banned facilitation payments outright. The United
Kingdom, you will remember, is one such country that says that facilitation payments
are illegal. The officials came back to us and said: “Oh, but they aren’t prosecuting
small facilitation payments.” They might not be, but they are still illegal. The Canadians
have moved to make facilitation payments illegal. Transparency International said that
the United States and Australia are also moving in that direction. My question to the

items.speaker: National Party is
items.text: if we are really proud of our reputation of being the least corrupt
country in the world, why are we not leading on this aspect of facilitation payments?
We ought to be. We ought to be leading on that to maintain our reputation for the
highest possible standards of integrity and transparency.
It is also true that other organisations that we are proudly part of have spoken out
against facilitation payments. APEC —the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation —has
opposed facilitation payments. The OECD,  which we are a member of, has opposed
facilitation payments. In New Zealand the Serious Fraud Office and Business New
Zealand, working in conjunction with Transparency International, put together a
programme where they recommend that facilitation payments  are not paid. Some
questions were asked of officials at the select committee about whether this would
hugely disadvantage New Zealand, if others are acting corruptly and we are not able to
do the same. Well, I do not think that is a good excuse, because i f we are encouraging
other countries in which we are conducting our business to stamp out corruption, why
would we then say that it is OK to make a facilitation payment? We would not because
that is a double standard.
There was a survey done of New Zealand  businesses in 2009, a business survey
conducted by Trace International. It found that more than three -quarters of the survey
respondents believed that it was possible to do business successfully without making
facilitation payments, if they planned carefu lly and they did proper management
support.
So I do not accept that facilitation payments are OK. In fact, in the United Nations
Convention Against Corruption, in article 16, there is nowhere where it says that a bribe
has to be a big bribe in order to be  a bribe. In fact, it defines that form of corruption —
bribery of foreign public officials —as when you promise, or offer, or give to a foreign
official or person in an international organisation, directly or indirectly, any undue
advantage for the official themselves. That is a payment. That is surely an undue
advantage. You are not paying customs officially to make the transaction; you are
paying the officials to grease their palms, to get something that gives you an advantage.
The other part of the defini tion is that it needs to be an act that does create undue
advantage, and if you are prepared to pay a facilitation payment, or, rather, if a business
is prepared to —I know you would not  personally do any such thing, Mr Assistant
Speaker—make a facilitation  payment, it is  to get an advantage. They do not want to
3516 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
queue up. They do not want it to take time. They want it now, and it gives them an
advantage. So I cannot see how anyone can read article 16 of the United Nations
Convention Against Corruption as all owing facilitation payments  because they are
small and they are perhaps not that important. If you believe in the process of having a
clear line, then you do not make a payment that is not an official payment, and a
payment that goes into the pocket of an official, to get an advantage. Yet in this piece of
legislation here we are saying that that is OK. I do not believe that it is OK.
The other criticism—in so far as I have a criticism of this bill —is the length of time
that it has taken to get here. The ma tters that this bill deals with are important matters.
They are matters of large -scale criminal activities. It is designed to make sure that our
law against organised crime is as tough as it needs to be. It needs to be a lot tougher
because we know that if  we take one aspect of organised crime, and that is the
manufacture and sale of methamphetamine, that is a business infiltrated by organised
crime that makes more than a billion New Zealand dollars a year in this country. That is
a billion dollars going in to the pockets of organised crime to promote drugs, and we
have taken a long time to bring our legislation up to the standard that makes it easier for
us to crack down on that sort of organised criminal activity.
The bill also provides for further action t o be taken against the crime of money -
laundering. Money -laundering is when you convert the proceeds of crime into a
legitimate payment by cleansing that money and making it a payment on property or
some such thing that makes it look legitimate. Money -laundering in this country, in the
Government’s own regulatory impact statement, is estimated to be at a value of over
$1.5 billion a year—$1.5 billion a year in criminal activity being laundered. So why is it
that we had to first be criticised by international  organisations about the inadequacy of
our money-laundering legislation before we acted? Those criticisms date back to 2009.
It is now 2015, and I ask the Government why it took 6 years to bring back to the House
this necessary piece of legislation dealing  with criminal activity to the value of $1.5
billion a year.
Of course, what this legislation also does is it enables us to ratify the United Nations
Convention Against Corruption. We were one of the first countries to sign it 11 years
ago, and we will be one of the last countries to actually ratify it. We will be one of the
last countries that signed the convention to ratify it and bring it into force. I want to
know why, if we are so proud of our role of being a good international citizen, it took
all of that time—the whole 7 years of this Government —to actually act on something
that needed to occur. It is not good enough that we turned a blind eye to these things.
We lowered the priority, we did all sorts of other legislation, but we did not crack down
on criminal activity.
There is a range of things that this bill enables us to do. We can not only now ratify
the convention against corruption but also improve our compliance with things like the
OECD Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officia ls in International
Business Transactions , the UN Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime ,
and the United Nations anti -trafficking protocol. If I take that instance of trafficking
again, why has it taken so long to crack down on that when we know the appalling
human costs and consequences of trafficking?
What is finally before the House we support, but it took too damn long for it to get
here, and we need some explanation of that from the Government, and some
explanation of why a small bribe is OK but we will criminalise a large bribe. Where is
the line drawn? Why are facilitation payments  exempted from being defined as bribery,
when clearly that is exactly what they are and what they are intended to do?

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak on the
Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill. I would just like to acknowledge
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3517
the chair of the Law and Order Committee, Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi, and the Minister of
Justice, the Hon Amy Adams, as well as the other members of the committee,
particularly those who have spoken already.
This was one of two of the first pieces of legislation that I was privileged enough to
work on in the Law and Order Committee and I have to say that it was certainly a piece
of legislation around which I think all parties involved and all representatives across the
House were certainly on the same page regarding the importance of this legislation. By
and large we were all on the same page when we were talking to officials and submitters
from the various representative agencies on the legislation and the importance of it.
I just want to acknowledge a couple of the agencies and organisations that provided a
lot of work and  guidance on this, particularly the Ministry of Justice, the Police, the
Police Association, the Privacy Commissioner, and Transparency International. I
acknowledge their guidance with regard to the international protocols and experiences
around how other countries have adopted and implemented this legislation. I would also
like to acknowledge the New Zealand Bankers’ Association and the three banks that
submitted separately—ANZ, Westpac, and BNZ. Collectively, for those organisations,
as well as for the ag encies involved, there was a high level of constructive, productive,
and pragmatic engagement, and I think everybody at the heart of it wanted the best
piece of legislation that could come out.
We have already heard from the Minister and a number of other  members tonight
about some of the changes that have taken place in response to the concerns that were
raised by the various submitters in order to make the legislation the very best it can be.
We have already heard from Mr Goff about the value of money -laundering, as reported
by the departmental report, at $1.5 billion. That is a serious aspect of the economy that
could provide, obviously, dangerous flow -on effects to some vulnerable New
Zealanders. Although we are talking about why this legislation may ha ve taken a little
bit longer to progress than it could have, while we are looking at vulnerable New
Zealanders we have passed other pieces of legislation that have tried to protect them as
well, such as that resulting from the White Paper for Vulnerable Children and a number
of education amendment bills.
So I think that we have given this piece of legislation the priority it deserves. One of
the advantages, potentially, of implementing the legislation behind some of the other
countries that ratified the UN  convention is that although we may have been one of the
first to sign and one of the last to eventually progress the legislation, it means that we
have had the luxury of being able to look at how other countries have articulated the
challenges that were r aised as they were progressing the legislation in their respective
countries. We have been able to take those perspectives and craft our own unique
legislation, which draws on the challenges and inconsistencies that may have been
experienced by others. So I think there is an advantage in that, and it means that New
Zealand has truly got a piece of unique legislation, picking the best from other countries
that we compare ourselves to.
There are just a couple of points that the Minister has raised that I thin k are
important, given that that probably draws into another reason why it has taken a little bit
longer to progress the legislation, and that is that a number of aspects and, indeed, the
changes that have been incorporated through the select committee process are minor and
highly technical in nature.
As we have heard from a number of the banks, such as the Banks Association, ANZ,
and Westpac, the nature of the systems and software that these organisations already
have in place, and already provide reporting mechanisms to the police, is complex and
unique and takes time to change. I think as a committee we did this legislation a lot of
justice by taking the time to get a greater understanding of some of those complexities.
3518 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
Westpac articulated that it  provides banking and insurance and investment services
across a broad range of industries to a broad range of clients. It estimates that it has
around 1.4 million customers. When this legislation does finally progress and the
regulations have been implemented, it estimates that it will be required to report around
2,000 transactions per day. So we have got a duty to be able to make sure that if it is
having to do this, we have got the right frameworks in place from the outset so that
when it spends million s of dollars on developing its software to meet the requirements
of Parliament and the regulations that follow, that money has not been wasted and it is
not having to go back and repeat and redo the software based on changes we may have
to make later on down the track.
BNZ is in a similar situation. Internationally, it expects that across the world it will
have about 5 million to 7 million reportable transactions annually. They are not small
numbers, and given the threshold of payments that are reportable —as low as $1,000,
and most of these are electronic transactions and they happen numerous times on a daily
basis—I think that if these organisations are going to be reporting these to the police,
they need to be able to have some clear understanding of what is actually necessary
from a police perspective and the collection agency of these transactions. They need to
have a clear understanding of what is actually required from the outset, because it will
be a hugely costly exercise to ensure that both sides of the spectrum have the necessary
software to be able to take on board the transactions that come about.
The Minister and other members have also reported that obviously this is a
borderless and global environment we are acting within. I do not think I can r emember
the last time I actually gave a cash sum of over probably about $100. If you look at most
members of this House, we do use our banks’ online mechanisms to make payments, so
it is very important. As we have heard from a number of members tonight, the organised
criminal networks—

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: You use cash?

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: Cash? I use cash every now and again. I use an Eftpos card, a
credit card from time to time. I do not use credit cards on undesirable things. I do no t
use my parliamentary credit card where I should not, either.
The all-of-Government response to organised crime has been an important aspect of
this, and we have heard that the Ministry of Justice has played a huge role. Another
aspect that the Banks Association raised in its submission on the bill  was that it felt that
the bill did not adequately identify the form of information reported that should take the
proposed method of delivery. It specifically raised an issue with new section 48B of the
Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act , where it requires
that the nature of the transaction be reported. The association raised questions as to what
kind of analysis is needed to be undertaken to make sure this determination was clearer.
That is an example of an aspect within the bill where the Ministry of Justice went back
and looked at it and took into consideration the views of the Banks Association.
Another aspect was the time of implementation. The bill initially set down that after
12 months following the implementation of the Act, the requirements will come into
force. But, as we know, the regulations will take a long time following that to
implement, and the Ministry of Justice was quite clear that it—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: It’s OK to not take the full 10 minutes.

items.speaker: TODD BARCLAY
items.text: I am enjoying this, Ms Dyson. It is very fascinating. The
ministry basically said that it will look at the legislation and will implement it as soon as
the banks and everybody are in order.
When Mr Goff was reflecting on money -laundering and why facilitation payments
were not included, I just wonder what hat he was wearing —whether he was wearing his
hat as a member of the Law and Order Committee, a former Minister of Justice, or a
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3519
former Minister of Trade. If this was such a huge aspect of this bill that absolutely
needed to be included, I am not sure why he did not feel compelled to pass the
legislation himself when he was the Minister of Justice, and take a world-leading step as
he said we should be here. Obviously, as a former Minister of Trade he will know more
than many of us that it is of the utmost importance that we ensure that our businesses
are not disadvantaged on the global scale. We are already disadvantaged by the tyranny
of distance; we do not need to be disadvantaged by other aspects that are just in the
general course of doing business overseas.
Mr Bakshi has reflected that there were 20 submissions and 11 were heard orally.
Particularly within two aspects of the bill, the money-laundering side as one and
organised crime as the other, the themes that were coming through were incredibly
consistent. We are comfortable that we have struck the right positioning of this bill to
provide the best legislation for all parties involve d to ensure that we are adhering to our
obligations under the international treaties that we have ratified. Thank you very much.
It is great to be passing this very important legislation and commending it.

items.speaker: DAVID CLENDON
items.text: I am also pleased to speak to this bill, the Organised
Crime and Anti -corruption Legislation Bill . It is an interesting bill. It has been around
for some time. It has had time to mature, clearly. The Greens are supporting it because it
does some good things, some necessary things.
Time and technology move on. Technological developments create new
opportunities for criminal elements to offend and to find ways to extract money in ways
they ought not to do. We are, however, in commo n with our Labour colleagues,
disappointed by this bill to the extent that it fails to do something that it could do, and
that is clearly about this notion of bribes. I will avoid the language of “facilitation
payments”. It is such a dainty expression. It simply overlooks or seeks to disguise the
fact that, actually, you are talking about bribes —small bribes, perfectly formed little
bribes, but bribes none the less. I will say more about that in a moment or two.
This bill does some good things, as I said. A mong other things, it will make it much
more difficult for people to launder money through improper transactions and pass
money through the banking system by various ways and means. It was quite an
education, I must say. Some of the early submitters to the  Law and Order Committee
were the banks and some of the major financial interests. It was genuinely interesting to
hear about novel ways people find to work electronic systems that to most of us look to
be quite impregnable and quite bulletproof.
We did ra ise some concerns, as did others, about the very low level of reporting. A
$1,000 remittance overseas by a New Zealander will be tracked and will be recorded. I
cannot recall now the number of transactions that that represents in the course of a year
going through the banks —most of them, the vast majority of them, legitimate —but it
was many millions of transactions. That is a difficult challenge technically for the
banks. They got somewhat nervous, I think, about the commencement date initially,
making the very good point that they need to develop their software and their systems to
accommodate that level of reporting. There was no opposition, as such, that I could see.
They were simply concerned about their ability to meet the requirements of the bill. So
those matters were dealt with.
I continue to have some unease about the level of data that is being gathered here. As
we know, massive data banks, information about people’s banking and their
transactions, can have value in all sorts of ways, not least of a ll for commercial reasons.
I discovered recently when visiting Spark in Auckland that there is a new and
interesting profession called a data scientist —people who can manage these massive
databases, extract information from them, and discover patterns and trends within them.
I am sure the police will do this for very good reasons, for good and sound reasons.
3520 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
They will be looking for the patterns and trends that represent offending in some way.
But, equally, that information is vulnerable to being mined and to being manipulated
and applied for purely commercial or other reasons, and for that reason I guess we will
continue to have some level of scepticism about these massive databases and will want
to be assured that over time they will be managed, they will be eliminated—whatever it
takes to protect individuals’ privacy.
The bill does some very useful things around people trafficking. It tidies up our law.
It stiffens up some of our regulations. It criminalises actions in New Zealand even if the
offending is carried out overseas, and that is as it should be. New Zealanders should not
be exempt from offences or from liability for offence s simply because what they are
doing is not currently criminalised in New Zealand. As I said , though, where we part
company wi th this bill  is that it  is the perfe ct opportunity , when it does deal with
matters around money laundering,  bribery, and anti-corruption measures, to remove the
section in the Crimes Act that allows for these so -called facilitation payments, these
small bribes. We have heard a number of justifications about why that is  OK, and they
are common enough justifications. The pragmatic argument, and Mr Bak shi made that
in all honesty, is that, yes, if you want your business matter to progress, you might have
to slip somebody a few dollars or whatever the currency is in order to progress that. But
that is simply a bribe. It also embeds in that culture the notion that it is OK.
Often the history of bribes and corrupt money exchanges is about the fact that people
are not properly paid to do jobs, not least of all in the public service in other countries,
where the income levels are so low that actually the brib es supplement the income and
allow those people simply to do well or at least to have decent lives, and, of course, the
potential to accumulate large fortunes. I think the pragmatic argument fails. I think we
as a country, with a very good reputation as a transparent country with very, very low
levels of corruption, should exercise some leadership and not be afraid to simply say
openly and publicly, even in environments where bribes are commonplace: “No, we
don’t do that. We don’t go there.” I think we would be supporting those countries.
Two of the countries with the most serious problems around corruption in the world
are China and India, two countries that are important trading partners for us. I think we
could stand up and be the example, in a sense. Yes , it is true that some countries do
allow for facilitation payments, although it is interesting to note that typically the
regulations, the laws, in those countries like Australia and like Canada are actually
tougher than ours. I think the provision in thi s legislation to require the reporting of
facilitation payments, of small bribes, catches us up with Australia, where that is
already obligatory. The penalties in those countries for overstepping the mark in terms
of bribery, internationally bribing foreign officials, are more serious than ours.
It is interesting to note that only 44 percent of the top 50 companies on the NZX have
policies prohibiting bribery, and 18 have policies that regulate facilitation payments.
Compare that with the UK, where of the t op 100 companies there, 72 explicitly prohibit
giving and receiving bribes. The figure in Europe is around 57 percent. Only five
companies in New Zealand on the NZX have codes of ethics that prohibit facilitation
payments. As I say, we have a very good rep utation as being a country with very low
levels of corruption. We also have a reputation as a clean, green country. I think
Transparency International is something like Mike Joy, in the sense that Mike Joy is
blowing the whistle on our water quality and on  the fact that our environment is not
pristine. In the same way, Transparency International is blowing the whistle on the fact
that to the extent that we continue to accommodate, accept and, even legally allow for
these small bribes, we are undermining our reputation.
It is interesting in respect of Transparency International that the patron is one Sir
Don McKinnon, whom we heard mentioned in an earlier debate today, a former MP of a
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3521
National Government and a Deputy Prime Minister, if my memory serves me.
Transparency International is lobbying very hard for us to include in this bill the
removal of that clause in the Crimes Act. It put out a media release just a day or two
ago, which I hope some members have seen and I would encourage those who have not
to have a wee look at it. I think I was the only MP who attended a workshop over at
Victoria University, hosted by Michael Macaulay. I can never recall the name of his
department. It is the Institute for Governance and Policy Studies. He calls himself the
“Professor of Corruption”. It was an excellent presentation from him, from
Transparency International, which put up, I think, an undeniable argument that
facilitation payments are bribes. We ought not in New Zealand to have provision in our
legislation that en ables New Zealand companies to be involved in bribing foreign
Government officials.
It is not the moment now to mention it, but I will anyway. In respect of the
Committee stage I have lodged Supplementary Order Paper 76, which seeks to remove
that provision from the Crimes Act. I would encourage Government members to have a
look at that, read what Michael Macaulay has had to say, read what Transparency
International is saying, what the Human Rights Commission is saying, and give some
serious thought to whet her now is the time to enhance our reputation as a country that
does not tolerate corruption. Kia ora.

items.speaker: MAHESH BINDRA
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise on behalf of New Zealand
First to speak to the Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill. But before I
do that, I would like to join the earlier speakers in paying homage to the late Ērima
Hēnare—and our sympathies to our Labour colleague Peeni Henare.
New Zealand First supported this bi ll to the Law and Order Committee and we will
continue to support this bill. This bill aims to strengthen the law to combat organised
crime and corruption. Proposals within this bill aim to improve New Zealand’s ability to
work alongside international efforts to disrupt and respond to organised crime. We have
an enviable reputation for being a corruption -free society. Well, that reputation may be
a little overrated because low corruption does not mean no corruption at all. We need to
keep it that way. We ar e one of the least corrupt countries in the world and I have seen
the whole spectrum, having grown up in a country that has the dubious distinction of
being one of the most corrupt countries in the world. So I have seen the whole spectrum
during my career and I am proud to say that I do now belong to a country that is one of
the least corrupt countries in the world.
New Zealand First supports the new offence criminalising the acceptance of a bribe
by a foreign public official. We are pleased that the new o ffence also identifies the
acceptance of a bribe in return for influencing an official. I know of countries where the
payment of a bribe is termed as —the nomenclature varies from country to country. I
look at this scenario in a certain country —which I woul d not like to name, and I have
just named—where, say, if you are an importer or an exporter and you expect a large
consignment of goods from another country, the customs officials are paid a certain
facilitation fee, which is called “speed money” over ther e, which actually expedites the
process of clearing those goods. That is perfectly acceptable in those cultures, but we do
not want to head that way.
New Zealand has one of the strongest reputations globally for being one of the least
corrupt countries, as I said. We demand honest and fair dealings in all aspects of our
lives. We expect our Governments to make laws that combat organised crime and
corruption. We expect our law enforcement officers to effectively enact those laws and
enforce those laws, and  advice from the New Zealand Police was welcomed by the
select committee. In the select committee process I contributed by way of a couple of
queries as to whether this bill will address the ambiguity of various nomenclatures, such
3522 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
as, in certain countries , if it is called “speed money”, will that be addressed by this bill
or are we going to just stick to our own ways of addressing these things and just leave
that and we will be there. I was assured by the officials that we will be addressing those
things, and we will also be addressing the issue of extradition of those suspects who are
involved in these activities in foreign lands.
The select committee recommended that a new clause 46B be added so that New
Zealand police could take identifying particulars from a person arrested on an
extradition warrant. This new clause recognises that police need to have the authority to
take these particulars, to ensure that they have arrested the right person. We expect our
legal system to respond quickly to punish those  who are involved in organised crime
and corrupt practices. The select committee was grateful to receive advice from the
Ministry of Justice, and I acknowledge the great work done by the other committee
members, and also the officials and a large number of  organisations and individuals
who gave some very meaningful submissions during the select committee process. We
have some very good legislation, and our Crimes Act will be enhanced by this bill. It
will allow New Zealand to ratify the United Nations Conve ntion Against Corruption, to
which we are signatories. It will also improve our compliance with a number of other
international conventions.
During this bill’s first reading, my colleague Denis O’Rourke welcomed the changes
made to the human trafficking o ffence in the Crimes Act. People  traffickers can be
prosecuted, regardless of whether the crime occurred overseas. The recommended
amendment to clause 15 ensures that money -laundering acts committed outside New
Zealand will be captured by this bill. Money -laundering is a growing criminal activity,
and it needs the strongest possible deterrent. The ability to detect and investigate
money-laundering is also improved through amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering
and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009.
The bill amends the Policing Act to expressly provide the police with the power to
share personal information with their international counterparts. New Zealand First took
special interest in this part of the bill, and challenged the select committee to  ensure that
any information sharing did not infringe on the right to New Zealanders’ privacy. So
there will not be this issue of the Privacy Act either. After consulting with the Privacy
Commissioner, the select committee recommended inserting a new secti on 95CA. This
section requires the Police Commissioner to consult with the Privacy Commissioner
when entering into or making changes to agency-to-agency agreements.
The bill will bring New Zealand into line with international best practice as set out
by t he United Nations conventions. It will update the definition of crime involving
dishonesty in the Crimes Act to ensure that those convicted of corrupt offences cannot
hold positions of trust in the community. New Zealand First supports the committee’s
recommended change to clause 6 for foreign bribery penalties. Including fines as
penalties for foreign bribery alongside the existing term of imprisonment is a positive
move and will strengthen our compliance with the OECD’s anti -bribery conventions.
Making fines available as well as imprisonment supports the OECD working group’s
findings that monetary sanctions are a fundamental deterrent for economic offences.
This bill will remove the dual -criminality requirement for foreign bribery offences in
the Crimes Ac t. New Zealand will be able to effectively prosecute foreign bribery,
regardless of whether it is an offence in the country where the bribery occurred.
In closing, as I said earlier, New Zealand First is heartened that the bill substantially
increases the penalties for bribery and corruption in the private sector. Some offences
will now be punishable by up to 20 years’ imprisonment or fines up to $500,000. This
bill has some very sound and useful clauses. New Zealand First will be supporting this
bill.
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3523

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I have found this debate
absolutely fascinating, as we have looked at this issue. And who would have thought, on
a Wednesday night at 9.25 p.m., t hat people might find Parliament interesting? But I
have found it very interesting, as I have heard different views around facilitation
payments and comments around bribery. I think that the previous speaker, Mahesh
Bindra, has brought out a very important point when he talked about—what did you call
them—“speed payments”. He said that in a number of countries around the world that is
absolutely normal and quite acceptable. And I think what we are discovering is the fact
that we live in a world of great cul tural difference. What might be perceived to be
wrong here is not so wrong in other places, for lots of reasons.
The very first time —to perhaps illustrate this in a benign way —that I went to the
United States of America, at the age of 17, to play rugby, I  went into a restaurant, or a
diner, actually, and ordered grits. A huge experience, the first time I ever had
McDonald’s in another restaurant. In those restaurants where people served you
personally, it was expected that you would show appreciation. So n ot only did you pay
for the product but you showed some appreciation.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I have never had
grits, so let us just say—

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Not you, Mr Assistant Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: That is right.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I have to say that when people talk about tips coming to
New Zealand, I was the first to think: “No, no, no, there is something wrong about that.”
And we are just discovering that there are cultural differences of understanding around
some of these measures. So when I am in New Plymouth in a restaurant and you get
great service, great attitude, you get so mebody who is doing their job very, very
professionally, very, very well, and you give them a tip, it feels good. They appreciate
it. It is not a facilitation payment, but it is something that was culturally difficult to
accept a decade or so ago. But toda y it is becoming increasingly part of how we show
appreciation.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: Yeah, that’s because you keep wages so low.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: No, it has got nothing to do with wages. It has got
something to do with appreciation of service. I think that is a generous way to look at it.
So I think that what we understand in this bill is that we have very strong principles
here in New Zealand when it comes to public service, or people giving a service for
what would be the bona fide and acceptable level and means of payment. But in other
countries it is slightly different. And so although we have in this bill something
described as facilitation, we also have measures in this bill regarding corruption here in
New Zealand. We are trying, in this bill, to live in a big world, where we participate.
And what we have got to understand is that trade, trade itself, is a great facilitating
process, where people become —can I use this term —civilised toward one another.
Because if I have something to sell, I have got to convince you that you want to buy it.
If I have got goods or products that come from this beautiful country, I have to convince
people in other countries that this is going to be of benefit. So we have to communicate.
We have to perceive that I have value, you have got value, and together we actually start
to dialogue and talk. So trade is a very good means by which we can facilitate
increasing harmony in interaction between nations.
Although I understand the purist po int of view around this debate that has been
defended by members on the other side, I also understand the pragmatic view that
actually has at the end of it a good result. What we need to understand is that the
democracy that we have come to appreciate, wit h all of its weights and balances, its
accountabilities, its checks and balances —all of these aspects do take generations,
3524 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
sometimes, to actually become part of the ethos and the cultural thinking of people. So
what are we to do? Because we find something in this bill offensive, do we withdraw
and say we are not going to participate in that nation? Well, I know companies here in
New Zealand that work in some of those nations of the world, and they understand what
we are talking about. If we were to say “No,  no. You ought not have a facilitation
payment because that is a bribe and that is corrupt.”, then what we would find is that we
would have lost a relationship that can have an ongoing beneficial process not only of
enhancing our economic strength and our trade in this country but also of the
relationships that we form having some influence upon thinking in other countries. In
that, I guess, brief analysis, I want to support what this bill says around facilitation
payments, and I want to say that this bill is a good bill.
I want to just touch on another area that the bill speaks on, and this is around the
amendment that people-trafficking offences apply to activities in New Zealand, not just
when victims are moved in or out of this country. If you would all ow me, let me just
read just a couple of sentences from the bill: “Every person is liable to the penalty stated
in subsection (2) who arranges, organises, or procures—(a) the entry of a person into, or
the exit of a person out of, New Zealand or any other State—(i) for the purpose of
exploiting or facilitating the exploitation of the person; or (ii) knowing that the entry or
exit of the person involves 1 or more acts of coercion against the person, 1 or more acts
of deception of the person, or both;”. It go es on to say in new section 98D(1)(b) that it
applies not only in and out of the country but also within New Zealand.
I just want at this point in time to put a shout -out to a group in New Plymouth that
tomorrow evening is organising a public meeting arou nd human trafficking and its
abhorrence of it. The shout -out goes to Tu Tama Wahine in New Plymouth and also to
Steph Lambert, a friend of mine, in her work as the executive director of Justice Acts
New Zealand. They invited me to be at that seminar and to  participate, but I am unable
to be there, so I want to wish them the very, very best for tomorrow evening.
Just if I can, I will talk very briefly in the next 2 minutes about what the United
Nations Office on Drugs and Crime says about trafficking. Based  on data gathered out
of 155 countries —and, of course, it is so difficult to get data around this subject,
because it is through such subterfuge that this happens —according to their most recent
report, the most common form of human trafficking is sexual exploitation; 79 percent of
it is that. The victims of sexual exploitation are predominantly women and girls.
Surprisingly, in 30 percent of the countries that provided information on the gender of
traffickers, women make up the largest proportion of traffic kers. In some parts of the
world, women trafficking women is the norm. So insidious is this that it affects even
those of the same gender. The second -most common form of human trafficking is
forced labour —18 percent, although this may be a misrepresentatio n, because forced
labour is less frequently detected and reported than trafficking for sexual exploitation.

items.speaker: This is the shocking figure
items.text: worldwide, almost 20 percent of all trafficking victims are
children. However, in some parts of Africa and the Mekong r egion, children are the
majority—up to 100 percent in parts of West Africa. It is very, very good and very
important that this bill places this issue at the heart and centre of it, and I commend this
bill to the House.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: I rise to take a short 5 -minute call for the Greens on the
Organised Crime and Anti -corruption Legislation Bill. We will be supporting this bill
despite the fact that we do not think that it really goes far enough. We agree that this bill
is overdue, and we fully support this bill being enacted, as it will allow New Zealand to
ratify and comply with international agreements and conventions —conventions like the
United Nations Convention Against Corruption, the United Sta tes and New Zealand
Agreement on Enhancing Cooperation in Preventing and Combating Crime, the OECD
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3525
Convention on Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business
Transactions, the United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organ ized Crime,
and also the United Nations anti -trafficking protocol. I agree with the previous speaker,
Jonathan Young, about this insidious crime, and it is well overdue that we are doing
something about it to ensure that we meet our international standards.
As the New Zealand Police Association outlined in its submission to the Law and
Order Committee—which I was not on, but I have read the submission —this bill will
improve New Zealand’s ability to address crime locally, combat crime internationally,
and tighten up the provisions in the Crimes Act around human trafficking as they apply
to the activity that takes place in New Zealand. There is no doubt that this is needed
and, quite frankly, it is well overdue.
But the area where we think the bill falls down—and others have spoken about it, but
I will add my 2 cents worth as well —is around what are called facilitation payments,
which are basically small bribes. The Ministry of Justice in its reports gives examples of
what these facilitation payments are: sma ll bribes for things like the granting of permits
or licences, the provision of utility services, or the loading or unloading of cargo.
Essentially, the bill as it is written at the moment would exempt these sorts of payments
from being recorded because th e ministry maintains that these payments would not
yield any undue advantage. That is exactly what it says: “undue advantage”.
But we believe that payments to grease the wheels should be resisted at every
opportunity. If we allow small -scale corruption to  continue and thrive, then where do
we draw the line? Where does it go from there? Does it escalate? Does it de -escalate?
Generally in these sorts of things it certainly escalates. Undoubtedly, it allows the
culture of corruption to continue, and given tha t countries like Australia and the United
Kingdom have taken a very strong stand to stamp out facilitation payments, and even
India and China are actively working to get rid of this type of small -scale corruption,
surely we should be doing more to ensure that our laws prohibit this type of bribery.
The bill is an opportunity to take a really strong stance. I believe that by not doing so
we undermine our reputation as a country that rates highly with Transparency
International for being an honest country, for having open and transparent government. I
note that this reputation is built not only on our laws like the Official Information Act
but also on our Public Service, which does not take bribes.
Transparency International released a statement yesterday th at said it was bitterly
disappointed about the opportunity that this bill has lost by maintaining the allowance
for small payments or small bribes to occur. It makes no bones about the fact that it
endangers our standing in the international community. I a gree with the president of
Transparency International New Zealand, who says there is no such thing as a harmless
bribe. I certainly hope that the Government will reconsider that clause in this bill when
it comes to the Committee of the whole House, and tha t it will support the
Supplementary Order Paper that will be brought to the Committee on this issue by my
colleague David Clendon. Thank you.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Assistant Speaker. I
am pleased to make a short contribution in this debate. Although I am not a member of
the Justice and Electoral Committee, which has considered this bill—

items.speaker: Ian McKelvie
items.text: Law and order.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: —oh, sorry, the Law and Order Committee —I have found
the debate very interesting. It is good to be actually supporting legislation to strengthen
the way we can combat organised crime and corruption. We support this bill. It has been
a long t ime in the making. It is quite ironic that it was introduced by the Hon Judith
Collins about 3 years ago, but it has finally made its way here to its second reading. It is
good that it brings New Zealand in line with various international conventions acros s a
3526 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
range of measures. I understand that it is amending, roughly, about a dozen pieces of
legislation, which will all be implemented as a result of the passage of this bill. So it is a
commendable piece of legislation. I just want to pick up on the—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Sorry, I have
reflected on what the member said in his recent comments, and I think they were
unparliamentary. I will ask him to withdraw his comments in relation to a nother
member.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: I withdraw. So returning to the bill —I raise a point of order,
Mr Speaker. Could I seek some clarification with you on that—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Well, the problem that I
have is that if I do clarify with the member what the inappropriate comments were, I
will in fact repeat and compound his offence. I think if the member reflects carefully on
what he said, he will understand what his offence was.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. Well, it certainly was not
taken as offensive by the members of the opposite backbenches there.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will
take a seat. When I make a ruling, it is not the role of the member to reflect on that
ruling. It is final and it is finished.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Thank you for that ruling. I would like to talk about
facilitation payments. I have experienced international trade in other countries. It is a
big, wide world out there. New Zealand is an exporting nation. We rely on selling our
goods and services to customers around the world, so it is very important that we break
into overseas markets. I have been working on behalf of the New Zealand Government
assisting New Zealand companies, and I have worked with New Ze aland companies
themselves to break into certain countries to expand our exports and grow our foreign
exchange earnings. It is difficult. It is a difficult business. I guess New Zealand
businesses have to appreciate the cultural differences that do apply. In certain countries
that I have been attempting to do business with on behalf of New Zealand companies
the culture is very much of facilitation payments, the greasing of the wheels —
baksheesh, as they call it. Whether it is just trying to park your car or whether it is
trying to get to an appointment or whatever level of decision making needs to be done,
in certain cultures it is endemic. I guess it is a business decision that, ultimately, New
Zealand companies have to make.
What I do find is that countrie s that are at the lower end of Transparency
International’s spectrum are the countries that we tend to avoid, because doing business
in those countries is too tough. But in terms of this legislation, there is an ambiguity. It
does not state when facilitati on payment ends and bribery begins, and by perpetuating
that ambiguity, it does not really help our own international reputation as being one of
the least corrupt countries in the world. I would have hoped that the Government could
take on board Mr Clendon ’s Supplementary Order Paper 76. It has some very sound
recommendations. If it is good enough for the United Kingdom and it is good enough
for Australia to outlaw facilitation payments, then surely it should be good enough for
Aotearoa New Zealand.
It is good that we can set the example, because New Zealanders know how to do
business. We are exporting all around the world and we will put our efforts into
countries and into overseas markets where we can form good relationships —but on a
sound business footin g. We are not perpetually trying to feed people who are trying to
extract demands, bribes, facilitation payments, and the like. That is one aspect that we
would hope could be improved in this bill, but otherwise there are some very positive
measures that we do support.
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3527

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: It gives me pleasure to take a call on the
Organised Crime and Anti -corruption Legislation Bill. The Government produced this
bill as a re sult of a report on strengthening New Zealand’s  resistance, I guess, to
organised crime. It was an all -Government department report and it encompassed the
whole of our legal fraternity, and you can tell by the number of bills that it touches on—
a dozen of them, I think—that it was quite a complicated bit of legislation for someone
like me to understand. I could understand the need to deal with some of the facts we are
dealing with, but it was pretty hard to understand how it all worked. Linking it together
was quite a task; it took a while. Primarily, the bill deals with the law enforcement
agencies that deal with instances of organised crime and corruption, not only in New
Zealand but internationally. As I said, I found it interesting but quite complicated,  and I
will endeavour to explain that during the contribution I am going to make to this bill.
We heard from some 20 submitters, almost all of them in support in one form or
another. Many of them related to the banks’ role in this bill. The banks’ role in  this bill,
although it seems minor, is actually quite important in that the banks give the law
enforcement agencies the ability to track financial transactions. There was a lot of
