discussion about how those financial transactions would be managed, who wou ld
manage them, and at what point they would be reported to the law enforcement
agencies. The law enforcement agencies needed this information as quickly as they
could get it and the banks needed time to be able compile it and put it together, and so
there were some changes made to the bill in respect of the amount of time the banks
had. I think the bill talked about 10 days and the bill now talks about 10 working days,
which satisfied the banks’ request in that respect.
A number of the submissions raised an issue that I have found to be very interesting,
and, of course, it has been talked about by almost every speaker tonight, though not all
with the same view. I really quite enjoyed the contribution that the last speaker, Rino
Tirikatene, made to this, because he touched on the fact that around the world things are
quite challenging. In fact, Jonathan Young touched on the fact a little earlier too that
trade is what makes the world go round, and in every part of the world trade is dealt
with in a different  manner. So the issue of facilitation payments —or bribes, as David
Clendon called them, and they could well be called bribes as well —is quite a complex
one, and I think that we have probably arrived at the right situation on this, and I will
explain why in a moment. But there is a very fine line between a bribe and a legitimate
payment being made to someone for, I guess, services rendered, or, as the bill words it,
a “routine government action”.
I remember when I was much younger I spent a lot of time on a  fairly large
continent, and I remember one night pulling up in quite a large passenger plane in the
middle of a runway. A fellow ran up the stairs of the plane when they dropped the stairs,
he paid the pilot off, and everyone walked off the plane and out through the back door.
We did not have to go through customs. It had nothing to do with me, I might add, but
that is the sort of thing that, I guess, this bill is attempting to manage. Obviously, in
some parts of the world, a lot of that sort of stuff happens.
Although these facilitation payments are legal in New Zealand and Australia —and I
think it was pointed out earlier that the law is worded slightly differently, certainly, in
Australia than it is in New Zealand, and, consequently, could have a differen t
interpretation made of it —they are illegal in the UK. Surprisingly, the Director of the
Serious Fraud Office and the Director of Public Prosecutions have issued a joint
statement in the UK saying that they are very unlikely to prosecute in the case of sm all
facilitation payments being made.
I do find this a really interesting topic, because I think that when you look all around
the world, trade varies so much and there are so many different ways of dealing with
3528 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015
this issue that I would be very reluctant f or us to support, I guess, the Supplementary
Order Paper that David Clendon is putting up, for that reason. I think it would preclude
us from some courses of action, particularly with our trade relationships, that we may
well want to make.
The types of crime talked about in this bill frankly make one’s hair stand on end. One
of them is human trafficking. The penalties for human trafficking in this bill are 20
years in jail or a $500,000 fine. I was kind of likening human trafficking —and I realise
it is a little different—to a topic that I am very interested in, and that is stock rustling. I
wonder whether there is a great deal of difference between stealing someone’s person
and someone’s sheep. I guess I would definitely struggle to get penalties of that or der
for stock rustling, but in fact it is a similar sort of thing when you think about it.
[Interruption] Well, hopefully—I do not know whether they do. I am not sure whether
more sheep do get stolen than people, actually. But bribery, of course, is a very  large
topic in the course of this bill.
The other topic that came to the fore, in its many forms, was money -laundering. I go
back to the days of the bookie in the local pub. They are outlawed now, of course. They
were then too, but they still operated. B ut I do go back to those days, and I am pretty
sure a lot of the money that went through those bookmakers’ hands was far from
legitimate. Humans have been, I guess, in the money -laundering business almost for
ever. Of course, the money -laundering business also impacts largely on a worldwide
scale on the gambling business. For many of us, gambling is —I was going to say it is a
way of life; I should not say that. Gambling is kind of, I guess, a hobby that is
undertaken by people, but at the same time gambling  is also undertaken by a large
sector of the criminal fraternity with a view to laundering the ill -gotten gains from some
form of crime or other.
The other issue that looms very large in the course of this bill is the matter of drug -
smuggling and the worldwide drug markets, how that money changes hands, and how it
is used once it has changed hands. This bill will go a long way to making sure that New
Zealand sits with the rest of the world in enabling the handling of these things in a very
strong and sensible manner.
It really strengthens the law enforcement agencies’ ability to track a whole lot of
stuff that we currently have the law in place to deal with, but not in the form that will be
put in place once this bill goes through Parliament and once the amendments are  made
to those 12 different Acts that need to be amended to get us to the point we need to be
at. The bill ensures we are able to cooperate with agencies worldwide. It encourages
better cooperation and understanding with our friends around the world. It wi ll enable
us as a country, as has been referred to a number of times tonight, to stand with the
United Nations and manage our way through a lot of these issues as we need to.
The bill was put through the Law and Order Committee under the leadership of
Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi. I think he did a pretty good job of getting this bill through
there. As I said, I thought it was a little complicated. It was also under the stewardship
of Minister Amy Adams. In the course of the discussion on this bill by the select
committee, there were some nine or 10 changes  in all, I think, made to the original bill
that was put to the committee. Those changes, I think, will ensure that this bill moves
smoothly through the next phase of the House. Obviously, there is a Supplementa ry
Order Paper coming from the Greens. I am also very pleased to note that the whole
House supports this bill pretty much in its entirety. I think that is a pretty good feat, as
well. So I have no problem supporting this bill going to the next step, and I thank you
for the opportunity to speak on it.

items.speaker: KELVIN DAVIS
items.text: Labour supports this bill almost in
its entirety, as the previous speaker, Ian McKelvie, said. We do have a bit of a hiccup or
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3529
a hang-up with facilitation payments, which is a topic that has been traversed by almost
every speaker here. I reflected on Jonathan Young’s contribution notwithstanding his
story about having to tip a service worker in the States f or a meal of grits. May I say
that that service worker was probably being paid about 70 cents an hour back when
Jonathan Young was 19 years of age on his trip to the States. You know, who would
begrudge offering a tip to somebody on that sort of income? I remember that in 2004 I
was in the States and I was talking to the girlfriend of the person I was staying with,
who was a service worker at that time, and she was paid $3 an hour. Working an 8 -hour
shift, she was earning $24 but she made over $100 in tips.  So we do not begrudge
people earning tips. But he tried to make the point that that was a custom in the States
and that facilitation payments are customs in other countries.
I take issue with that. I think there is a fine line being drawn between what is  called a
facilitation payment and a bribe. If we look at what Transparency International says
about facilitation payments, it says: “There is no dressing this up. Facilitation payments
are bribes and by failing to address them, we are enshrining bribery i n New Zealand
law.” It almost sounded like Jonathan Young —and I know he did not mean to make it
sound like this —was defending bribery and corruption. The payment of money to an
official to speed up a transaction —it does not matter how small or how large th at sum
of money is, a bribe is a bribe. It is a bit like saying that you are only just pregnant. You
are either pregnant or you are not. When I reflect on Ian McKelvie’s story about landing
somewhere in an aeroplane and someone running up the steps and giv ing the pilot a
payment, which enabled all those passengers to get off without having to go through
customs, it makes you wonder what sorts of crimes were hidden by that act. How many
drugs went out of the airport without being picked up? How much laundered money had
gone through the airport without having to go through customs? How many people were
trafficked on that aeroplane? We do not know. So I do not think it is right that we can
stand here and defend facilitation payments.
The Hon Phil Goff was very  eloquent and passionate in his summation of them.
Basically, bribery is bribery. It does not matter how big the sum of money is or how
small the sum of money is, facilitation payments are bribes. I think that we should
absolutely follow the lead of Transp arency International and not enshrine these in law.
In fact, Transparency International says it believes that ratification of the United
Nations Convention Against Corruption will not be possible unless the proposed bill
amends its stance on facilitation p ayments. We cannot stand here and say that we are
going to ratify that convention and, yet, still have the capacity for officials to be bribed.
I have to say that when this bill came in front of the Law and Order Committee, I
was quite concerned. I unders tood the arguments that, yes, it may facilitate speedy
process for New Zealand businesses to do work overseas, but in my heart of hearts I
knew that there was something wrong with this and that it cannot be justified by our
continuing to support it.
The other comment that Jonathan Young made was around trafficking. I was quite
astounded to hear that 70 percent of people -trafficking is for sexual exploitation. As
most people know, this is an issue that I am particularly concerned about.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3443 
 
WEDNESDAY, 20 MAY 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
ORAL QUESTIONS  
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus 
1. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement in his Budget speech last year, “we are in surplus”? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : Yes, because the Treasury forecasts then 
showed a small surplus for 2014-15. 
Andrew Little: Why has he persisted in making that promise or that undertaking to 
New Zealanders, including after the election, when he knew he could not keep it? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I do not believe that that statement is at all accurate. 
Andrew Little: Why does he or other Ministers in his Government persist in making 
excuses about milk prices and inflation when he knows that dairy prices began falling 
last February and inflation has been stagnant since 2013? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: The member may have such a lack of  grasp of economics that 
he does not realise the impact that inflation has on the Government’s books. We know 
that Grant Robertson has got his training wheels on, so he does not know what $15 
billion worth of less expenditure means. By the way, during the entire election 
campaign, Labour got up and said that the Government should take no credit for higher 
dairy prices, because that is just a function of something else. But, apparently, with 
the— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I have heard enough. 
Andrew Little : Now that he is set to be the first Prime Minister since Robert 
Muldoon to deliver seven straight deficits, why should the public believe him when the 
Government promises a surplus next year? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: What the New Zealand public have done , year after year after 
year, is judge this Government on its economic performance. They have see n the mess 
we inherited from Labour when it came to ACC, the massive build -up in expenditure, 
the failure to have a competitive tax  system, and the fact that it left the books in such a 
shocking state, and they have actually seen us get that down, get debt down, and get 
growth up. That is why business confidence is high. That is why New Zealanders in 
droves have voted for National. Ma ybe the member needs to look in the mirror and ask 
himself why his messages are not getting through. Here is an idea: he does not have any 
messages. He has not— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order!  
Tim Macindoe : What reports has the Prime Ministe r received on getting back to 
surplus based on the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update  forecasts before the 
election last year? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I have seen one report from last year’s election campaign on 
the 2014 -15 surplus: “Oh, lo ok, absolutely stand by the numbers, calculated and 
checked on the same basis as the Government’s own numbers and absolutely verified, 
all banked, all paid for. We are still running a surplus every year. It is absolutely 
fantastic and people can have every confidence in it.” That was David Cunliffe claiming 
that Labour was running a surplus, even from Opposition. 
3444 Oral Questions  20 May 2015 
 
Andrew Little: What other promises for Budget 2015 are now also under threat, and 
will the Budget show we are on track for the 150 ,000 extra jobs by 2016 and a $7,000 
average wage rise by 2017, as promised in his open letter after last year’s election? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : The member will have to wait —only one more sleep, 
actually—until the Budget tomorrow. I am sure he  will be able to do that. What he will 
see tomorrow in the Budget, though, are  good growth numbers . He will see surpluses 
out in the years in front. He will see debt levels that are the envy of the Western World. 
That is why I can be absolutely sure that when New Zealanders look at this Government 
and its economic leadership they do not have buyers’ remorse; they are very happy that 
they dispatched Labour to Opposition for 3 more long years. 
Tim Macindoe : How much can the fiscal numbers move around between Budget 
forecasts and the Government’s annual accounts being published the following year? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: According to that economic powerhouse Grant Robertson, not 
at all. But, actually, history shows that fiscal forecast s and out-turns move around quite 
substantially. For example, in Budget 2008 the then finance Minister was forecasting a 
$1.3 billion operating balance before gains and losses surplus in 2008 -09. As it actually 
turned out, he left the Government’s books in  deficit by $3.9 billion that year. I say just 
this one thing: why in this country do we have the Public Finance Act? I know —
because Labour rorted the books so much that they could no longer be trusted. That is 
why. 
Andrew Little: In light of that answer, and returning to reality, what happened to his 
promise to act on child poverty and make it the centrepiece of his third term? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: One more sleep. 
Andrew Little : Is not the truth of it that this  is a Government with a surplus of 
empty promises and a deficit of ideas, a Government that took credit for a short patch of 
economic golden days on the back on high dairy prices and the Canterbury rebuild but 
has no plan now that the storm clouds are gath ering? Is that not the truth of this 
Government? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: Here is the truth of this Government. Unlike the countries that 
we actually compare ourselves with, we have got on top of deficits despite the 
Christchurch earthquakes. We have got employment rates that are rising. Of the OECD 
countries, of which there a re 36, only four have higher levels of employment than us, 
and 31 have lower levels of employment. We have low inflation and we have strong job 
creation. We have low levels of public sector debt  and we have high levels of consumer 
confidence. The record ac tually speaks for itself. It happens to be a record I am very 
proud of. 
Child Poverty—Government Initiatives to Address 
2. METIRIA TUREI (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he stand  
by all his statements? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes. 
Metiria Turei: How can he be “proud of the Government’s record in tackling child 
poverty” when he said this week that it is probably numerically correct that the number 
of children in poverty has grown under his watch? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : As we know with this, there are many, many measures, but 
what I can be absolutely sure of is that  there are 42 ,000 fewer children, for instance, 
living in benefit-based households over the last 3 years. I can be sure that we have done 
a great deal for those children who live with hardship, including free GP visits and 
prescriptions, including the work we have done  with charitable organisations that , for 
instance, provide breakfast in schools, including the work we have done with social 
workers, including the work we have done with Children’s T eams, and including the 
20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3445 
 
work we have done on insulating homes. During the worst of all times, this Government 
actually maintained benefits and entitlements for New Zealanders. There were plenty of 
people who wanted to slash them; this Government supported them. 
Metiria Turei: How many, if any, of the 260,000 chi ldren currently in poverty will 
no longer be in poverty as a result of the Budget tomorrow? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY: I do not have an exact answer for that, and even if I did have, I 
would not give it to the member a day before the Budget. What I can say, though, is that 
the fastest way out of poverty is through work, and this Government is doing two things 
in that regard. One is it is underpinning, with its policies, strong economic growth and 
strong job creation. We know this because there are 4 2,000 fewer children living in 
benefit-based households than there were 3 years ago. The second thing that this 
Government is doing is invoking the investment approach when it comes  to people who 
are on benefits —making sure that they have got skills, makin g sure that they have got 
training, and making sure that they have access to the opportunity to look after 
themselves. Again, I am actually very proud of what this Government is doing to help 
people to help themselves. 
Metiria Turei: Why did the Prime Minister abandon the thousands of children who 
turn up to school hungry every day by voting against my bill to feed them lunch at 
school, and even stood in this House and denied that those children existed? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Well, I reject the last part of the member’s question. I think 
she overexaggerated those numbers, and I think we demonstrated that on the day. 
Metiria Turei : Why is the Prime Minister abandoning young New Zealanders in 
their 30s, for whom hom eownership has plummeted under his watch faster than it has 
for any other age group? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Again, I reject that proposition. If the member cares about 
young people in their 30s getting a home, why did the member not support the  
HomeStart package that we have? Why does the member not support Resource 
Management Act reform? Why does the member not actually support the work we are 
doing with special housing areas? I know: because the member likes to jump up and 
down and complain, b ut when it comes to actually doing anything, she has never done 
anything because she has never been in Government. 
Metiria Turei: Why is the Prime Minister abandoning young parents by refusing to 
fix Working for Families so that young parents who lose work hours or who fall on hard 
times do not also lose the $60-a-week in-work tax credit lifeline that they rely on? 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : As the member knows, that policy, which was introduced by 
Labour—and I think, in this instanc e, was correctly positioned that way —ensured that 
there was always a gap between welfare and work. And if there are not those incentives, 
all of the academic evidence shows you, actually, that there will be less incentive for 
people to move off welfare int o work. I think that if you have a welfare system in New 
Zealand, it is a sign of a decent society that looks after people. But it is also a system 
based on obligation, and, actually, we owe it to the millions of New Zealand taxpayers 
who work hard to pay their taxes that people who are on welfare feel the obligation that 
they should go out and work if they possibly can. 
Metiria Turei: Will the Prime Minister at least agree—[Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Would the member ask her supplementary question. 
Metiria Turei: Would the Prime Minister at least agree that an economy that is not 
working for everyone —that includes young New Zealanders under 40 who are 
struggling to buy a home, who are struggling to get dece nt paid work, who are trying to 
raise their children in increasing financial insecurity —is an economy that is simply not 
working? 
3446 Oral Questions  20 May 2015 
 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : Far from not working, the economic credentials and 
performance of this Government over the last 7 years, even in contrast to like -minded 
countries, demonstrate that this Government has been performing well. We live in the 
real world, and in the real world there has been a global financial crisis and many other 
issues. Actually, some of these iss ues, when it comes to either people on benefits or 
children living in benefit -based households, have been very longstanding, complex 
issues. They will not actually be resolved overnight, but the work that this Government 
is doing, breaking down the silos and the barriers that are there, is working pretty well. I 
think the member actually speaks with great ignorance when she rejects what the 
Government is doing there. 
Budget 2015—Future Investment Fund 
3. JAMI-LEE ROSS (National —Botany) to the Minister of Finance : How will 
the Government’s responsible fiscal management support better public services for New 
Zealanders in Budget 2015? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : The Government has managed the 
finances that are paid for by the taxpayer by being careful with new spending and 
focusing consistently on reprioritising —that is, shifting money from programmes that 
either do not  work or are low priority to new, more effective spending. For instance, 
over the previous six Budgets the total new discretionary spend of this Government has 
been around $3 billion. Over the last six Budgets of the previous Labour Government 
the total new spending was $20 billion. The Government has, over the last six Budgets, 
been able to shift around $15 billion of spending from ineffective or low -priority 
programmes to more effective programmes, and that has been at least as important as 
the new spending. 
Chris Hipkins : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I wanted to wait until the 
Minister had finished his answer before raising this, because he had already begun his 
answer. I was expecting that you may have had a comment on the primary question set 
down because of the assertion that it contains within it and your previous rulings on our 
questions that contain such assertions. If it is acceptable for Government members to 
ask about “responsible” fiscal management, can we ask about “irresponsible” fiscal 
management? 
Mr SPEAKER: I certainly examined the questions and did not pick up that at 11.30.  
It was accepted and tabled in the House. It was only when an interjection came from my 
left during the question that I really focused on the meaning of that word. I think it 
would have been a better question without that word there. I should have picked it up at 
11.30, but I did not. 
Jami-Lee Ross : How is the Government using capital reprioritisation to improve 
public services and avoid further overseas borrowing? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The main tool the Government is using is the Future 
Investment Fund. Th e sale of electricity assets raised $4.7 billion, which was allocated 
to the Future Investment Fund, and we are now able to use that money to invest in other 
public assets. So far the Government has invested around $700 million in health, nearly 
$400 milli on of the fund in education, and $1.9 billion in other public assets. That 
means we have not had to go to foreign lenders for more money. We have been able to 
use the savings of New Zealanders who bought the shares to invest in New Zealand 
assets. [Interruption] 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The level of barrage I am getting from two or three members 
on this side means they can take this as their final warning. If it continues at that 
volume, I will be asking those members to leave the Chamber. 
20 May 2015 Oral Questions  3447 
 
Jami-Lee Ross : H ow have dividends paid by mixed -ownership companies to the 
Government increased since the part sale of those companies? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : At the time there was some suggestion the Government 
would be giving up dividends if it sold down the shares, but I can inform the House that 
the Government, as a 51 percent owner, is now receiving more dividends than it did 
when it was, on average, a 100 percent owner of the companies. For instance, the 
highest annual dividend rec eived from Genesis Energy at any time in the previous 10 
years was $57 million. The average dividend was $32 million when we were the 100 
percent owner over those 10 years. This year we will receive $76 million in dividends. 
As a 51 percent owner, we will get more than twice the dividend we got on average 
from Genesis Energy. We can apply that to more high -priority Government social 
programmes. 
Jami-Lee Ross : How will Budget 2015 continue the Government’s ongoing 
programme to improve public services for New Zealanders while helping to support 
more jobs and higher wages through careful fiscal management? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: In many ways that will be talked about in detail in the House 
tomorrow, but it will be against the background of growth over the next 4 years forecast 
to deliver more jobs through to 2019, in addition to the 194,000 jobs that have been 
added to the economy since 2011. Wages are expected to continue increasing ahead of 
the cost of living. Budget 2015 will be a  responsible Budget from a responsible 
Government. 
Budget 2015—Youth Unemployment 
4. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Minister for Tertiary 
Education, Skills and Employment : What plans does the Government have in the 
Budget tomorrow to get the 146,000 officially unemployed New Zealanders, as 
measured by the Labour Market Statistics, into work? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and 
Employment): The Government will continue to operate the same sensible economic 
and fiscal policies that have delivered 194,000 jobs to New Zealanders in 4¼ years, and 
23,000 more jobs than the 171,000 jobs forecast by Treasury in Budget 2011, with more 
than one quarter to run. In fact, this Government and businesses around the country 
have delivered job growth in 16 out of the  last 17 quarters, and I am confident that the 
Budget tomorrow will project further job growth. I thank the member for his question. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : What are the Government’s plans in tomorrow’s Budget 
for Māori and Pacific yo uth, where unemployment under this National -led Government 
has increased by over 40 percent for Māori youth— 
Hon Dr Nick Smith: Rubbish! 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : —and almost 50 percent for Pacific youth —no, no, I am  
not dealing with your speciality: rubbish; I am talking facts. 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : I am not sure about the member’s figures, but I certainly 
would agree with him that Māori and Pasifika youth unemployment is  too high. I agree 
with him. We have got a number of measures under way alongside the Ministry of 
Māori Development to improve that situation, including, of course, the Māori and 
Pasifika Trades Training Initiative, which is a programme that is delivering great 
opportunities for young Māori and Pasifika in the trades around New Zealand. And 
there may or may not be more information about that in the Budget tomorrow. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : How is his Government going to be able to claim  to be 
working for New Zealanders when we have tens of thousands of youth who are 
3448 Oral Questions  20 May 2015 
 
currently unemployed, yet, his Government has approved over 47,200 international 
student visas with work rights in our current financial year? 
Hon STEVEN J OYCE: The member may not be excited about international 
education, and I am reasonably confident from all his past statements that he is not, but 
international education creates for this country around $2.85 billion worth of value a 
year and some 33,000 jo bs, and a relatively small number of international students 
actually participate in the employment market. But I thank the member for his question 
and say that international education is very important for New Zealand’s future. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I did not ask about 
international education, did I? 
Mr SPEAKER: Yes. [ Interruption] Order! The member will resume his seat. If he 
wants to go back and look, he included in his question the  47,200 people here on 
student visas. That is the part the Minister chose to address.

WAITANGI NATIONAL TRUST BOARD AMENDMENT BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon MAGGIE BARRY (Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage) : I move, That 
the Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill be now read a second time . Kua 
hinga te tōtara o Te Wao -Nui-a-Tāne. Ka tangi a Ngāti Hine, ka tangi te motu. Ko te 
poutokomanawa o Te Reo kua wahangū. A tree has fallen in the great forest of Tāne. 
Ngāti Hine mourns and the nation mourns with them. A mainstay of the Māori language 
has been silenced. I begin by acknowled ging the passing of Ērima Hēnare, the widely 
respected and beloved Ngāti Hine leader, who, among his many roles, was a member of 
the Waitangi National Trust board, and who made an excellent contribution to that 
board.  
This bill amends the Waitangi National Trust Board Act 1932. Its principal purpose 
is to make changes to the membership of the trust board and to provide fixed terms of 
appointment for board members. In doing so, it will provide a new framework for the 
ongoing relationship between the Government and the board. The responsibility of 
caring for the birthplace of our nation, the place where the Treaty of Waitangi was first 
signed, is a significant task. It is one that the Waitangi National Trust Board has 
discharged since the Waitangi estate was gifted to the nation in 1932 by Lord and Lady 
Bledisloe.  
The Waitangi National Trust Board’s aspirations extend beyond maintaining the 
Treaty House and its grounds, to making sure New Zealanders can learn about their 
history and understand the historical and contemporary role of the Treaty of Waitangi. 
The board is doing this partly through a major development programme to build a new 
museum and education centre at the Treaty grounds. Work on the new museum is 
progressing well, and when completed, hopefully by Waitangi Day next year, it will 
further enrich the visitor experience and enable the unique story of the development of 
our nation to be told in a more detailed and accessible way.  
I am sure that such developments  would have been very much approved of by Lord 
and Lady Bledisloe, whose gift of the Treaty grounds and its surrounding estate to New 
Zealanders has enabled the constitutional and heritage values embodied in the site to be 
shared with current and future ge nerations. In this spirit, it is essential that the 
organisation responsible for one of our most significant historical sites has a suitable 
governance structure to support its aims and aspirations for the future while also staying 
true to the original intent of the board when it was formed.  
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3485 
 
The purpose of the Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill is to create a 
clear separation between the Government and the board while also setting up a new 
framework for positive relations between the board and th e Crown. This bill is 
deliberately narrow in its focus. It specifically removes the Governor -General, the 
Prime Minister, and two Government Ministers from ex officio positions on the board. 
It addresses the real or perceived potential conflict that could arise under the current 
structure by virtue of such ex officio members being on the board while also having a 
constitutional role.  
Clause 6 inserts new section 4A, which establishes a statutory Crown representatives 
group, comprising the Prime Minister, t he Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage, and 
the Minister for Māori Development. This group will provide a clear link between the 
board and the Government and will encourage open and positive dialogue. The bill 
allows for the Governor -General to be an h onorary patron of the Waitangi National 
Trust, should he or she so choose. The bill also provides for two members of Parliament 
to be appointed to the board. New section 4B, in clause 6, requires one new full board 
member to be nominated by the Prime Minis ter and one to be nominated by the Leader 
of the Opposition. Creating these two new positions ensures ongoing Government and 
parliamentary input into the work of the board and a direct link to the elected 
representatives of New Zealand.  
The bill restricts the length of time a board member can serve. It creates 3 -year terms 
for most board members, who will then be eligible to serve for up to three terms —that 
is, 9 years in total. The two members of Parliament being added to the board will serve 
for the dura tion of the parliamentary term in which they are appointed, unless they 
become Ministers or leave Parliament first.  
The Māori Affairs Committee received three written submissions. The committee has 
recommended an amendment to the bill to increase the repr esentation of Māori families 
on the board so that each of the four families currently represented on the board would 
have its own member. At present there is only one representative for four Māori 
families. The committee recommended this amendment in respo nse to a submission 
from one of the families. The amendment has been included in the bill as clause 3A, 
which amends section 2 of the Act.  
In recent years the board has standardised appointment processes for new board 
members. It has taken steps to make these appointments transparent, through advertising 
and disseminating widely the call for nominations. I would expect that the appointment 
of additional Māori family representatives to be in accordance with this rigorous 
selection process.  
Although I under stand the committee’s reasons for recommending the amendment 
concerning representation of Māori families, it raises questions about whether the 
current basis of representation on the board should be reconsidered more broadly. I am 
therefore initiating a wi der review of the Waitangi National Trust, with the aim of 
ensuring the best possible governance and management of the Waitangi estate.  
The review will also respond to issues raised by the board in its submission on the 
bill. Although supporting the intent of the bill, the board asked for changes to its powers 
and to penalties for offences and by -law breaches under the Act. These matters are 
outside the narrow focus of the current bill but will be considered as part of the wider 
review. Generally speaking,  it is my intention that the review will look at the role, 
composition, and powers of the board; the appointment process and criteria for board 
members; how best to provide for iwi Māori involvement in the governance of the trust; 
offences and by-laws on the Waitangi estate; and the financial sustainability of the trust. 
By establishing a framework for continued positive relationships between the board and 
3486 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015 
 
the Government, I believe the bill will create the necessary conditions for a wider 
review of the trust to take place. 
I wish to thank the chair and members of the Māori Affairs Committee for 
consideration of submissions during the select committee process. I am pleased to note 
that there is broad, cross -party support for the bill, and I am confident that the bill will 
provide for a positive and cooperative relationship between the Government and the 
board. I look forward to progressing the bill through the House.

I am proud to stand as a member of this House, and as the chair of the Māori Affairs 
Committee, for the second reading of the Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment 
Bill. I tautoko the previous speakers, who have done a sterling job of giving a very good

Many consider the first Waitangi Day to be 6 February 1932, although Waitangi Day 
was not celebrated annually for another 15 years after that, and even then there were no 
Māori present. So 1932 is a special year in Waitangi history. It was on that day  that the 
then Governor-General Lord Bledisloe gifted the former home of James Busby, where 
the Treaty was signed, to the nation. The house and surrounding grounds were dedicated 
as a public reserve and placed under the guardianship of the Waitangi Nationa l Trust 
Board.  
We have come a long way since 1932. Waitangi Day is now widely recognised as 
our national day —the day that marks the birth of our nation. The historic Treaty 
grounds now play a central role in our annual celebrations. If Waitangi Day marks the 
birth of our nation, then the Treaty grounds are indeed its birthplace. As such, it is 
appropriate that we stand here today, in this House, having recently marked the 175 th 
year since the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi, to consider a bill that updat es and 
modernises the arrangements for guardianship of this great taoka, this national treasure. 
That was 79 years ago.  
The Waitangi National Trust Board was legally established by the passing of the 
Waitangi National Trust Board Act 1932. The Act appoint ed two types of members to 
the board. Under the original Act, the trust deed, there are seven members representing 
the following groups: the family of Archdeacon Henry Williams, the families of Hone 
Heke, Maihi Kāwiti, Tāmati Waka Nene, and Pōmare, Māori l iving on the North 
Auckland peninsula, Māori living in the rest of the North Island, Pākehā living in the 
Bay of Islands, Māori and Pākehā living in Te Wai Pounamu —the South Island —the 
family of Edward Gibbon Wakefield, and the eighth member is to be a pro minent 
person in the life of this country Aotearoa. In addition, there are four ex officio 
20 May 2015 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 3489 
 
members: the Prime Minister, the Minister of Conservation, the Minister for Māori 
Development, and the Governor-General if he or she chooses.  
This bill is the resul t of a review of the Waitangi National Trust Board Act 1932 
undertaken by the Ministry for Culture and Heritage between 2006 and 2008. That 
review concluded that there is a risk of an actual or perceived conflict of interest 
between the constitutional roles of members of the executive and the roles they serve on 
the trust board. So that is the first point, particularly, about part of the make -up of the 
board and the roles. It would not be good enough to just remove the Governor -General 
and Ministers as this  would sever an important link, a very important link, between the 
trust board and the Crown. Instead, the Prime Minister, the Minister for Māori 
Development, and the Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage will make up a Crown 
representative group. This g roup will ensure continued communication between the 
trust board and the Government. In addition, the Governor-General may choose to be an 
honorary patron of the Waitangi National Trust and this preserves the historic link 
between the Treaty grounds and th e Governor-General, stretching back to the original 
donation by Lord and Lady Bledisloe.  
To replace the ex officio members on the board, two members of Parliament will be 
appointed. One will be chosen by the Prime Minister and the other by the Leader of t he 
Opposition. Of course, members of Parliament can also be members of the board in 
representative roles, and I acknowledge Pita Paraone for his work as chair of the 
Waitangi National Trust Board.  
The bill, as it was sent to us on the Māori Affairs Commit tee, also introduced terms

which we on the Māori Affairs Committee have recommended. We rece ived a

The families of James Busby, Edward Gibbon Wakefield, and Archdeacon Henry

for engaging with the committee and for providing us with the details of what the 
3490 Waitangi National Trust Board Amendment Bill 20 May 2015

After the signing of the Tre aty in 1840, the Busby family continued to own the land

February 1934, commencing a tradition of what is now known, obviously, as Waitangi

from this histo rical site, and there is nothing better than to be at Waitangi at dawn for 
the service or to watch the changing of the guard and the raising of the flag on those

This amendment bill addresses the representation on the trust. At present t he board 
has two sets of representatives: one being ex officio members —the Prime Minister, the

Governor-General—and the second group being the representatives of the families o f

In the case of the second group, there is obviously a current disparity between the 
representatives of the Pākehā families, where there is one member for each family, an d 
the representative for the Māori families, being one member only. The Māori Affairs

representative. Although this will increase the number on the trust board, it is a lo gical

group is going to consist of the Prime Minister, the Minister for Arts, Culture and

appointed to the board, one from the Government and one from the Opposition.  
The removal of the Governor-General and the Ministers from the ex officio positions

roles as trustees. A clear separation between the Government and the board will, 
therefore, exist while at the same time ensuring that positive work continues to exist on 
that board.

ORGANISED CRIME AND ANTI-CORRUPTION LEGISLATION BILL 
Second Reading 
Hon AMY ADAMS (Minister of Justice) : I move, That the Organised Crime and 
Anti-corruption Legislation Bill be now read a second time . This bill reflects the 
Government’s ongoing commitment to combat organised crime and corruption both i n 
New Zealand and globally. Can I take this opportunity to thank the Law and Order 
Committee for its work on the bill. I understand the committee received 20 submissions 
and has recommended that the bill proceed with a number of amendments, mostly of a 
minor and technical nature.  
This bill addresses a serious issue faced by societies around the globe. Organised 
crime is a corrupting influence worldwide, undermining public safety, economic 
development, good governance, and national security. New Zealand has  robust legal 
frameworks to combat organised crime and corruption and high levels of international 
engagement in responding to these threats. However, we are not immune to organised 
criminal activities such as money -laundering, identity theft, people -trafficking, and a 
range of conduct that constitutes bribery and corruption. This bill tackles such conduct 
in a number of ways. It enhances New Zealand’s ability to collaborate with international 
efforts to disrupt organised crime and ensures that law enforcem ent agencies are able to 
quickly and effectively respond to new challenges. Measures in the bill will also 
increase New Zealand’s compliance with a number of international agreements.  
One of New Zealand’s core assets internationally is its reputation as o ne of the least 
corrupt countries in the world. However, we can never afford to be complacent. This 
bill will send a strong signal that New Zealand values having, and is committed to 
maintaining, corruption -free institutions. This is vital for maintaining New Zealand’s 
reputation as a reliable trading partner and enhancing our influence in international fora. 
The 2011 all-of-Government response to organised crime outlined a range of measures 
that this Government had introduced to target and disrupt organise d crime. However, 
we also recognised that more work could be done and identified a range of areas for 
improvement. This bill implements many of these reforms by making a number of key 
changes.  
I will begin by outlining two important amendments to the mone y-laundering 
offences under the Crimes Act. Firstly, the bill removes the requirement that the 
proceeds of money -laundering be generated from offending punishable by 5 years’ 
imprisonment or more. This requirement places the police in the position of havin g to 
establish that the proceeds of crime are generated solely from such offences. This 
20 May 2015 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 3509 
 
burden is both difficult to meet and inconsistent with the reality of these crimes, as the 
proceeds are often intermingled and arise from a range of criminal activities.  
The second change simply clarifies that the prosecution need not prove that a 
defendant had intent to conceal the proceeds of crime, although this may result from the 
money-laundering transaction. This is a return to early case law on the money -
laundering offence, which held that intent to conceal was not an element of the offence. 
More recent decisions, however, have required the prosecution to prove that element, 
creating unnecessary hurdles to successful prosecution. Removing this requirement will 
help deter those who exploit the current limitations and responds to the concerns raised 
by the Financial Action Task Force, which sets the international best practice for 
combating money-laundering.  
In addition, the bill introduces new reporting requirement s under the Anti -Money 
Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act for two high -risk classes of 
transactions that we know criminals use to launder money and finance terrorism. Under 
the new requirements, financial institutions will need to report international wire 
transactions of over $1,000 and all physical cash transactions of $10,000 or more to the 
financial intelligence unit within the police. This amendment will improve our ability to 
detect and investigate money -laundering and align New Zeal and with international best 
practice for combating money -laundering. The fact that the banks are already required 
to collect identity information from their customers means that the public should not 
notice any change as a result of these new requirements. 
The bill also addresses the issue of identity theft. Identity theft and the misuse of 
personal information is estimated to impact over 190,000 New Zealanders each year, 
and this bill deals with gaps in New Zealand’s identity crime framework by adding new 
offences of selling or distributing unlawfully obtained identity information, and of 
making or possessing goods intended to facilitate identity crimes, such as credit -card 
skimming devices. By addressing the gaps in our identity crime framework, we will 
ensure that a full range of identity crimes can be prosecuted.  
Other important amendments in the bill expressly provide police with the power to 
share personal information, including fingerprint information, with their international 
counterparts. This amendment will allow implementation of the Agreement on 
Enhancing Cooperation in Preventing and Combating Crime with the United States. The 
Law and Order Committee has recommended inserting a new requirement in this part of 
the bill for the Commissioner of  Police to consult with the Privacy Commissioner 
before entering into international information -sharing agreements. This was already a 
requirement in accordance with a Cabinet decision. However, including the consultation 
in the bill will ensure that the o versight role performed by the Privacy Commissioner is 
more transparent. In addition, the bill makes an amendment to allow information stored 
in the DNA Databank to be provided to assist criminal investigations and prosecutions 
overseas, subject to the Att orney-General’s authorisation. I have great confidence in 
New Zealand’s law enforcement agencies, which have a successful history of 
prosecutions against those who engage in organised criminal activities. The measures I 
have outlined will further enhance i nternational law enforcement cooperation and 
capability.  
A range of amendments in the bill will also strengthen New Zealand’s ability to 
combat bribery and corruption. These will enable the Government to ratify the United 
Nations Convention Against Corrup tion, which is the first global instrument to address 
corruption in both the public and private spheres. Although New Zealand already 
broadly complies with the convention, the bill contains a number of legislative 
amendments that are required before we can  formally ratify it. These changes include 
increasing the penalties for private sector bribery and corruption offences under the 
3510 Organised Crime and Anti-corruption Legislation Bill 20 May 2015 
 
Secret Commissions Act 1910 to bring them into line with public sector bribery and 
general fraud offences. 
The bill also create s new offences to address gaps in our anti -corruption framework. 
The new offences criminalise the acceptance of a bribe from a foreign public official 
and the acceptance of a bribe in return for using one’s influence over an official. Other 
amendments in t he bill will enhance compliance with the OECD Convention on 
Combating Bribery of Foreign Public Officials in International Business Transactions. 
The foreign bribery offence is amended to ensure that it applies to bribery in relation to 
the provision of international aid and clarifies the circumstances in which a company is 
liable for foreign bribery. The Law and Order Committee recommended a further 
amendment to make specified fines available as sanctions for foreign bribery, in 
addition to a term of impri sonment. The amended penalties reflect the serious nature of 
foreign bribery and send a very clear message that those who engage in corrupt 
behaviour will be meaningfully held to account.  
A final amendment to the foreign bribery offence addresses the exis ting exception 
for small payments made to foreign public officials for the sole purpose of expediting a 
service to which the payer is already entitled, commonly known as facilitation 
payments. It is important to note that this exception has been part of ou r law for many 
years and is important to ensure that New Zealanders acting in good faith are not 
unintentionally criminalised. However, the bill tightens this already narrow exception, 
such that it will not now apply to payments that provide an undue mater ial advantage to 
the payer or an undue disadvantage to anyone else. This maintains compliance with the 
UN convention, which requires parties to criminalise payments that provide the 
recipient with an undue advantage. This measure, combined with a new requi rement for 
companies to record such payments in their books, will ensure that the exception is not 
open to abuse. I note that this is consistent with the treatment of such facilitation 
payments in Australia, in the US, and in South Korea, and with operatio nal practice in 
the UK.  
Let me conclude by outlining three final sets of reforms in the bill. The bill extends 
the Crimes Act offence of people -trafficking to ensure it applies to trafficking within 
New Zealand and not just in or out of the country. The r evised section also expands the 
trafficking offence to include the movement of a person for exploitative purpose —for 
example, prostitution or slavery. These amendments enhance our compliance with the 
UN anti -trafficking protocol, bringing us into line with  best practice. The bill also 
amends the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act to allow foreign restraining orders to be 
registered without notice and enable the court to extend the registration of these orders 
more than once if necessary. A further amendment r ecommended by the select 
committee ensures that extensions are not limited to extradition cases. Finally, the Law 
and Order Committee recommended a minor amendment to the Extradition Act to 
ensure that the police are able to take identity information from those arrested under that 
Act in relation to offences committed overseas. 
Collectively, the amendments in the bill will ensure that New Zealand has a robust 
legislative framework that complies with best practice. The bill will ensure that those 
engaging in organised or corrupt criminal activities will be subject to the full force of 
the law by removing current limitations in domestic law and enhancing New Zealand’s 
ability to internationally cooperate. I commend the bill to the House.

I raised a number of questions, particularly when Transparency International was

I think that what Transparency International said made a lot of sense. It pointed out

Kingdom, you will remember, is one such country that says that facilitation payments

It is also true that other organisations that we are proudly part of have spoken out 
against facilitation payments. APEC —the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation —has

Zealand, working in conjunction with Transparency International, put together a

other countries in which we are conducting our business to stamp out corruption, why

that is a double standard. 
There was a survey done of New Zealand  businesses in 2009, a business survey 
conducted by Trace International. It found that more than three -quarters of the survey 
respondents believed that it was possible to do business successfully without making 
facilitation payments, if they planned carefu lly and they did proper management

So I do not accept that facilitation payments are OK. In fact, in the United Nations 
Convention Against Corruption, in article 16, there is nowhere where it says that a bribe

bribery of foreign public officials —as when you promise, or offer, or give to a foreign

advantage for the official themselves. That is a payment. That is surely an undue 
advantage. You are not paying customs officially to make the transaction; you are 
paying the officials to grease their palms, to get something that gives you an advantage.

MAHESH BINDRA (NZ First) : It is a pleasure to rise on behalf of New Zealand

do that, I would like to join the earlier speakers in paying homage to the late Ērima 
Hēnare—and our sympathies to our Labour colleague Peeni Henare.  
New Zealand First supported this bi ll to the Law and Order Committee and we will 
continue to support this bill. This bill aims to strengthen the law to combat organised

work alongside international efforts to disrupt and respond to organised crime. We have 
an enviable reputation for being a corruption -free society. Well, that reputation may be

keep it that way. We ar e one of the least corrupt countries in the world and I have seen 
the whole spectrum, having grown up in a country that has the dubious distinction of 
being one of the most corrupt countries in the world. So I have seen the whole spectrum 
during my career and I am proud to say that I do now belong to a country that is one of 
the least corrupt countries in the world.  
New Zealand First supports the new offence criminalising the acceptance of a bribe 
by a foreign public official. We are pleased that the new o ffence also identifies the 
acceptance of a bribe in return for influencing an official. I know of countries where the 
payment of a bribe is termed as —the nomenclature varies from country to country. I 
look at this scenario in a certain country —which I woul d not like to name, and I have 
just named—where, say, if you are an importer or an exporter and you expect a large 
consignment of goods from another country, the customs officials are paid a certain 
facilitation fee, which is called “speed money” over ther e, which actually expedites the 
process of clearing those goods. That is perfectly acceptable in those cultures, but we do 
not want to head that way.  
New Zealand has one of the strongest reputations globally for being one of the least 
corrupt countries, as I said. We demand honest and fair dealings in all aspects of our 
lives. We expect our Governments to make laws that combat organised crime and 
corruption. We expect our law enforcement officers to effectively enact those laws and 
enforce those laws, and  advice from the New Zealand Police was welcomed by the 
select committee. In the select committee process I contributed by way of a couple of 
queries as to whether this bill will address the ambiguity of various nomenclatures, such

as, in certain countries , if it is called “speed money”, will that be addressed by this bill 
or are we going to just stick to our own ways of addressing these things and just leave 
that and we will be there. I was assured by the officials that we will be addressing those 
things, and we will also be addressing the issue of extradition of those suspects who are 
involved in these activities in foreign lands.  
The select committee recommended that a new clause 46B be added so that New 
Zealand police could take identifying particulars from a person arrested on an 
extradition warrant. This new clause recognises that police need to have the authority to 
take these particulars, to ensure that they have arrested the right person. We expect our

and corrupt practices. The select committee was grateful to receive advice from the 
Ministry of Justice, and I acknowledge the great work done by the other committee 
members, and also the officials and a large number of  organisations and individuals 
who gave some very meaningful submissions during the select committee process. We 
have some very good legislation, and our Crimes Act will be enhanced by this bill. It 
will allow New Zealand to ratify the United Nations Conve ntion Against Corruption, to 
which we are signatories. It will also improve our compliance with a number of other 
international conventions.  
During this bill’s first reading, my colleague Denis O’Rourke welcomed the changes 
made to the human trafficking o ffence in the Crimes Act. People  traffickers can be 
prosecuted, regardless of whether the crime occurred overseas. The recommended 
amendment to clause 15 ensures that money -laundering acts committed outside New 
Zealand will be captured by this bill. Money -laundering is a growing criminal activity, 
and it needs the strongest possible deterrent. The ability to detect and investigate 
money-laundering is also improved through amendments to the Anti-Money Laundering 
and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009.  
The bill amends the Policing Act to expressly provide the police with the power to 
share personal information with their international counterparts. New Zealand First took 
special interest in this part of the bill, and challenged the select committee to  ensure that 
any information sharing did not infringe on the right to New Zealanders’ privacy. So

Commissioner, the select committee recommended inserting a new secti on 95CA. This 
section requires the Police Commissioner to consult with the Privacy Commissioner 
when entering into or making changes to agency-to-agency agreements.  
The bill will bring New Zealand into line with international best practice as set out

hold positions of trust in the community. New Zealand First supports the committee’s 
recommended change to clause 6 for foreign bribery penalties. Including fines as 
penalties for foreign bribery alongside the existing term of imprisonment is a positive 
move and will strengthen our compliance with the OECD’s anti -bribery conventions. 
Making fines available as well as imprisonment supports the OECD working group’s 
findings that monetary sanctions are a fundamental deterrent for economic offences. 
This bill will remove the dual -criminality requirement for foreign bribery offences in 
the Crimes Ac t. New Zealand will be able to effectively prosecute foreign bribery, 
regardless of whether it is an offence in the country where the bribery occurred.  
In closing, as I said earlier, New Zealand First is heartened that the bill substantially 
increases the penalties for bribery and corruption in the private sector. Some offences 
will now be punishable by up to 20 years’ imprisonment or fines up to $500,000. This 
bill has some very sound and useful clauses. New Zealand First will be supporting this 
bill.

of money is, a bribe is a bribe. It is a bit like saying that you are only just pregnant. You 
are either pregnant or you are not. When I reflect on Ian McKelvie’s story about landing 
somewhere in an aeroplane and someone running up the steps and giv ing the pilot a 
payment, which enabled all those passengers to get off without having to go through 
customs, it makes you wonder what sorts of crimes were hidden by that act. How many 
drugs went out of the airport without being picked up? How much laundered money had 
gone through the airport without having to go through customs? How many people were 
trafficked on that aeroplane? We do not know. So I do not think it is right that we can 
stand here and defend facilitation payments.  
The Hon Phil Goff was very  eloquent and passionate in his summation of them. 
Basically, bribery is bribery. It does not matter how big the sum of money is or how 
small the sum of money is, facilitation payments are bribes. I think that we should 
absolutely follow the lead of Transp arency International and not enshrine these in law. 
In fact, Transparency International says it believes that ratification of the United 
Nations Convention Against Corruption will not be possible unless the proposed bill 
amends its stance on facilitation p ayments. We cannot stand here and say that we are 
going to ratify that convention and, yet, still have the capacity for officials to be bribed.  
I have to say that when this bill came in front of the Law and Order Committee, I 
was quite concerned. I unders tood the arguments that, yes, it may facilitate speedy 
process for New Zealand businesses to do work overseas, but in my heart of hearts I 
knew that there was something wrong with this and that it cannot be justified by our 
continuing to support it.  
The other comment that Jonathan Young made was around trafficking. I was quite 
astounded to hear that 70 percent of people -trafficking is for sexual exploitation. As 
most people know, this is an issue that I am particularly concerned about. 
Debate interrupted.
